points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The book is titled Isʿaf al-Talib fi Jamiʿ al-Matalib (The Student's Aid in All Demands), begun on 7 Rajab in the year 1051 of the Prophetic migration.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author wrote at the repeated request of a patron, to gather into one place what is scattered across the books of the saints and their callers — the paired and authoritative books, the brief abridgements on Sharia matters, and expansive treatments of juristic paths and legal opinions — so that these paths become easier to travel.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The work is situated in the Tayyibi Ismaili dawa, dedicated to the caller Jafar ibn Sulayman ibn al-Hasan ibn Yusuf ibn Sulayman and his successor the caller Muhammad ibn al-Fahd, in service to the Imam al-Tayyib.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author disclaims originality: whatever is correct in the book derives from the guardian of his favor and his successor, while every slip or error is his own shortcoming.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: Quoting some noble books, the author reports the teaching that faith has eight levels, the first of which is charity toward parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is a relative, the neighbor nearby, the companion at one's side, the traveler, and those whom one's faith obligates one to care for — a list established in the Book of God.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The same source asserts that whoever undertakes the worship of God and the call of the People of the House without knowledge and without action cannot bear the name of faith, and has no bond with God nor covenant or honor with His guardian, because he has departed from it.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author announces that he will next distinguish faith (iman) from Islam, setting out what each encompasses and what lies beyond them.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: Reporting from the fourth of the Mustansiriyya Councils (the Councils of Exposition and of Wisdom), the author states that the Imams of religion are seven, recurring in the world as the days of the week recur until the rising of the Qa'im, while the twelve proofs (hujjas) are spread throughout the world — and that this constitutes knowledge of the sum of the limits of the testimony.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author interprets that saying to mean the limits of testimony only, and holds that fulfilling the rights owed to those limits consists of seven obligations of religion — guardianship, purity, prayer, almsgiving, fasting, pilgrimage and struggle — corresponding to the seven Imams.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: Corresponding to the twelve proofs are twelve incumbent practices: honoring parents, maintaining kinship ties, protecting the neighbor, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, truthfulness in one's home, good conduct with one's spouse, kindness to dependents, spreading the greeting of peace, feeding others, keeping the bond among the brethren, and visiting the sick.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author states as a qualification that these twelve practices are not obligatory upon women.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author cites 'Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts to the effect that the Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects and this community will divide into seventy-three, of which one is in the Garden and the rest in the Fire.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: The author cites Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman's Book of the Foster-Suckling, which reads 'the righteous of the believers' in Q 66:4 as designating 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Imam of every believing man and woman.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: On the same authority, Qur'anic uses of 'righteous' — 'their father was righteous' and 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' — are interpreted as referring to an Imam and to the Imams among God's servants.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: The Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, in a Friday sermon, likened himself in the physical world to the Pen in the spiritual world, setting four ranks beneath it, each preceded by a spiritual rank guiding it upward, so that the foundation faces the tablet and engraves upon it what it derives from the spiritual world.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: In an account from Uns al-Afidah al-Muniba, a messenger of the king of Rum brings money to Medina to test the Prophet's successor with three questions: what is not God's, what is not with God, and what God does not know.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: Abu Bakr and 'Umar each fail to answer and instead accuse the questioner of disbelief, which 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas criticises for not even admitting ignorance, before directing the group to 'Ali.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: 'Ali answers that what is not God's is a partner, what is not with God is injustice, and what God does not know is that the Messiah is God's son — citing 'Do you inform God of what He does not know?' — since the nonexistent has no object of divine knowledge; the questioner then professes Islam and 'Ali's walaya, and 'Ali has al-Hasan and al-Husayn distribute the money to the Muslims.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: In a report from Abu al-Jarud via al-Harith al-Awar, a Syrian sent secretly by Mu'awiya brings eleven questions originally posed by Ibn al-Asfar (the Byzantine ruler), who promised to follow and pay tribute to whoever could answer them.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: 'Ali first detects the stranger's foreignness, grants him safety on the principle that 'when war lays down its burdens there is no harm,' and denounces Mu'awiya and the community that severed his kinship, denied his right and diminished his station.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: 'Ali defers the questioning to his sons, presenting al-Hasan and al-Husayn as the sons of the Messenger of God and Muhammad (ibn al-Hanafiyya) as his own son, and the Syrian chooses al-Hasan.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: Al-Hasan answers all eleven questions — truth and falsehood are four fingers apart (the eye sees truth, the ear hears much falsehood); heaven and earth are separated by the oppressed one's prayer and the reach of sight; east and west by the sun's day-course; the galaxy is the lamps of heaven from which rain descends; the rainbow is God's bow and safeguard from drowning; the moon's darkening is God's erasure of the night's sign per Q 17:12; the first thing to appear on earth was the valley of Dab and the first to stir the palm tree; the polytheists' souls flee to a spring called Salma; the hermaphrodite is identified by emission, menstruation or breasts, else by how the urine strikes a wall; and the ten ascending strengths run stone, iron, fire, water, cloud, wind, angel, Angel of Death, death, and the command of God.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: The Syrian testifies that al-Hasan is the son of the Messenger of God and that 'Ali is Muhammad's guardian with more right to the affair than Mu'awiya; and Ibn al-Asfar, on receiving the answers, tells Mu'awiya they come only from the mine of prophecy and the seat of the message, not from him, and refuses him even a dirham.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: In a further report, 'Ali resolves four of 'Umar's unanswered puzzles: dreams seen while the soul is loosened from the body (per Q 39:42) are true visions of the kingdom while those seen as it returns are Satan's delusion; instinctive love or hatred stems from souls meeting and scenting one another in the air two thousand years before the bodies; and forgetting and recalling are caused by a film over the heart like the film of the moon — after which 'Umar affirms his truthfulness and prays not to outlive him.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The author, citing the twenty-third of the Mustansiriya councils, states that the revelation of peace divides into seven sections from above (from God and His angels) and twelve sections from below (those coming from human beings).

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The seven higher instances are enumerated in descending order of exaltedness: God's 'Peace be upon you'; 'O Noah, descend in peace from Us'; 'Their greeting on the day they meet Him is peace'; 'they will be met therein with greeting and peace'; the angels' entry saying 'peace be upon you'; the command that believers pray for the Prophet and submit; and 'Peace be upon the family of Ya Sin'.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The author interprets 'Ya Sin' as our Prophet Muhammad and 'the family of Ya Sin' as the family of Muhammad, the family of Ali, so that the seventh Qur'anic peace is addressed to the Imams of the Prophet's house.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: Citing the twenty-fourth assembly, the author holds that the offering of peace is an obligatory Sunnah of Islam expressing affection and submission, and that al-Salam is one of the names of God, possessed of majesty and honor.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: Of the twelve human greetings, the first four are named as: the greeting of the people of the right hand to the Prophet and his noble family ('Peace be upon you for your patience'); the greeting on entering houses/the mosque; the peace concluding the ritual prayer; and the believer's 'peace' answer when the ignorant address him.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The fifth through ninth divisions set an order of precedence in initiating the greeting: the camel rider greets the horse rider, the horse rider the donkey rider, the donkey rider the walker, the walker the one standing, and the one standing initiates and then returns it.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The author distinguishes three kinds of reply to a greeting: the virtuous reply (better than what was offered), the complete reply (in kind), grounded in 'return it with something better, or return it as it is', and the just reply.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The just reply is reserved for dhimmis, who do not initiate the greeting; if one does, the answer is 'And upon you', because some were reported to say 'al-sam alaykum' ('death be upon you') instead of 'al-salam alaykum', so that whoever said good receives its like and whoever said evil receives its like.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The author cites al-Muizz li-Din Allah's Sunday prayer naming the five lower borders — the spokesman, the foundation, the culmination, the successor, and the wing — and his Saturday prayer over the seven days and twelve months.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: Prayers of the saints of the religion are reported invoking blessings on the seven proclaimers, seven culminations, seven caliphs and twelve successors, together with their gates, proofs, and preachers, and on the Imams of Muhammad's station and the proofs of their ages.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: From the Four Hundred Counsels of Amir al-Muminin the author reports the command to return a greeting better or in kind, to shake hands with an enemy even if he dislikes it on the authority of 'Repel with that which is better', and to answer 'May God greet you with peace' with 'You are the peace of God, and the finest of abodes and stations'.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: Citing the questions of Shaykh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi answered by Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris, the author records the ruling that peace to sheikhs and teachers should be proclaimed aloud rather than by the Indian custom of bowing, that is better.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The same source rules that audibility in returning a greeting and in blessing a sneezer is a courtesy and not an obligation, with no fault in omitting it — except that returning a greeting in general remains required, whether aloud or silently.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Jafar bin Mansour al-Yemen, in the book of the Esoteric Nursing, interprets the Quranic verse 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' as referring to the Imams among God's servants.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: On the same authority, 'those who were made weak in the land' whom God will make Imams and heirs means the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib, weakened in the person of Ali himself, who is the proof of Muhammad and whose likeness is the earth.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Al-Muizz li Din Allah, in his Sunday supplication, sets out a descending order of ranks: beneath the Foundation (al-Asas) the Terminus (al-Mutimm) facing Israfil, beneath the Terminus the After (al-Lahiq) facing Michael, and beneath the After the Wing (al-Janah) facing Gabriel.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Al-Muizz holds that these three (the Grandfather/al-Jadd, the Opener/al-Fath, and the Imagination/al-Khayal — i.e. Israfil, Michael, Gabriel) transmit to the respondents from the Speaker and the Foundation in the bodily world, just as three transmit from the two roots, the Pen and the Tablet, in the spiritual world.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: In his Friday supplication al-Muizz enumerates seven hudud — the Speaker, the Foundation, the Terminus, the After, the Wing, the Authorized (al-Madhun) and the Respondent (al-Mustajib) — together with twelve proofs ranked across twelve regions, which the author correlates with the Quranic 'over it are nineteen'.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's supplication of victory and awe invokes numbered ranks — the six transmitted, the seven beheld, the nine signs, the ten words, the twenty-one, the eight who encircle the Throne, the eleven who prostrate and the twelve counted ones who bow.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: In his Four Hundred Manners Ali names seven Imams, seven successors, seven witnesses and seven substitutes, and declares that whoever holds fast to them joins the truth while whoever holds to another way is undone.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Muhammad bin Tahir, in a supplication, seeks nearness to God through the Imams' gates, proofs, preachers, authorized ones, the respondents of their cycles, and all who incline toward, shelter in, follow or are guided by them.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Ali prohibits both exaggeration and falling short concerning the Imams: believers must say the Imams are servants under a Lord, though they may say whatever they wish of their excellence — and he adds that the exaggerator will return to them and they themselves will raise up the one who falls short.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Ali's commandment to those who love the Imams requires doing their work with God-fearing restraint, not sitting with those who revile them, and not praising them openly before the enemy — so that love of them be plain and hatred of them concealed — together with truthfulness, patience, and not burdening the Imams with intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Further maxims from the Four Hundred Manners: beware disputation, for it bequeaths doubt; reckon speech as part of deeds; hasten to good works and let most speech be remembrance of God; sins withhold provision; the best deed of the believer is awaiting the relief; and blessed is he admonished by another's case.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: The nineteenth of the Mustansiriya councils teaches that the kinship God commands to be joined contains a seven and a twelve, the seven being the Imams of the religion indicated by 'I ask you no reward except affection toward my kin', recurring like the days of Friday.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred manners, forbids despising weak believers (saying God belittles and detests whoever despises a believer, and will not bring the two together on the Day of Resurrection unless he repents), forbids making a brother ask when his need is already known, and commands mutual visiting, tenderness, and giving, warning against being like the hypocrite who describes what he does not do.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Ali teaches that the Muslim is the mirror of his Muslim brother: on seeing a brother's slip one must not band together against him but guide, counsel, and treat him gently, and must avoid discord, which leads a person away from the path.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Ali forbids backbiting, citing the Qur'anic rebuke about eating the flesh of one's dead brother, and commands that believers meeting one another shake hands and show a bright face, so that by parting their burdens have lifted.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: In a reported question-and-answer, Shaykh Shimon bin Muhammad al-Ghuri al-Hindi asked whether the Indian custom of asking neighbors for water, salt, or food (when one could afford to buy but lacks them at the moment) is permitted, and Sayyidina Hassan bin Idris (Badr al-Din) answered that there is no harm in it, since it belongs to the purity of affection and the excellence of brotherhood.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The Mustansiriya councils (seventeenth) place righteousness toward parents as the first of the twelve practices corresponding to the letters of the testimony, after the seven obligatory rights corresponding to its seven clauses.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The author notes that in both Qur'anic verses enjoining goodness toward parents, God commands goodness to both yet credits the child's account with the mother's deed alone (carrying him in hardship, in weakness upon weakness), so the one God distinguishes by mention must be distinguished with honor and righteousness.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Righteousness toward parents (eighteenth council) has seven obligatory parts and twelve manners, and extends to four levels: the bodily parents who caused his physical form, the two parents in religion who cause his form in knowledge (the Imam of the age and his proof), the two fathers of the community (the Prophet and the legatee, per the report 'I and you, O Ali, are the two fathers of this community,' and the Imams from their progeny), and finally righteousness toward one's own soul.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Righteousness toward one's own soul, the seal of this righteousness, consists in making the truth plain to the soul and establishing it there, magnifying it so as to awaken longing, placing fear in it, dealing gently with it, delivering it from what would destroy it, and rescuing it from what has bound it.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The twelve manners toward parents include honoring their dwelling, rising for them, answering their call, lowering the voice, not rebuking them, lowering the wing of humility, not walking ahead of them in light or darkness, never opposing their command or saying a word of complaint, desiring life for them in old age as they desired it for him in childhood, and providing for their needs as they provided for his.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The twenty-fourth council names three obligatory rights God will not accept unless discharged in full: the right of God (to leave what He forbade and enter what He commanded), the right of parents (thankfulness for what has passed and obedience in what remains), and the right of the child (to be raised with tenderness, nourished, and taught the Book and wisdom); Ali adds that whoever goes against his parents has been undutiful to them.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The nineteenth council divides a person's relatives into twelve categories (children; full brothers al-ashqa'; half-brothers by another mother banu al-'allat; half-brothers by the mother al-akhyaf; paternal grandfathers and grandmothers; maternal grandfathers and grandmothers; paternal uncles and aunts; maternal uncles and aunts), with anyone related through one of these taking that one's ruling, and requires keeping the tie, giving, drawing near, and loving even when the relatives cut off, withhold, push away, and abandon — and Ali adds that no oath binds in the severing of kinship.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The twentieth council divides safeguarding the neighbor (per the verse on the neighbor who is kin, the neighbor who is a stranger, and the companion at your side) into seven ranks — the believing kin-neighbor with three rights (neighborliness, kinship, faith); the kin-neighbor without faith with two; the believing stranger-neighbor with neighborliness and faith; the companion at your side who differs in religion with the right of neighborliness; the companion aboard the ship with the right of nearness; the sharer of one's litter; and the one who sits with you to receive wisdom, whose sanctity is the most binding and whose claim is most obligatory.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Twelve manners of neighborliness are enumerated — not peering into the neighbor's house, not listening in on his speech, not disclosing what one learns of him, not letting him hear or see what he would hate, not withholding a household implement when asked, not acting haughtily when of higher station, not envying him when he is above, helping when he seeks help, covering his 'awrah if exposed, causing him no injury, and bearing his injury with patience — these being the deeds of a people whose hearts God has tested for piety.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred maxims are cited for rules on study: no daylong silence except in remembrance of God, no reverting to desert life after the migration, and no recitation of the Quran while ritually impure until one purifies oneself.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Ali is cited warning believers not to let the Murjiah prevail over them with their opinion, marking certain schools as sources whose word must be refused.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: In a question from Shaykh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi answered by Sayyidina Hasan ibn Idris ibn al-Hasan ibn Abdullah al-Anf, it is asked — citing Hamid al-Din's al-Hadi wal-Mustahdi, al-Numan's al-Daaim, and Idris ibn al-Hasan's Zahr al-Maani — whether al-Sadiq's concealed license to al-Shafii later lapsed as with al-Mughirah and Abu al-Khattab, or whether the ignorant merely invented his school as factions falsely claimed the Imamate for Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and Abdullah ibn Muawiyah.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: The answer given is that al-Sadiq had granted al-Shafii license solely because of his acknowledgment of the excellence of the Ahl al-Bayt, and for no other reason.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Asked how the Prophet's saying that whoever looks into his brother's book without permission is as one looking into the Fire squares with members of a school freely consulting each other's books, the answer distinguishes the book of inner truth (haqiqa), which may be opened only by permission of the one who granted access, from all other books, where the rule is mere good manners and not binding.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: A borrower who finds a Quran or other book damaged and disordered may correct and set it right without the owner's permission — there is no harm in doing so, but it is not obligatory upon him.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Books of the dawah belonging to a deceased man may not be used to settle his debts, because they belong to the dawah and are not inherited.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Those granted license (al-mafsuhin) may read the benefits of religion to women in a mixed gathering only if a screen stands between them so she hears without being seen, and no man may be alone with a woman unless another woman is with her or another man is with him.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: The obligatory knowledge no believer may lack is enumerated as: knowledge of God's oneness and His transcendence above likeness (tashbih), above the stripping of attributes (tatil), and above nonexistence; acknowledgment of all messengers and their delivery of the message; acknowledgment of Muhammad as Seal of the Prophets and all he brought; acknowledgment of the Imams of his progeny whom God commanded be taken as guardians and to whom questions must be referred; and recognition of the Imam of the age, belief in his Imamate and walaya, submission to his command, and taking knowledge from him.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: This obligation rests on the doctrine that God has never left the earth without a proof (hujja) against His servants and an Imam calling them to obedience, supported by 'Obey God, obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you,' 'On the day We shall call every people by their Imam,' 'You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide,' and 'Ask the people of remembrance if you do not know'; and a believer's degree is raised in proportion to what he knows after acknowledgment.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Analogy in religion is prohibited outright: Ali is cited that the religion cannot be measured by analogy, that a people will come who do so and they are its enemies, and that the first to reason by analogy was Iblis.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan in Mafatih al-Nimah cites al-Sadiq distinguishing referring an obscure teaching back TO the Imams — so they may establish its proof and disclose its interpretation (tawil) — from throwing it back AT them by calling it false and turning away, the latter being forbidden.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: The duty of concealment and precaution is affirmed by Ali's maxim that whoever divulges the secret of the Imams, God will give him the cold of iron to taste.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: A Question-and-Answer book arranged on the order of the doors of Daaim al-Islam, containing questions from teachers of the Indian lands and answers from the summoners (duat) of the Yemeni lands, is cited as an authority on purity.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Asked whether the prohibition on urinating beneath fruit-bearing trees means trees actually bearing fruit or trees whose property it is to bear fruit, the Yemeni respondents answer that it covers both.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Though the dawah books forbid greeting or speaking to one in a state of hadath, the answer given is that once he has risen from that place (having cleansed himself with a stone or otherwise) he may be greeted, must return the greeting, and may speak.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Reusing a stone or clod of earth used for cleansing after urination is permitted once it has dried, provided no impurity and no moisture are evident upon it.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf lists the nullifiers of ablution as sleep, whatever issues from the front or rear passage (including a stone or wind), an enema, fainting, insanity, and the disappearance of the glans into the front passage of a living or dead person.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Tawil al-Daaim reports that one who interrupts his ablution may build upon what he has already done, so long as the water has not dried upon the limbs already washed; and Mukhtasar al-Musannaf holds that one whose hands are amputated above the elbows is relieved of the obligation to wash them.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The Trusted of the Imam, the Banner of Islam, in the fifth council of Majalis al-Bayan and Majalis al-Hikma (the Councils of al-Mustansiriyya), teaches that each of the seven obligations of Islam itself contains seven obligations and twelve practices, mirroring the honored number nineteen formed from the testimony's seven and twelve letters.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Walaya is the first and most excellent of the obligations, and in every allusion made by these numbers the ranking of the friends of God is the utmost aim and intention.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Purity follows walaya in rank, and its lesser purity (ablution) has seven obligations: pure water, intention, washing the face, washing the hands, wiping the head, wiping the feet, and order — beginning with what God began by mentioning.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The twelve practices (sunan) of ablution are istinja, washing the hands before entering the vessel, pronouncing God's name on sitting down, rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose, moving the ring, combing water through the beard, wetting the eyes, giving the right precedence over the left, wiping the inner and outer ears, the second and third washings of the face (the first being the obligation), and the siwak.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The greater purity — washing of the whole body — likewise has seven obligations: washing from janabah, from menstruation, of the unbeliever entering Islam, of one recovering from unconsciousness, from the blood of nifas, after immersion in impurity, and of the dead, which is an obligation upon the living until one of them performs it.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The twelve practices of the greater purity are the washings of Friday, of Eid al-Fitr, of Eid al-Adha, for ihram, for entering the Haram, the Kabah, and Madinah, on the day of Arafah, on the nights of the nineteenth, twenty-first and twenty-third of Ramadan, and after washing the dead.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred maxims of conduct, commands cleansing with water from foul odor, prescribes invocations on entering the privy and on looking at what has passed, and states that when sleep mingles with the heart ablution becomes obligatory.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The book of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of Daaim al-Islam rules that one who prayed while a known impurity was upon him — having forgotten the istinja — must repeat the prayer, since prayer is not permitted while a man carries an impurity of which he knows until he washes it away.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The same source distinguishes obligation from excellence: the Imams' concealment of themselves in water was mentioned for the excellence of good manners, so a man who uncovers himself where no one sees him commits no harm and prays validly with that purity, though concealment is better.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah lists twelve manners of the wudhu governing the privy — entering with sandals, advancing the left foot, covering the head, not facing or turning the back to the qiblah, concealing oneself, leaning on the left leg, not sitting long, not cleansing with human excrement or worn bone or animal droppings but with three fresh stones, cleansing with the left hand, not pouring water on excrement, not speaking, and advancing the right foot on leaving.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The section holds, on the authority of the Prophet, that prayer is not valid or accepted without ablution and purification, and reports his forbidding urination in burrows because they are the lairs of serpents and snakes.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Manners is cited for rinsing the mouth and drawing water into the nose as Sunnah purification, istinja with cold water cutting off piles, ablution after purification earning ten good deeds, the formula 'In the name of God — make me among those who repent and purify themselves' said before touching water, concealing oneself because Satan covets the uncovered man, not baring the thigh before a company, and washing children's hands of food-grease lest Satan smell it and harm the two recording angels.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: A key distinction is drawn between acts that are Sunnah and acts that are obligatory for another reason: rinsing the mouth, drawing in water and istinja are Sunnah practices not to be deliberately abandoned, and omitting them does not spoil the prayer — yet the istinja remains obligatory insofar as the removal of impurity is itself obligatory.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Rulings of accommodation are given for the injured and incapacitated: one with a wound or boil that water cannot touch wipes over the bandages, and performs tayammum if removal would harm him through cold or severe injury or if he is sick; in the greater purification he pours water in a stream, and performs tayammum if he fears for himself, whether traveling or at home; and a man whose hands are cut off has the wudhu performed for him by his bondmaid or wife, failing which he performs tayammum and prays.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: On water, the answers hold that water above the Shariah-stated measure which overpowers impurity remains valid for purification, whereas water in a vessel in which an impurity has become apparent becomes impure and is not made valid by pouring more water in a stream unless it rises above the measure after the vessel is purified; a pool eight cubits in length and breadth, even a span deep, is valid; rainwater running with filth into a great pool is valid so long as color, taste and smell are unchanged; and used water and used dust may be used for purification once and many times.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The saying 'Whoever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him' is interpreted esoterically: water purifies and is not itself purified, and likewise the knowledge of the Imam — whomever it does not purify, nothing else will purify him.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Majalis al-Bayan enumerates the seven obligations of wudhu (pure water, intention, washing face, washing hands, wiping head, wiping feet, and the order in which God mentioned them), its twelve Sunnah acts, the seven obligatory forms of ghusl (including washing the dead as a collective obligation on the living), the twelve Sunnah forms of ghusl, and the twelve places where prayer is disliked.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl in al-Risalah al-Maknunah divides purity and filth into two kinds: outward purity is achieved by outward water, cleansing the outward filth of urine and excrement, while inward purity is achieved by inward water — which is knowledge — cleansing the inward filth of doubt and ignorance.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The same author reads the seven acts of wudhu as seven bounds — three Sunnah (rinsing the mouth, drawing in water, istinja), two washings and two wipings, one of each bounded and one unbounded — and interprets the mouth as the sole conveyor of nourishment to the senses, the nostrils as the breath by which the body lives, and the face, with its seven openings, as bearing the meaning of the Speaker, since as a person is known by his face so no one is known except through his prophet and there is no deliverance except by turning toward him.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The section closes with Ali's ruling that there is no dissimulation (taqiyyah) permitted in the drinking of intoxicants or in wiping over the socks, consistent with Tawil al-Shariah's report that the Prophet forbade wiping over the socks and forbade abandoning the audible saying of the basmalah.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: The answers given hold that one who fears harm from water — whether resident or traveler, weak or sick — performs tayammum and prays, and is NOT required to repeat the prayer later, contrary to the ruling in certain Shariah books that he must wash and repeat it.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: The esoteric interpretation given is that the washing from janabah is a likeness of the removal of doubt, since marital relations are a likeness of imparting and receiving, and doubt arises precisely at the moment of imparting and receiving.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Doubt itself triggers obligation: one who revives from unconsciousness not knowing his condition, and one who wakes finding traces of semen without recalling an emission, must perform the ghusl.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: The one in janabah, the menstruating woman and the woman in post-natal bleeding are ruled alike: it is better that they leave off removing hair or nail until purified, and neither may deliberately recite the Quran, nor Quranic matter within supplications or books, nor the basmalah with the intention of Quranic recitation.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Procedural rulings from Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: one who forgets the ablution until after the ghusl simply performs it with no penalty; and if minor impurity occurs mid-ghusl, he completes the ghusl and performs the ablution afterward for prayer.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Yemeni summoners answering Indian dignitaries ruled that when water suffices for only one of a living junub and a corpse, the living one in janabah performs the ghusl and tayammum is performed for the deceased.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: The author of al-Risala al-Maknuna grounds the ghusl in Quran 'and if you are junub, purify yourselves' and the Prophetic saying 'beneath every hair there is janabah,' and defines junub etymologically as 'the one far from a thing,' concluding that the obedience of one in janabah is void and false.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his Four Hundred Manners, forbids the Muslim to sleep while junub or without purity, prescribing tayammum with earth if no water is found, because the believer's spirit ascends to God who receives and blesses it — keeping it in the finest form if its term has come, or returning it by trusted angels if not.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: On material purity the answers hold: vomit does not render impure what it falls upon (though washing is better); ground is pure once the impurity's substance and smell are gone, since sun and light purify it, unless it is ground set aside as a privy; and a small amount of impurity — wet hair, the produce of filth-eating animals — is excused.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Ali's ruling that touching a corpse after it has grown cold necessitates ghusl is interpreted to mean 'after it has become impure' — the corpse's moisture transmits impurity to the living — while the corpse-washer's own washing is Sunnah.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Garments made by polytheists are pure until the polytheist has worn them or visible impurity appears, per al-Daaim's dispensation; but the answer of the master insists that what polytheists have bleached and washed with soap is not pure except by washing, while cloth merely sprinkled with impure water during weaving and then dried may be prayed in.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Against the common people's claim that a garment large enough that moving one end does not move the other may be prayed upon at its pure portion, the answer rules that prayer upon such a mixed garment is not permitted at all; likewise prayer is not complete without a pure garment, tayammum being prescribed for ritual impurity and never for the impurity of garments.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: The section closes by interpreting Ali's saying 'whomever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him' esoterically: water purifies and is not itself purified, and so likewise is the knowledge of the Imam — whomever it does not purify, God does not purify.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The section's rulings are taken chiefly from a book of questions and answers that one of its compilers arranged according to the chapter order of Daʿāʾim al-Islām, supplemented by Sharḥ al-Akhbār, Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim, Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf, al-Muntakhaba, and question-sets addressed to Yemeni masters.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: On the siwāk, the answer given is that the tooth-stick is the mainstay and there is no objection to the Indian custom of scraping the tongue afterward with split bamboo, though one should not pick the teeth with a knotted stalk of dried grass, and using the siwāk while in janāba (major ritual impurity) is disliked.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Two definitions of al-rayḥān are reported: Sharḥ al-Akhbār says it is every fragrant plant, with the myrtle (al-ās) singled out by that name; Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim says it means linguistically the tips of any sweet-scented plant when its blossom appears, and is a comprehensive name for fragrant plants, the myrtle being singled out as the most lasting and strongest.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is quoted from his four hundred points of etiquette as saying the siwāk pleases the Lord, sweetens the mouth, and belongs to the sunna.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Tayammum is not permitted to a settled (non-traveling) person except for cause; it is licit for the traveler who is far from water, or who cannot perform ablution before the prayer time lapses, or for whom reaching the water would endanger his person or property.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Tayammum requires dust: on a smooth rock fixed in the ground one may perform it only if dust lies on it, and al-Muntakhaba directs one who finds no earth to beat out felts and garments and use that dust even if nothing is seen to fly up.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: A series of traveler's cases is resolved: tayammum suffices for both prayer and fast for one who forgot the ghusl; one who fears illness from ablution performs tayammum; the dead on a journey are given tayammum; prayer with tayammum is valid both in its time and as a make-up; a junub imam who performs tayammum leads only those who have likewise performed it; scarce water goes first to washing an impure garment; and a new convert who finds no water performs tayammum and prays.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Where a deceased person and a person in janāba compete for water enough for one washing, the junub washes himself and the deceased is given tayammum — a ruling repeated in both the question-collection and Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Finding water breaks a tayammum performed for janāba and returns the man to that state, so he must repeat tayammum until enough water for the full washing is available; once he is pure from janāba, remaining water is used for ordinary ablution rather than tayammum.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Al-Nuʿmān's book of purity is cited for the case of a traveler with only a little water: he cleanses himself after relieving himself with stones or the like and then performs the ablution, since the absence of water is itself the cause, and no tayammum is called for.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Tayammum is made valid by intention for oneself: of two men who prayed together, the prayer of the one taught the tayammum was valid while the teacher's prayer, who struck the earth only to instruct, was invalid because he formed no intention for himself.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: A woman who becomes pure from menstruation in Ramadan before sunset and fears harm from the full washing, and a man who has a nocturnal emission and fears illness from washing at night, may each perform tayammum and fast, and neither must make up that day; a traveler's wife who becomes pure and finds no water likewise performs tayammum, after which intercourse is lawful — and a Christian or Zoroastrian wife is to be taught the tayammum by her husband.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: On food, the governing principle is that any liquid in which an animal with flowing blood has died may not be eaten and may not be fed to animals lawful to eat, though soap may be made from it provided the buyer is told of its corruption and the washed garment is afterward rinsed with pure water; and the dung of any animal unlawful to eat is impure, so neem oil pressed from stones passed by crows may not be eaten, sold, or bought.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Small admixtures are tolerated — a little lime chewed with betel, or a little earth in drinking water — unless gross enough to harm the one who takes it.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The food of unbelievers is treated by distinction: their slaughtered animals were forbidden only because they neither pronounce God's name nor turn the animal to the qibla, while their other foodstuffs are lawful in themselves and defiled only by their wet touch — so one must avoid their handiwork where an alternative exists, but in need nothing is forbidden except their slaughtered animals and their moisture.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Corroborating positions are cited: Ḥusayn ibn Idrīs answering Shaykh Ḥasan ibn Nūḥ holds that slaughtered animals of the People of the Book may be eaten if a Muslim witnessed the qibla and God's name, and their other food is lawful by the text of the Qurʾān but impure if touched with their moisture; and the Yemeni masters answering Shaykh Ḥasan al-Hindī permit eating the cooking of a serving girl who is not careful about ritual purity.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: A collection of questions and answers, arranged by the chapter order of the book Daaim al-Islam, supplies rulings on cleanliness and the purifications of the natural disposition (fitra).

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: The responding authority rules that no uncircumcised male is left so in Islam even to eighty years, and that a woman who has grown old without the circumcision of girls (khafd) still undergoes it rather than being left without it.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: On hair, the answers require that the head be parted in two halves from front to back (against the Indian custom of parting toward the middle), permit trimming only from the two sides of the beard (al-aridayn) and nothing else from the beard, and allow shaving, shortening or plucking of other body hair.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Several Indian customs are dismissed as having no basis — the dislike of a husband and wife sharing one comb, and the belief that leaving the hair uncombed on Friday night is binding — with the reply 'no reliance is to be placed upon that.'

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: The answers distinguish forbidden from permitted adornment: the engraving of dye (tattooing with henna patterns) is forbidden, while dyeing the teeth, filing uneven teeth for women, and piercing the ears of women and infant girls carry no harm.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Henna for men is ruled discouraged but not sinful in the question-and-answer collection ('no sin upon one who does it'), whereas Jafar ibn Sulayman's epistle condemns men's henna as imitation of women and an act of disobedience to God.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Ali is reported as instructing women not to take the circumcision of daughters to the utmost but to leave something of it, as better for the face and more favored by the husband, and the respondent confirms one acts accordingly.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: The Prophet's prohibition of a menstruating (adult) woman taking a qassa or jumma is glossed: the jumma is plaiting hair from the side locks to the nape, the qassa is cutting the head hair leaving about a quarter at the front, and the qunzua — gathering the hair with portions left standing — is likewise forbidden.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Qadi al-Numan, answering his district governor al-Khattab ibn Wasim, ruled that an uncircumcised married father must still be circumcised, with the exceptions that one born circumcised (as some prophets were) is excluded and that a man whose glans or most of it is exposed is not compelled.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: In his epistle al-Sayf al-Aqta fi Ibtal al-Bida, addressed to his people in the Island of Yemen, Jafar ibn Sulayman argues that women shaving their heads or their crown-edges and temples inverts the God-given order — men's adornment being the beard, women's the length of their head hair — citing the Prophet that hair is 'one of the two beauties.'

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Jafar's decisive proof against women shaving is Qadi al-Numan's ihram ruling in Daaim al-Islam: the bald and scalp-diseased man passes the razor over his head, while the woman released from ihram only cuts from the ends of her plaits and shaves neither it nor anything of it — so if shaving is barred even there, it can never be a standing custom.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Jafar condemns a double inversion of timing: girls are circumcised too early (within ten to forty days) when Ali forbade it before seven years, while boys are circumcised too late though Ali commanded haste — even the People of the Book circumcise on the seventh day.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Jafar further rules that the circumcision of girls must be done in concealment — known only to the girl, the woman performing it, and a few household women — without gathering, hospitality or call to prayer, since such public ceremony belongs only to the purification of male children and the matter falls under modesty, which the Prophet called part of faith.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: On a girl who dies before seven, Jafar ibn Sulayman (answering the author's questions from Yemen to India) holds the stated age-limit may not be transgressed, and Muhammad ibn Fahd al-Mukarrami rules explicitly that she is not circumcised — whereas a male child who dies uncircumcised is, by preferred sunna, circumcised after death.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Ali's four hundred counsels close the section with the command to circumcise children on the seventh day regardless of heat or cold, since it purifies the body and the earth cries out to God from the urine of the uncircumcised upon it.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The author draws this section's rulings chiefly from a previously mentioned book of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of Daʿāʾim al-Islām, supplemented by Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim, Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf, Mukhtaṣar al-Āthār, Kitāb al-Akhbār, al-Iqtiṣār and Kitāb al-Zīna.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The answer given is that impure garments, the skins of carrion, the skins of beasts of prey, or garments washed by polytheists' hands transmit impurity to the body when contact occurs while either is wet, so the body must then be washed.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim rules that the goat, unlike the sheep, is not shorn while alive — hair shorn from a living goat counts as carrion — but its hair, skin, flesh and bones become lawful and pure if taken after proper slaughter, so prayer upon them is permitted.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: Regarding wool, fleece or hair shorn from a lawful animal while it is alive, the text is reported as holding that prayer in it is not permitted until it is washed, yet the material is not itself impure — a qualified position, not a declaration of impurity.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On vessels made of carrion skins in Waghar used to carry ghee or oil to Ahmedabad, the answer is that the contents become impure and a garment they touch cannot be prayed in, but the ghee and the soap made from it may be sold and bought provided the buyer is told they are impure, whereas the carrion skins themselves may never be sold or bought.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf rules that a broken human bone may be patched only with the bone of a properly slaughtered edible animal; one who used carrion bone, inedible-animal bone or human bone must remove it and repeat every prayer prayed, and the ruling authority compels him if the case becomes known — but it is not removed after death if it was unknown and he himself did not know.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On menstruation, the answer permits the husband to touch his menstruating wife's whole body short of intercourse, but holds it better that he avoid what is beneath the wrapper worn from navel to knees, lest fluid reach her womb.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The reported norms are that the least of menstruation is three days, the least of purity is ten days, and the most of menstruation is ten days; if bleeding exceeds ten days the woman is a mustahadah, distinguished by the fact that menstrual blood is thick and turbid while istihadah blood is thin.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The mustahadah does not pray, does not enter the mosque and is not approached by her husband while the menstrual blood is present; when it departs and the flow thins she purifies herself, prays, fasts, enters the mosque and her husband may come to her, performing ablution whenever blood appears, since it is an ailment.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On the term of nifas the authorities differ: Hasan ibn Nuh and Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf make it depend on the woman's customary duration; the Sharia texts give forty or sixty days; Hasan ibn Idris answers that it may be less than forty days though forty must be reckoned; and a book of the people of the House sets the least at twenty days, the middle at forty and the most at sixty.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The author himself concludes decisively that the postpartum woman is pure once clean of blood after twenty days, thereafter relying on her custom, and that if blood exceeds her custom she judges by whether it has changed — changed blood being istihadah, unchanged blood keeping the original ruling.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: Citing al-Nuʿman's al-Muntakhaba, the author rules that when postpartum blood turbid, thick and foul exceeds her custom she abstains from prayer, fasting and her husband until two months pass; if it continues beyond two months she is unquestionably a mustahadah, washes, and makes up the abandoned prayers and fasts from her customary term to the two months by way of precaution, since menstruation may have followed the nifas.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: Hasan ibn Idris answers that neither the menstruating woman nor the one in janaba may recite any portion of the Quran, whether in supplications or books, nor recite the basmala with the intention of Quranic recitation, and the menstruating woman does not touch the mushaf.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On istibra, the clearing of the womb: a marriage contract with a woman one has fornicated with is invalid until her womb is cleared; Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf sets the withdrawal at two months; Kitāb al-Akhbār transmits forty-five nights for a mature woman who has not menstruated and nine months for such a virgin deflowered by the seller; and by the maxim al-walad lil-firāsh wa-lil-ʿāhir al-ḥajar the fornicator has no claim on the child's lineage.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author reports Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts as teaching that night prayer benefits the body, earns God's pleasure, opens one to mercy and conforms one to prophetic character, and that one must not pray in laziness or drowsiness, must limit wandering thought (receiving only as much of the prayer as one attended to), and must not look aside, since God says 'I am better for you than that toward which you have turned.'

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Also from Ali: prayer is the offering (qurbān) of every godfearing person, no deed is more beloved to God than prayer, and worldly affairs must not distract from its appointed times — God having reproached those 'neglectful of their prayer' (Q 107), meaning heedless of it.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author cites riddle-questions from a book of legal questions: the man for whom prayer is impermissible yet inexcusable is the one drunk to unconsciousness ('Do not approach prayer while intoxicated'); prayer in a state of purity may still be invalid if performed behind a bedouin (a'rābī), since bedouins are harder in disbelief and hypocrisy and it is impermissible to pray behind them; and an obligatory prayer without bowing or prostration is that of a swimmer unable to reach dry land.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The governing distinction throughout the question-and-answer material is between adā' (prayer performed within its appointed time) and qaḍā' (making up after the time has passed), applied separately to the obligatory prayer, its sunnah, and its optional (nāfilah) prayer.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Responsa rule that missed prayers (fawā'it) take precedence over the current prayer if time remains — one sins by neglecting them — that the sunnah's time is before the obligatory prayer except in Maghrib, whose sunnah is prayed as adā' after the obligatory prayer provided nothing separates them, and that one arriving while the imam prays 'Asr during the Dhuhr time intends Dhuhr with him if Dhuhr's time still holds.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Making up missed prayers or praying voluntarily at sunrise, at the sun's meridian standing, and at sunset is disliked (makrūh), on Friday and other days alike; and the reports record agreement that there is no prayer after Fajr until the sun declines except for making up or obligatory prayers (the consecration prayer, the two rakahs of circumambulation, the two festival prayers and the like), with Friday excepted on the ground that 'the fires are not stoked on it.'

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author holds that one who abandons the prescribed prayers for a long period without excuse is not counted a Muslim during that period and has no deed accepted — citing the Prophet's 'There is nothing between the servant and disbelief except the abandonment of prayer' and Ali's 'Prayer is the pillar of religion' and 'There is no share in Islam for one who abandons prayer.'

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author expressly qualifies this 'disbelief': it means only that nothing is accepted from him since he stands in a disbeliever's position — he is not subject to the poll tax, killing, enslavement of offspring, ritual impurity, or prohibition of his slaughtered meat, because the two testimonies place him within the rulings of Islam.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Upon sincere repentance (tawbah naṣūḥ, Q 66:8, whose 'you who believe' the author glosses as those affirming the two testimonies) God accepts him, he becomes truly a Muslim with all lawful deeds accepted, and he is not required to make up the prayers missed before repentance — though doing so is rewarded — whereas deliberately broken Ramadan fasts from that period must be made up with expiation.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author reports, from questions of Sulayman ibn Hasan answered by Dawud ibn Ajab, the same ruling: one who cut himself off from prayer and cannot reckon what he missed bears no guilt for the past if he repents sincerely and enters the noble covenant and does not lapse again — and from Muhammad ibn al-Fahd ibn Salah's epistle, that a bequest paid for making up a dead person's prayers is applied in order (obligatory portions, then shaf' and witr, then sunan), prayer taking precedence over the obligatory fast.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: In the same epistle the case of the boy who killed his mother before puberty is answered: he should undertake her release and discharge as known in the books of the friends of God, and convey good deeds to her — above all Hajj, since Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq told a wealthy questioner that charity equal to the weight of Mount Abu Qubays would not attain the reward of Hajj — but if she was not a believer or did not pray, he must make up her prayer as far as he is able, since prayer is the first deed God examines.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man ibn Muhammad, in the book of the interpretation of the Sharia, defines the five prayer times as hidden and known only by indications (Dhuhr when a thing's shadow equals its length, 'Asr when double, Maghrib at the setting of the disc, Isha' al-Akhirah at the vanishing of the white twilight, Fajr from daybreak to near sunrise), so that ten things are present each day and night — five outward prayers and five inward times.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Al-Nu'man further sets prayer's four boundaries, like a house's — the time, the qibla, the wudu, the intention — and its seven obligatory elements: takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, glorification, tashahhud, and the sealing.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Al-Nu'man reports Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah's answer that the Fajr prayer belongs neither to night nor day — for if to night the faster could eat at its time, and if to day its recitation would not be aloud — since two prayers belong to the day's portion, two to the night's, and one stands midway, this being 'the far-reaching wisdom.'

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inward Nursing, prescribes the witr as three units reciting al-A'la, al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas respectively with the standing qunut after bowing, followed after a separation by two seated units reciting al-Falaq and al-Nas, and identifies the dawn prayer — four units, two voluntary and two obligatory, containing the qunut — as the 'middle prayer' of Q 2:238.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author closes with Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim's answer (sent from Yemen to Hind in 1145 AH to Muhammad 'Ali ibn Salih al-Badri) that making up prayer follows the rule of fasting — only men make it up on behalf of men — while an aged man too weak to make up prayer prays what he can, another makes up on his behalf, and expiation is made.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: A question-and-answer book arranged by the chapter order of Daa'im al-Islam records that a man of the call appointed by a tyrannical sultan as imam, muezzin or teacher and paid from the port levy or jizya may lawfully consume such pay only if the public treasury (bayt al-mal) is administered by the judgment of one appointed by the friends of God, and not otherwise.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Idah reports from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ali that giving the call while walking or mounted is permissible provided one faces the qibla at the moment of the testimony, while the author states that the books attributed to the Ahl al-Bayt agree that the iqama is invalid unless the person is standing upon the ground.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf holds that the muezzin should say inwardly 'I bear witness that Ali is the friend of God' after each testimony to Muhammad's messengership, and 'the family of Muhammad are the best of humankind' after each 'Come to the best of deeds'.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf further rules that no one in the mosque should leave after the call before praying, except for a necessity or to perform ablution with the intention and expectation of returning, and that one who misses the congregation prays alone or with another congregation without fault.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Tawil al-Shari'a rules that the adhan may be given without ritual purity but the iqama only by one who is pure, that the muezzin faces the qibla and forms intention first, and that the obligatory prayer is prayed at the iqama while the supererogatory is joined to the adhan and comes first.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Idris ibn Sayyidina Hasan records in the sixth part of Uyun al-Akhbar that under the caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah the muezzins publicly proclaimed 'I bear witness that our mawla Ali is the friend of God' and 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of humankind and their kindred the best of kindred', in confirmation of the Prophet's Ghadir declaration.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The author argues from Ibn Abbas's answer that the 'near kindred' are Ali, Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and rejects the report from Abu Bakr that 'we are the kindred of the Messenger of God' on the ground that Abu Bakr's only tie was remote Qurashi lineage.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The objection of many common people — that Muhammad may be granted best of humankind but not Ali, since prophets are among humankind — is answered by the author as obstinate and self-refuting, since all Muslims accept that Muhammad's community is 'the best community brought forth for the people' though earlier communities contained prophets.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The author supports Ali's pre-eminence with the Prophet's hadith of the two weighty things and the ark of Noah, and the saying 'Ali is the best of humankind, and whoever refuses this has disbelieved'.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The narrated anecdote of al-Hakim at al-Gharafa has him settle a dispute at Atfih between a preacher who rejected the new call and the dai who gave it, by a chain of reports the preacher himself concedes sound.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Al-Hakim's argument runs: al-Hasan and al-Husayn are masters of the youth of the people of the Garden, the people of the Garden are youths who never age and include Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and the Prophet said their father is better than the two of them — therefore Ali is the best of humankind alongside the Prophet; the preacher then professes belief and al-Hakim tells the dai to give the call as he wishes, since none will oppose him.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The author announces that he will next reproduce in full the epistle al-Muriba 'amma jarat bihi al-mubahatha by his sayyid and father Muhammad ibn Fahd, which debates whether the formula 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of humankind' is an illicit innovation or a thing commanded by the Noble Book and upheld by obedience to those whose command must be obeyed.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The section is framed as a recorded debate in which one jurist challenges another over the call-to-prayer formula 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of human beings, and their kindred are the best of kindred,' noting no other Islamic group says it.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The respondent's first reply is that, per Q 41:46 and Q 6:164, a righteous act benefits only its doer and a wrong burdens only its doer, so the formula harms no one else; the questioner accepts this but demands a plain proof that Ali equals the Prophet in excellence, conceding the Prophet's primacy as master of the messengers is already established.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof one: the purification verse (Q 33:33) establishes the people of the household as equal to the Prophet in purity, and since Ali is the most excellent of them and the Prophet's guardian and successor, likeness to the Prophet is established for him.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof two: 'Peace be upon the family of Yasin' (Q 37:130) refers to the Messenger's household, and only the best of human beings could be the most excellent of that family, which is Ali, whom the Prophet chose as guardian over his community.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof three: 'You are the best community brought forth for humankind' (Q 3:110) is read as addressed specifically to the Prophet's household, and since Ali is first and most excellent among them, he is the best of human beings after and alongside the Prophet.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof four: because Moses' request for Aaron as minister, back-strengthener and partner in his task was granted (Q 20:29-36, 28:34-35), and because God's way admits no change or alteration and Muhammad is told to follow earlier prophets' guidance, the Prophet was obliged to appoint Ali as his minister, brother and partner — confirmed by the hadith 'Ali stands to me in the station of Aaron to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me.'

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof five: the guardianship verse (Q 5:55) — 'Your guardian is only God, His Messenger, and those who believe who give alms while bowing' — designates Ali as the Messenger's partner in guardianship over the believers, reinforced by the Ghadir Khumm declaration 'whoever's master I am, this Ali is his master.'

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proofs six, seven and eight argue respectively that Q 98:7 makes the household 'the best of creation,' that Q 3:33-34's election of Abraham's and Imran's families implies the Prophet's family surpasses them since he surpasses Adam and Noah, and that Q 44:30-32's choosing of the Children of Israel over the worlds shows the Prophet's kindred are best not only in their era but over all prior eras.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: An objection is reported: that Umar's removal of 'hayya ala khayr al-amal' from the adhan is unproven from the opponents' books, was in any case a legitimate exercise of judgment, and that if it were an error then the added testimony 'I bear witness that our master Ali is the guardian of God' would equally be an error, since adding to the adhan is like subtracting from it.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The author answers that even conceding error in both, adder and subtractor are not of equal degree, for four reasons: the subtractor misled vastly more people; he preceded the alleged addition by over four hundred years; he not only subtracted but also added the feeble sentence 'prayer is better than sleep'; and he dropped the Prophet's phrase from all five prayers while attaching his own only to the dawn prayer.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The author rejects as void slander the ascription of the wilaya testimony to al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah — noting the Twelver Shia use it despite differing from him in school — and instead traces the phrase to Ali himself testifying to his own guardianship after the Prophet, as the Prophet testified to his own prophethood and God testifies to His own oneness (Q 3:18).

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The author dismisses the appeal to the opponents' books (Sahih al-Bukhari, the five, al-Mishkat) on the ground that their own scholars dispute those books' soundness and they contain fabrications, and holds that al-Qadi al-Numan's narration from Jafar al-Sadiq predates their compilation and was likely suppressed by them to avoid censure.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: A hadith of the Prophet cited in the questions states that the earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification except for the bathhouse, the cemetery, and the latrine, and the answer given is that one prays in none of those places at all and builds no mosque beside graves.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: The compilation distinguishes a mosque given over to public use, which its owner may not pull down (though he owes nothing if it collapses on its own), from one belonging to him alone and not so dedicated, which he may pull down.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: A man who builds the congregational mosque or another on his own property does as he wishes and need not seek the governor's permission.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: The 'neighbor of the mosque' is defined as the one who hears the call to prayer; the prayer of a man without congregation counts as a single prayer, and for the neighbor of the mosque it is disliked to pray alone at home without an excuse.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Answering a question about the Prophet refusing to plaster his leaking mosque and saying 'No; a shelter like the shelter of Moses,' the reply explains it to mean that this is not like the plastered shelter of Moses.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
