points.text: The rulings distinguish a mosque opened to the people, in which the greeting prayer is prayed and which may not be relocated, from a prayer-place confined within a house and never made open, in which no greeting prayer is prayed and which the owner may absorb into his house.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Two imams do not lead prayer at one time in one assembly, and a congregational prayer is not held twice in one mosque — a later imam and his people pray individually — except that an imam overtaken by something breaking his state may appoint a substitute; yet a separate congregation on the mosque roof is allowed.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: A worshipper is permitted to pass the nearer mosque for a farther one because its licensed man is of greater rank, and no blame attaches to him.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: The greeting prayer is not prayed while an obligatory prayer is owed (except the Sunnah of dawn, which is joined to the obligatory prayers) and only at times when supererogatory prayer is permitted.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: On the qibla: one ignorant of it exerts his judgment and prays; learning of error mid-prayer with little time left, he turns toward the House and completes it if he was between east and west, but if his back was to the Kaaba only repetition suffices; and if two (or four) directions are confused with none prevailing, he prays toward them all — a ruling repeated from Mukhtasar al-Musannaf.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Muhammad ibn al-Fahd rules in his epistle that prayer is permitted in a dome or mosque built for prayer into which a grave was later introduced, but that a structure built on account of a pre-existing grave has the ruling of a cemetery and prayer in it is never permitted — matching the rule given earlier in the answers.
entities: The Clear Highway of the Path of Guidance

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Muhammad ibn al-Fahd further rules that the greeting prayer is obligatory only within the mosque proper and not its courtyard or forecourt, though performing it there is good since they fall within the mosque's bounds, so that one who steps out to the courtyard and returns need not repeat it.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Majalis al-Bayan lists twelve places where prayer is disliked, including the cemetery, slaughterhouse, bathhouse, latrine, camel resting places, facing a sleeper, without a screen, on impure ground, on food, in places of worship, churches, and Magian houses unless sprinkled with water.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Al-Majalis al-Mustansiriyya grades prayer in seven ranks by place — house (one), market mosque (twelve), tribal mosque (twenty-five), congregational mosque (one hundred), the Farthest Mosque (one thousand), the Mosque of the Messenger (ten thousand), and the Sacred House of God (one hundred thousand).

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib in his four hundred rules of conduct teaches that sitting in the mosque from dawn to sunrise is swifter for seeking provision than travel, forbids spitting toward the qibla (with forgiveness sought if done forgetfully), blowing on the place of prostration, food or incense, praying with a sword before one, and approaching the mosque after eating offensive foods.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The section is compiled from a question-and-answer book arranged according to the chapter order of Daʿaʾim al-Islam, supplemented by Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, Mukhtasar al-Athar, al-Ikhtisar, al-Muntakhaba, al-Idah, al-Majalis al-Hatimiyya, al-Majalis al-Mustansiriyya, and epistles of al-Qadi al-Numan and later summoners of Yemen answering Indian questioners.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: A list of twelve disqualifications from leading prayer is given: the sick may not lead the healthy, nor the leper, nor one with white leprosy, nor the madman, nor one on whom a prescribed penalty (hadd) has been carried out, nor the child of adultery, nor a bedouin leading emigrants, nor one in fetters leading the unfettered, nor one who performed dry ablution leading those who used water, nor the mute leading those who speak, nor a traveler leading residents, nor one hostile to the Prophet's household leading those who follow it.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The disqualification is relative, not absolute: each of these persons may validly lead others who share his own condition.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Precedence in leading prayer is ranked among seven, per Jafar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq: earliest in emigration, then best reciter, then most learned in jurisprudence, then eldest; the owner of a mosque has the better right to his own mosque; and the Imam and whomever the Imam appoints outrank all of them.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: A woman may lead women in prayer but does not stand ahead of them — they stand to her right and left — and a woman may never stand ahead of a man while he prays behind her.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Recitation that alters the meaning of the Quran voids the leadership: one who substitutes or distorts vowels (e.g. a kasra on the lam in "Allah is free of the polytheists and His Messenger," or a fatha on the ha in "and among them are those whom God guided") may not be taken as imam, must correct his recitation lest he exchange a verse of mercy for one of punishment, and one who does recite well is obliged to lead when the people call him and he is acceptable to them.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Taqiyya licenses modification but not omission of prayer elements: the licensed imam may lower the recitation of the basmala so only he hears it, and may omit "rabbana laka al-hamd" when common people are present — but he must not omit it for any cause other than taqiyya.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: A man of the summons who repeats a prayer outside its time purely for taqiyya before those not of the People of the House commits no sin, even if others of the summons follow him with him as their intended imam.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The blind man's imamate is conditionally allowed: al-Ikhtisar permits it when there is need, al-Muntakhaba requires that he be set straight on a given day and sets aside the nasib if he led from the side, and al-Qadi al-Numan wrote that there is no harm if he is set straight — but in every case he is not to be taken as a standing (permanent) imam.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The follower must never precede the imam: he begins each act after him, returns to his prior position if he forgets and precedes, may not stand in front of him (that follower's prayer is void though the imam's is valid), and the Prophet warned that one raising his head before the imam risks having his head turned into a donkey's.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The Prophet, injured by a fall from a horse, led his companions seated and signalled them to sit, then declared that the imam exists to be followed — when he magnifies, magnify; when he recites, be silent; when he says "God hears him who praises Him," say "our Lord, to You be praise"; when he gives the greeting, greet; and when he prays seated, all of you pray seated.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Rank among licensed men governs multiplicity and substitution: two imams are not gathered in one unpartitioned place unless the later is the more excellent; only one granted unrestricted leave may appoint a substitute if his prayer is interrupted; a broken ablution requires appointing a replacement before the imam leaves the mosque or the congregation's prayer is spoiled; and only one whom the summoner designates may step forward to the niche.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Rows must be complete and continuous with the space of a prostrating body between them, none in Mecca closer to the Kaaba than the imam, and a latecomer finding no room prays alone alongside the imam without joining his row — save the imam's hujja, who alone may step level with the imam, by explicit text.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: On women praying behind a screen, Sayyidna Jafar ibn Sulayman answers Sayyidna Ali ibn Sulayman that if the place is connected by an opening or lattice the prayer is complete and looking at the men is forbidden before or after entering the sanctified state, cutting off the prayer if directed at non-kin; if the place is not connected, the woman nearest the men takes a single glance at their garments before the sanctified state, and that suffices for all of them — this against the Daudi position that she must keep her gaze on the men during bowing and prostration or none of them has a prayer.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: A question-and-answer compilation arranged by the chapter order of Daaim al-Islam divides al-mufassal into long (al-Hujurat to al-Mujadila), middle (al-Mujadila to 'Amma yatasa'alun') and short (from 'Amma yatasa'alun' to al-Nas) portions, and explains that Ali's recitation of 'So be patient' against Ibn al-Kawwa was a rebuke to silence him, not the opening of a surah in prayer.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The same source lists acts that break the covenant: abandoning prayer or any prescribed work without excuse, disbelieving a believer who has sworn by God after being accused, fornication, killing a believer, reviling the summoner or his appointee, and refusing without excuse the summoner's command to strive with person and wealth.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that if the intention for prayer slips away before one enters it — through preoccupation, forgetfulness or anything else — the prayer subsequently performed does not suffice, and that one may not recite inwardly what the tongue has not uttered.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: On the tashahhud, performing the first does not excuse one from the second, though the second does suffice in place of the first.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Al-Ikhtisar sets the minimum by which prayer is completed at five limits — opening takbir, standing for whoever is able, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the tashahhud — valid for one who forgets or does not know more, whereas one who knows the limits and deliberately omits an obligation or sunnah has no prayer and must repeat it, and the ignorant person is obliged to learn.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Particular bodily rulings are given: a woman places her hands above her knees on her thighs so as not to raise her hindquarters, the seated worshipper folds the left leg beneath him and keeps the right upright, and tawajjuh comes after the takbirat al-ihram with recitation beginning after it.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Those behind the imam answer 'God has heard the one who praised Him' quietly with 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise,' the sole exception being the appointed relayer who raises his voice with that and with the takbir but not with the tasbih.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman's epistle al-Sayf al-Aqta fi Ibtal al-Bida rebukes Yemeni adherents who profess walaya yet never prostrate, arguing from 'between the servant and unbelief is abandoning the prayer' and Ali's 'there is no portion in Islam for one who abandons the prayer' that no one may claim walaya to the friends of God except by holding fast to the hem of the prayer.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: That epistle classifies neglecters of prayer into two kinds — those of tribal temper wholly absorbed in animal nature, and those of arrogance and coarse insolence, especially women — and notes that even unbelievers, including those of India, retain an inherited worship, so that such arrogance falls under the threat that those too proud to worship God enter Hell abased, worship benefiting only the worshipper since God has no need of it.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah numbers the obligations of prayer as seven — first takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, tasbih, greeting, taslim — and forbids moving the foot, speaking, or shifting place from the opening takbir to the taslim, along with prophetic prohibitions on reciting while bowing, disturbing pebbles, turning like a fox, squatting like a monkey, pecking like a crow, and drooping the head below the level of the back.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The Dai Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives a different seven obligations — intention, first takbir, standing, recitation, bowing, prostration, taslim — plus four limits of prayer (place, time, purity, intention), and interprets 'the one who abandons my sunnah is cursed' esoterically as abandoning the Prophet's legatee, adding that the outward prayer itself neither forbids nor commands.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya enumerates seven obligatory prayers (residence, travel, Friday, fear, tawaf of Hajj, tawaf of Umrah, the bier) and twelve sunnah prayers, and in each of the five daily prayers seven obligations and twelve sunnahs, the twelfth being that a prayer lacking a first sitting has a qunut counted in its place while one with two tashahhud sittings has no qunut.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Ali's Four Hundred Etiquettes forbid clasping the hands while standing in imitation of the People of the Book, treat gross turning about as cutting off the prayer so that it must be begun again with adhan, iqama and takbir, and direct the solitary worshipper to make himself hear his recitation and to turn to his right when finishing.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Answering Muhammad Ali ibn Salih al-Badri, head of the island of India, the master Hibat Allah rules that since no text of the friends of God forbids it, reciting al-Falaq and al-Nas in an obligatory prayer leaves the prayer complete — one who recited al-Nas first repeats it in the last rakah, one who recited al-Ikhlas first recites al-Falaq in the second — but one should not deliberately recite so, putting it in the position of the sunnah.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: In the question-and-answer book arranged by the chapters of the Pillars of Islam, it is answered that the guiding call's teaching that supplication is not recited after the afternoon prayer applies both to the supplication of drawing near and to all other supplications, yet no sin falls on one who does supplicate.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The same source answers that wiping the face at the place of prostration is permitted only after the afternoon and dawn prayers, this being commanded by the masters as received from the pure Imams, and that prolonging supplication after the afternoon prayer, though discouraged, incurs nothing.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The book on the interpretation of the Sharia holds that daytime prayers are recited low, night prayers aloud, and the dawn prayer, offered in the last darkness, is announced aloud.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: In the Eleventh Mustansiriyya Council, the author states that having completed the jurisprudence of prayer — outward given exposition, inward given sign and intimation — he now treats the supplication closing the prayer and its seven and twelve.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The seven supplications are distinguished by bodily posture: asking (palms facing the face), seeking refuge (backs of palms facing the face), humble submission (grasping the shoulders, done only in solitude), devotion (pointing with the index finger), entreaty (moving the finger), fervent appeal (both palms spread and raised to the sky), and abasement in the dust (cheeks turned upon the ground).

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The author states that each of the seven supplications has a mention in the Quran to be brought forward later, since all set down so far are roots awaiting the branching of boughs and bearing of fruit.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The twelve foundations of answered supplication are: sending ahead repentance, charity, a fast, or a prayer (per the verse that to God ascends the good word and the righteous deed raises it); purifying intention; beginning with God's praise; blessing the Prophet at start, middle and end; drawing near through the imams of religion named one by one up to the imam of one's own age; seeking access through him and them; asking the good of this world and the hereafter; seeking refuge from their evil; and finally asking whatever one loves.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib is quoted in his Four Hundred Etiquettes teaching that God accepts supplication when His right is remembered and guarded, that the gates of heaven open at six times (rainfall, the advance of battle ranks, the call to prayer, Quran recitation, the sun's decline, and dawn), that supplication turns back even a firmly settled decree, that it should be used to repel affliction before it descends since affliction reaches the believer faster than a mountain torrent or galloping horses, and that one who supplicates without deeds is like an archer with no bowstring.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Ali is further quoted that whoever recites Surat al-Ikhlas ten times and Surat al-Qadr until sunrise will not be touched by sin however hard Iblis strives.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The question-and-answer book rules that deliberate throat-clearing without excuse cuts off the prayer — the imam being alerted instead by words of glorification or a gesture — and that habitual deliberate throat-clearing requires repeating the prayer.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The same source rules that a woman may not occupy herself in prayer by carrying her child even to quiet his weeping, that food placed in the mouth out of necessity for pain incurs nothing, that a braid wound inside the turban around to the forehead is permitted since the forbidden binding is turning hair back on its root and gathering it to the middle of the head, and that holding a gemstone, dirham or object in mouth or hand does not void the prayer if it does not prevent proper formation of letters or fulfilling the prayer's limits — though being free of all such things is more fitting.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The abridgment of the compiled book rules that eating or drinking in prayer cuts it off whether done forgetfully or deliberately, and the interpretation of the Sharia adds that recitation precedes bowing, that one must not raise his voice above the imam's, that noon and afternoon recitation is kept low while night recitation is aloud, and that the Prophet forbade wiping over leather socks and forbade omitting the audible basmala; once the opening magnification is pronounced the worshipper does not speak until the salutation.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in his book on the inward nursing, enumerates fourteen "doors" that are the supporting pillars of prayer and without which it is not complete: ablution, opening, call to prayer, standing call, turning toward God, recitation, bowing, praise, glorification, prostration, testimony, salutation, the supplication of the standing invocation, and the supplication of the odd-numbered prayer.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: The answer in the question-and-answer collection arranged by the chapters of Daaim al-Islam holds that prayer on a mat or cloth bearing depictions is permitted only if the depiction does not occupy the worshipper's attention, with the standing exception that one does not pray toward images.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: A later answer in the same collection states more strictly that prayer in or upon a rug or garment bearing figures is not permitted when the figures are seen, and permitted when they are not seen.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Questions of dye and fabric are assigned to the domain of etiquette rather than validity: wearing safflower-dyed or deeply red cloth does not invalidate the prayer of man or woman, and only pure silk is singled out as disliked for men.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Because the whole of a woman is 'awra, the answer given is that prayer is not permitted to her if any part of it is exposed, and this holds whether she knew the ruling or was ignorant of it — a ruling applied directly to the women of the people of the dawa in India who do not wear the long shift and head-veil.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: The abridgment of the Musannaf draws an asymmetry: a man who prays with his 'awra uncovered unknowingly repeats the prayer once he learns of it, whereas a free or slave woman's prayer with uncovered 'awra is spoiled whether she knew or not.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Prayer is valid only in pure garments — the worshipper strips off whatever is impure — yet carrying wrought or unwrought gold and silver in the waistband does not affect the prayer's validity.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: On impure clothing the rule is that one who has only an impure garment and no water prays in it and repeats when a clean garment or water is found, and one who has two garments of which one is impure but unidentified must pray the prayer in each, intending the fulfilment of the obligation.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Obligatory prayer is not permitted upon stone, unbaked brick, or the like — only supererogatory and sunna prayer — and Idris ibn al-Hasan grounds the general principle in the Prophet's saying that the earth was made a place of prostration and a means of purification, concluding that whatever of the earth is unfit for dry ablution is unfit to pray upon.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman holds in the book of the obligations and limits of religion that a man may lawfully uncover his head and pray bareheaded, and that holding an object in mouth or hand does not void the prayer so long as it does not impair the letters or the required postures, though being free of it is better.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Another transmitted position holds that a man is not to pray bareheaded without turban and mantle unless he finds neither, and that praying with only a small handcloth on the shoulders is impermissible when another garment is available.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: The interpretation of the Daaim explains the technical garment terms — belting a single thick shirt so the private part does not show when bowing, the 'two wings of the swallow' wrap used when nothing else is found, and the forbidden ishtimal al-samma, which is invalid because it pins both hands and prevents bowing, prostration, and the raising of the hands.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred counsels of etiquette require a clean garment before God, forbid praying in a loosely draped shirt as the practice of the people of Lot, and forbid prostrating upon an image, a rug containing one, a heap of wheat or barley, anything edible, or bread — while allowing coins to be carried in a clean money belt or cloth.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Ancillary rulings permit prostration on plaster over which carrion was burned because fire purified it, deny validity to prayer in the resting places of camels while allowing it in sheep folds once swept and sprinkled, and tolerate a small amount of milk or butter from animals that feed on filth.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: A cited question-and-answer collection, arranged by the chapters of Daaim al-Islam, rules that Friday prayer may be established in two congregational mosques only if three miles or more separate them — and the answer extends this: if the distance is less than three miles, Friday is established in only one of them, whether the mosques belong to one city or two.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Against al-Muayyad's sermon wording that condemns abandoning Friday prayer 'under a just imam or an unjust one', the answer distinguishes two senses: praying behind the people of injustice is impermissible except under taqiyya (dissimulation), whereas 'the unjust' in the sermon means an appointed summoner in whom transgression has appeared, behind whom prayer remains obligatory while the people refer the matter to the holder of authority.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali is reported as instructing that prayer behind a nasib or a haruri not be counted, the leader being treated as a mere pillar of the mosque while one recites for oneself as if praying alone.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Al-Husayn ibn Ali is reported to have let Muawiya's governor lead the prayer over al-Hasan, saying 'were it not for the practice I would not have put you forward', which the text glosses as the People of the House's practice of dissimulation, summed up in an Imam's saying that 'dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my fathers'.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf supplies the practical rules of Friday: prayer behind the Imam of the Muslims surpasses prayer behind his deputies; the binding call is the one given before the seated preacher; a broken purity lets the Imam withdraw, wash, and either repeat the sermon or simply pray; a seated sermon suffices for illness; and omitting the sitting between the two sermons is disliked but not grounds for repetition.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: The number of cycles depends on when the congregation disperses: if all but one man leave after the sermon the Imam prays four, if they leave after one completed cycle he prays Friday as two, and if they leave before he bows he restarts as the four-cycle noon prayer.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah states that the sermon precedes the two-cycle Friday prayer, is divided in two by a sitting, is distinguished from ordinary noon prayer by the raised voice, and that the call to stand comes after the sermon; it also makes the summoner's assembly parallel to the Friday congregation, so that silence and attentive listening become obligatory once the preacher faces the people.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah forbids the respondent to 'give suck' unless appointed to it by his summoner, and forbids him to press proposals or demand branches of knowledge from the summoner, who 'knows better how to raise his children'.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl's Hidden Epistle reads Friday esoterically: it points to Muhammad, gate of the Garden, who has an outward summons to the zahir of his law and an inward summons to its interpretation; the two cycles replace four because the sermon substitutes for two, and the sitting within the sermon is the separation between the upper and lower lights with which the Qaim rises.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: The section reports that tashriq, said to be incumbent only in a congregational city, means the prayer of the two festivals — so named because it is prayed at sunrise and its performer is called al-mushriq — and that the twenty-three magnifications from Arafah to the last day of tashriq are a likeness of the summons of the five speakers of firm resolve corresponding to the five prayers, the ten spiritual and ten bodily ranks, and the speaker of the cycle, his executor, and the Imam of the age.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: The festival prayer has neither call to prayer nor call to stand, requires a congregation of five including the Imam like Friday, is obligatory where someone establishes it, and is not prayed in congregation at Mina — where, per al-Numan's Tawil al-Daaim and Idris ibn Hasan, each prays it alone.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: The Hidden Epistle derives fitr from the sense of splitting open, appearing and beginning — as earth, tree and camel's tooth 'break forth' — so that, fasting being silence and concealment as in Maryam's vow of a fast of silence, the breaking of the fast is the day the veiled command and hidden secrets are manifested; and the festival-of-sacrifice sermon uniquely begins with four magnifications rather than praise, signalling that the command appears otherwise than in past cycles.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The author distinguishes omission (sahw, inattention) from doubt: the one who commits an omission is certain of what he omitted, whereas the doubter is not certain of what he doubts — a distinction many jurists confuse by treating doubt as if it were omission.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The two prostrations of omission are called al-murghimatan, 'the two that rub down the nose', because they rub down the nose of the devil when the corruption of forgetfulness is repaired by them.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The Mustansiriyya councils (ninth council) enumerate seven places of omission in prayer, in six of which the two prostrations of omission are proper — including forgetting a prostration, forgetting the first or second tashahhud, saluting after two rakahs in a four-rakah prayer, and rising to a fifth rakah — while the seventh, inattention behind the Imam, requires none because the Imam bears it for the worshipper.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The same source divides doubt into twelve cases: in five (doubt about bowing while still praying, or over one/two, two/three, three/four, two/four rakahs) the worshipper builds on what is certain — the lesser — and prostrates for omission; in the remainder, where the doubt arises only after the relevant act has been passed (e.g. doubting the takbir after bowing, or anything after the salaam), nothing at all is due.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع) is quoted in his four hundred manners: whoever is certain of something and is then struck by doubt should act on his certainty, for doubt neither dispels nor diminishes certainty.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: If a doubter is certain of nothing at all — not knowing whether he added to or fell short of his prayer — he begins the prayer again from the beginning, and so likewise does the Imam.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The prostration of omission is not multiplied: repeated omissions in a single prayer, or three separate omitted obligations, still require only the two prostrations.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Where no explicit text (nass) exists — as with neglecting the first tashahhud and remembering before the salaam, or repeating a single surah after the Opening — it has not been stipulated that the worshipper must prostrate, though the answerers add that such things should not be done deliberately.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Against the maxim that deeds are accepted only with intentions, the answer given is that the intention resides in the heart and the tongue's utterance is merely verbal expression, as stated in the Pillars, so that an act intended in the heart is complete even if never voiced.
entities: Book of the Pillars of Islam

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The Imam bears responsibility for a follower's omission, except in the bowing and the opening takbir, which the follower must not neglect; conversely a latecomer prostrates for his Imam's omission even if he caught only the opening takbir with him, and prostrates on his own account for errors made while praying alone.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: On interruption, the author cites the report that three things interrupt the prayer — a woman, a donkey, and a black dog — alongside the Prophet's own statement that nothing interrupts a believer's prayer but one should ward off what one is able, and Ali's dictum that smiling does not interrupt the prayer while loud laughter does.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Broken purity or bodily impurity during prayer is governed by position and orientation: one who breaks purity before the tashahhud repeats the prayer but one who breaks it after the peace upon the Prophet and the righteous need not, and one who cleans blood or vomit without turning his face from the qibla builds upon his prayer, whereas turning from the qibla obliges repetition from the beginning.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd, in his epistle The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided, answers that a latecomer who reaches the Imam before the Imam raises his head from the bowing and enters with a single takbir has attained that rakah, provided the intention is contracted in his heart.
entities: The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib is reported as instructing that boys be taught the prayer and held to it when they reach eight years, and more generally taught what God will benefit the parents by.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Ibrahim ibn Husayn al-Hamidi reports in Ibarat al-Bishara a saying of Amir al-Muminin that the boy sheds milk teeth at seven, reaches maturity at fourteen, completes his stature at twenty-one, and completes his intellect at twenty-eight.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Athar directs that children be separated in their sleeping places at that stage, as a precaution since they have drawn near to maturity and the stirring of desire.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: The governing rule for the traveler is that he shortens the prayer and breaks the fast from leaving his dwelling until he returns to it, but he prays and fasts in full if he stops for five prayer times with his wife or with a resident blood relative (kin of lineage), while relatives by marriage and by nursing do not produce this effect.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: A distinction is drawn between the two grounds for praying in full: stopping five prayer times with blood kin or a resident wife, and forming the intention to reside ten days, the latter being the stipulated limit of residence.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Idris ibn Hasan answers that residence-intention governs: one prays in full while the intention of residence remains and shortens from the moment he resolves on travel; an intention to return to the first lodging carries over to a nearby lodging, otherwise a fresh ten-day intention is required.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Distances are defined: the barid is four farsakhs, the farsakh three miles, and the mile three thousand cubits, being a thousand even paces of a single leg.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Whoever enters Mecca prays in full without shortening, on the basis of the Quranic words that the resident and the visitor stand equal, though Ismail ibn Sayyidina Hiba held that the full prayer applies only within the sanctuary of the House of God and that in Mecca itself the prayer is shortened.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Six categories are reported from Amir al-Muminin as not shortening prayer or fast despite travel: collectors on circuit, merchants moving market to market, princes circuiting their emirate, hunters, shepherds seeking rain-fed pasture, and warriors who cut the road — and Idris extends this to shaykhs touring villages to visit believers, likening them to the prince.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: A traveler may lead residents when he is the more excellent, saluting after two rakahs while they rise to complete, and a traveler following a resident imam may either withdraw after two rakahs or wait for the imam's salutation — though Muhammad ibn Fahd restricts the traveler-as-imam dispensation to the people of the high ranks.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd reports that one who has performed tayammum may lead those who performed ablution only among the people of the high ranks, citing the Dai Jafar ibn Sulayman, who at Haraz performed tayammum unseen and led the congregation, then explained the dispensation as granted for weighty matters serving the guiding dawa.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Jafar ibn Sayyidina Sulayman answers in Ghurufat al-Jinan that an imam with only a shortening follower behind him need not raise the takbir aloud once that follower has withdrawn, since raising the voice exists for the follower.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states in Kitab al-Rida al-Batin that shortening applies to three four-rakah prayers — the first, afternoon, and late evening — reducing twelve rakahs by six.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: The sick man prays seated or cross-legged with bowing and prostration; if unable to gesture with his head he gestures with his eyes, and failing that with his heart, and he need only make up the obligatory prayer, the sunnah and supererogatory being meritorious but not obligatory to make up.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that one who loses his reason through a medicine or any act of his own must repeat the prayers missed in that state, regardless of whether the act was obedience or disobedience.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: The answer to the eclipse question, attributed to the pure Imams and the ranks below them, is that a lunar eclipse falls at the dawn of the fifteenth or sixteenth while a solar eclipse may fall at either the beginning or the end of the month, contrary to the Brethren of Purity's treatise on astronomy which said a solar eclipse occurs only at the month's end.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: The eclipse prayer may not be prayed until the eclipse is actually seen with the eye: it is not prayed on the word of an astrologer or anyone else, and if cloud intervenes it is postponed until visible (book of purity).

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: A latecomer to the eclipse prayer counts his joining as the beginning of his own prayer, follows the imam in bowing and prostration, sits poised while the imam testifies, and after the imam's salutation completes the remaining bowings himself, not counting the first two prostrations done with the imam.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: In extreme combat — crossing of swords and thrusting of spears — prayers are converted into takbir, one takbir in place of each bowing, and the takbir is shortened just as shortening is obligatory in the prayer of fear.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Per مُخْتَصَرُ الْمُصَنَّفِ, the prayer of fear requires at least three men praying with three standing guard, since the term 'party' does not apply to fewer than three; and if eclipse, funeral, and fear coincide the imam prays the funeral, the eclipse prayer, and the prayer of fear.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: The rain prayer includes a hundred takbirs facing the people, a hundred glorifications to the right, a hundred declarations of oneness to the left, and a hundred praises, with two sermons as at the two feasts, delivered leaning on an Arabian bow as the Messenger of God did; and whoever delivers the sermon before the prayer must pray and then deliver it again.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: On the qunut the answers distinguish: deliberate abandonment in the witr requires repetition, forgetting it requires no repetition since there are no prostrations of forgetfulness in sunnah prayers, its least measure is three glorifications or three takbirs, and it is recited after 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise'.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Judge al-Numan in المنتخبة holds the witr may be divided by the salutation without intervening actions or speech, though if one is compelled to speak there is no harm provided the talk is not prolonged.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd, in لاحبة سبيل الهدى للمهتدين, answers that one who prayed dawn before the true dawn keeps his shaf and witr but must repeat both the sunnah and obligation of dawn — unless dawn was close upon him, in which case the sunnah prayer stands, on account of a noble inner meaning permitting it.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Praying tarawih behind an imam who recites the whole Quran is permitted only for the sake of protective concealment (taqiyya) and with the intention of a voluntary prayer, and the believers do not take him as a leader; likewise the reliance for numbers of sunnah bowings is upon الدعائم, and sunnah omitted for concealment must be made up.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman rules that the prayer of Umm Daud has a text from Mawlana al-Sadiq only for the month of Rajab and for the day of 'Arafah, so Qasim ibn Fir of the Daudi faction, who commanded it in Rabi al-Awwal and Ramadan of 1042, acted without a text — for no practice is valid without a supporting text, and 'little action in a sunnah is better than much action in an innovation.'

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim answers (year 1135) that the prayer of the prophets and Imams at times of calamity was praise and thanksgiving for what God disclosed to them, and that followers may pray it at all times when sunnah and voluntary prayers are permitted, prohibition applying only to the forbidden times.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: For the Quranic prostration a distinction holds: the binding prostration verses oblige all present to prostrate (though not a second time in the same sitting), while the remaining ones are optional, prostrating being better; and 'Ali's four hundred points urge prolonging prostration since Iblis was commanded to prostrate and disobeyed while the son of Adam obeyed and was saved.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The 'dying state' (siyaq) is defined as the moment when death draws near and the passage from this world to the hereafter is imminent, per the book interpreting the pillars.
entities: book of the interpretation of the pillars

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Asked whether people may relocate to flee epidemic and plague believing they will escape it, Idris ibn Hasan answered that they may go wherever they wish, since the matter is in Allah's hand.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman's epistle 'The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations' — written to admonish his heedless followers among the people of the island of Yemen where he had settled — rebukes them for being slow to visit the sick, citing the pillars' report from the Commander of the Faithful that seventy thousand angels pray for a Muslim who visits a sick person from the hour of his visit until sunset (or sunrise, if by night).
entities: The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The Prophet forbade the visitor from eating in the sick person's presence, and Allah nullifies (in another wording, casts behind him) the reward of such a visit, the stated reason being that eating in a poor sick man's house burdens him and inwardly galls his household.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Whoever knows such rulings is obliged to pass them on, since the learned are few, and the one who gives the warning has thereby discharged his duty.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: From 'Ali's four hundred points of conduct: one must not sleep in the prohibited posture nor on one's face (and the sleeper on his face is to be woken), a woman is not to sleep stretched on her back, and refuge is sought from severe affliction because the gravest affliction is loss of one's religion.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: On lifespans: they are fixed terms that neither increase nor decrease, yet the reported 'increase and decrease' is sound in the sense that what is diminished in the past cycle is added in the future one.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The saying that 'the wretched is he whom the Hour overtakes while alive and not yet dead' is interpreted to mean that the Hour comes upon him while he is still in the animal (bahimi) condition, not having passed to the angelic life.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Husayn ibn Idris ruled, answering Hasan ibn Nuh's tenth question, that a living formed child in a dead mother's womb must be extracted if a skilled woman is present and it is possible, or if the fetus is six months or more with hope of life; otherwise the mother is not buried until the child's death is confirmed.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: 'Ali taught frequent remembrance of death, the rising from graves and the standing before Allah so that calamities sit lightly, described fever as death's forerunner and Allah's prison on earth which strips away sins as hair is stripped from a camel's pores, and said that a Shi'a who departs from a prohibition is afflicted in property, child or self so that his sins are purged before meeting Allah — the dead of their Shi'a being a truthful witness (siddiq shahid).

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Innovations of mourning are condemned: no shaving hair, lighting lamps or cutting nails for the dead; placing weapons beside the corpse or holding a vigil beside it obligatory has 'no reliance to be placed upon it'; and the gathering of women to lament for nights and days with singing and play, as if it were a prescription at fixed times, disgraces the believers before Allah and His friends.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Wailing is forbidden by narration: Jafar ibn Muhammad bequeathed that no cheek be struck and no collar torn for him (the woman who tears her collar has a rent in Hell that grows as she adds to it), 'Ali wrote to Rifaah ibn Shaddad his judge over al-Ahwaz to forbid wailing where he held authority, and the Prophet named two accursed voices — howling at calamity and a voice raised at a blessing — i.e. wailing and singing.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The account of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah shows the dead/dying are punished by the living's words: he saw an angel with a fiery iron mace who struck at his skull each time a woman shrieked 'O my mountain!' or 'O my might!', desisting only when he answered 'No, rather Allah', and the Prophet confirmed it saying, 'What is the matter with your dead, that they suffer by the words of your living?'

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The decisive distinction: the Prophet wept at the death of his child and declared he had not forbidden weeping but only wailing and lamentation, weeping being a tenderness and mercy Allah places in whom He wills; he licensed tears at calamity ('the soul is stricken, the eye sheds tears') while commanding only speech pleasing to Allah and forbidding foul speech (hujr).

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Correspondingly, the singing forbidden at calamity is permitted at weddings and banquets solely to distinguish lawful marriage from fornication — the Prophet, hearing music among the Banu Zurayq, approved it, saying there is no secret marriage until smoke is seen or a tambourine heard, and that the beating of the tambourine is what separates nikah from sifah.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: 'Ali commanded households to speak well over their dead, citing Fatimah — when the daughters of Hashim mourned with her at her father's death she said 'Grieve with restraint, and hold fast to supplication' — and he ruled that whoever strikes his thigh at a calamity forfeits his reward.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The washing of the dead requires the ablution performed three times together with three washings, though performing the ablution at the last washing suffices, as stated in the Book of Reports.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Where water is scarce, the answer given is that a living man in janabah uses the water and the dead is given tayammum with earth; another report permits a washer in janabah to wash the dead, performing tayammum first if washing would harm him, when no one else can be found.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: A martyr is normally not washed, but the Mukhtasar of al-Musannif rules that a martyr who was in janabah is washed on account of that janabah, and one found dead with no mark upon him is washed, given hanut, and shrouded.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The Mukhtasar al-Athar rules that the drowned and the burned are washed, as is any severed limb whose separation would preclude life, each detached limb being washed and set in its own place before shrouding; no hair is shaved and no nail trimmed from the dead.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Answering the author's question from Hind, Jafar ibn Sulayman rejects the wrapper arrangement used by the Daudi group and by unbelievers, ruling that the Pillars prescribes only an izar from navel to knee with water passed beneath it and the washer's cloth-wrapped hand reaching under it, while conceding that a screen is the better course, especially for a woman.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The best shroud, per Jafar ibn Muhammad in The Pillars of Islam, is three garments: a shirt neither buttoned nor hemmed, a wrapping sheet, and a waist wrapper.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan's term 'tajir' for a woman's shrouding is defined as gathering the shirt at the navel down over the clothing and tucking it into the izar's fastening — a mark distinguishing women from men, like the head covering.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Ali's counsel that whoever touches the body of the dead after it has grown cold must perform the washing is glossed as meaning after his end has come and he has been washed according to the sunnah, since the dead body has become impure and its moisture renders a living man impure.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: For conjoined twins, the summoners of Yemen rule that separation is done only if slight and safe; if dangerous they are left, their life and death counting as one, and if one dies the adhering part is cut from the dead one only where the living feels no pain.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The shroud and outfitting are taken from the estate first — before debt and bequest — according to the deceased's station even if costly and even if the debt exceeds the estate.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Hanut is any perfume placed on the places of prostration and named parts of the body, but wars and saffron are excluded for men and included for women; the dead himself is not incensed — only his shroud and the place of washing — and Ali forbids any fragrance but camphor since the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: One who dies in a state of pilgrim consecration has his head and face left uncovered and no perfume brought near him, because he remains consecrated during days that are numbered.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Walking before the bier is disliked only for an enemy of the family because angels of wrath attend it; for believers, encompassed by angels of mercy, position does not matter though walking behind is more excellent, and the call to prayer at the bier is disliked while announcing the death without a public call is permitted.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The Prophet turned back women following a bier, telling them they neither pray over it, carry it, lower it, nor cover it, and so should return excused but unrewarded.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The funeral prayer is a communal obligation on every Muslim who knows of it until one performs it, may be offered anywhere and even in disliked hours or at an eclipse, and the supplication between takbirs may be recited or left to the imam.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: In the absence of the imam of the age, the right to lead the funeral prayer belongs first to his appointed judge or officeholder, then to the highest in station among those the imam has advanced, then to the appointed prayer leader, and only if none is present to the most entitled guardian.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The funeral prayer is offered over martyrs, grave sinners, those executed under prescribed punishment or retaliation, and even one who has taken his own life; the supplication is quiet by day and aloud by night.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The dead is buried in the burial ground of the town where he died and not carried to another, unless he dies in open wilderness, in which case he may be carried to the nearest burial ground.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Burial in another's land requires his leave, but once done without consent the owner may claim only the value of the grave sites and may not have the bodies removed.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Baked brick, stone, and whatever else is available may be placed over the dead, contrary to the dislike of it held by the people of the outward sense, and the questioner is told to rely on this except where prudent concealment requires otherwise.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Ali counsels visiting the graves of those who have a claim upon one and seeking provision there, since the dead rejoice at such visits, and a man should ask his need at his parents' graves after praying for them.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Prophet is cited as saying that charity (sadaqa) is not lawful for him nor for the people of his house, and a later answer specifies that 'people of the House' here refers to the Imams.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman teaches that whoever pays the khums is thereby excused from the tithe except voluntarily, but paying the tithe alone does not excuse the khums, because the tithe does not encompass the khums as the khums encompasses the tithe.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman also holds that one whose standing in the call, after his obligations are discharged, is shown by outward abundance of wealth pays from it what he wills, apart from the fitra, of obligatory rights and voluntary giving.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Prophet is quoted as saying there is no prayer for one who does not pay zakat, and that the withholder of zakat is in the Fire.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the Hidden Epistle, lists ten things upon which God imposed zakat: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, dates, raisins, wheat, barley, and grains.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in the Four Hundred Counsels, says: treat your sick with charity and fortify your wealth with zakat.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils place zakat after the jurisprudence of guardianship, purity and prayer, as one of the rights of the testimony, and assign it seven obligations and twelve sunnahs, matching the number of the clauses and letters of the testimony.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: According to the Mustansiriyya Councils, zakat must be received by the Imam and is taken from seven things: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, crops, and minerals.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Councils name eight recipients falling into seven divisions — the poor and needy, the collectors (as wage), those whose hearts are reconciled (as bond of protection), the freeing of necks, the debt-burdened among the people of allegiance, the way of God as a struggle of sufficiency, and the wayfarer understood as those cut off from the road of guidance.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The twelve sunnahs of zakat include waiting for the year to run its course, nisabs of twenty dinars for gold, two hundred dirhams for silver, five grazing camels, thirty grazing cows and forty sheep, taking the middling livestock rather than the best or poorest, not joining what is separate nor dividing what is joined, exempting the stud animal, giving from crops below the nisab of five awsaq by bundle and handful on the harvest day per Qur'an 6:141, and no zakat on dwellings, ornaments, or things for use.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: In the question-and-answer book arranged after Daaim al-Islam, the prohibition on concealing zakat from one's imam is explained as applying to one who brings out only part of the zakat, whereas one who withholds it entirely has abandoned the obligation altogether.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The same source explains that the 'hamala' which makes charity lawful for a recipient means either a penalty imposed by a tyrannical ruler or the bearing of blood money on behalf of the 'aqila.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Ali's covenant to Muhnaf ibn Sulaym forbids a resident of his domain to pay charity to the enemy, and the answer interprets the exemption for territory not encompassed by his horsemen as meaning zakat is not demanded from one seized by the enemy who is not of the Shia holding the allegiance.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: It is transmitted from the people of the House that zakat handed to other than the one God commanded does not suffice, even if it is afterwards plundered or stolen, until it is handed to the guardian of the affair or one who receives it by his command.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils hold that one who keeps the outward prayer and believes its inner reality but does not spend the zakat of his wealth, the khums of his earnings, the purchase of his own self and the redemption of his pledge falls short of the one God praises as spending from what He provided.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: In the questions-and-answers collection attributed to our master Idris, the obligations owed from a dead man's estate are ranked in a fixed order of priority: zakat first (because it is a debt and not part of his wealth), then the Hajj, then the khums, then expiation, then al-Shurwa.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: The same responsa hold that these debts take precedence over inheritance, that khums is taken from the entire estate including houses and servants, and that a guardian or kinsman who discharges them secretly, without the other guardian's knowledge, commits no wrong.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Where heirs refuse to purify the deceased's wealth by paying the khums, the answer invokes the Quranic verse 'There is no compulsion in religion' rather than coercion.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: The nisab that defines 'means' (yasar) is ownership, after a full hawl, of either two hundred dirhams of silver or twenty gold dinars — specified in Arab ounces and in Gujarati kadiyana and wal weights — and since gold and silver prices vary by age, the pious believer should reckon by whichever of the two coinages is the cheaper.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Once khums has been paid on capital, khums on subsequent profit is due only on what remains in hand after household expenses; paying khums on the whole profit is a merit (fadl), not a binding obligation.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf sets the general condition of zakat — that the property reach its nisab unencumbered and that a hawl pass over it — and applies it to altered deposits, to undivided estates (assessed per heir's share, not on the whole), to debtors (zakat only on the surplus over the debt), and to trade goods exchanged for trade goods.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Al-Akhbar reports that an apostate begins his zakat afresh and owes nothing for the period of his apostasy, and that there is no zakat on the wealth of an orphan or of one who has lost his reason — to which Ta'wil al-Da'aim adds the qualification that this exemption covers only wealth held for the owner's own use, while any part held for trade is valued and does bear zakat.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, cited in Ta'wil al-Shari'a, taught that zakat is five dirhams for five classes of poor and that its meaning is mutual consolation, since all creation is a single soul whose limbs all turn to treat the one limb that suffers pain, and he added that if anyone were untouched by defect death would never reach him.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inner Nursing, enumerates five zakats paralleling the five prayers: the khums of earnings (which belongs to the Imam), the zakat of already-purified wealth at one dinar in forty (due to the Hujja), the tenth of crops, one head in forty of livestock, and the zakat of the soul — the shurwa redeeming the believer's neck and the fitra of his fast.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad's al-Risala al-Maknuna gives the graduated livestock scales — a sheep for every five camels up to twenty, then bint makhad at twenty-five, bint labun at thirty-five, hiqqa at forty-five, jadha above sixty and two hiqqas at one hundred and twenty; tabi' at thirty cattle and musinna at forty; one sheep at forty sheep rising to two sheep at two hundred — with defective animals and the flock's ram excluded, and he explains the hiqqa at sixty as resembling the stallion in what she can bear.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: On produce, the responsa note a tension: the Pillars make zakat due on everything the earth brings forth and the masters' practice was to take the tenth from little and much alike, whereas the Shari'a sets a nisab of five awsaq (the wasq being sixty sa') — and the tenth is due on what sky and rivers water, half the tenth on what wheels and beasts water.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Al-Akhbar distinguishes land of the tenth (Arab land and mountain land cultivated by its own people, unconquered by horse or mount) from kharaj land (Sudan and lands taken by force), and holds that the ruling attaches to the land's produce and not to its owner, so that sale between Muslim and protected non-Muslim does not change it.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: The Book of the Inner Nursing reads the tenth as an outward ruling by which the Messenger judged: whoever pays it in truth and keeps back only nine tenths has discharged his outward obligation even unasked, while whoever retains more than nine tenths has not truly obeyed the ruler over his outward affairs.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: The khums is grounded in the Quranic spoils verse naming five recipients — God, the Messenger, the near of kin, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer — is extended by Da'ud ibn 'Ajab to the seed of lands already purified (seeds falling under the word 'thing'), and is taken from mines, treasures and spoils, as Ja'far al-Sadiq's report of the Prophet's distribution confirms.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Answering a question about the Indian custom of mixing four grains (rice, maize, wheat, salt) and taking their monetary value, the reply is that reliance is on the Book of the Pillars: a sa of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins.
entities: Book of the Pillars of Islam

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: A reported saying holds that the fitra should be from the best of what one eats and the purest of what one stores, yet mixing it from everything eaten during Ramadan suffices, and one who ate nothing but barley may give barley.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Against the objection that obligatory duties may not be performed outside their appointed times, the answer given is that delivering the fitra to a rightful recipient suffices whenever done, since no fixed time was set for advancing or delaying it — the sole prohibition being that one must not break the fast before delivering it.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that a dhimmi who accepts Islam before dawn on the day of Fitr owes zakat al-Fitr, while one who converts after dawn owes nothing.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Reports state the fitra is paid on behalf of the mukatab; the Landmarks of Religion that it is due for a child born before dawn on the day of Fitr; and the Book of the Pillars that it has also been said to be paid for the child still in the womb.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The Landmarks of Religion gives the sa as four and a half Meccan ratls, five ratls less a third by the ratl of Medina, and nine and a tenth Baghdadi ratls, while the Selected Book allows a sa of dried curd or half a sa of wheat.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The thirteenth Mustansiriyya session, following on the prior session about zakat owed by the wealthy, presents zakat al-Fitr as the zakat obligatory in every condition and even upon those of small means, comprising seven obligations and twelve Sunnah practices.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The seven obligations are that a man pay it for himself, for the elder and the younger of his household, the free and the enslaved among them, and the males and the females among them.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The Sunnah practices include bringing it from the middle sort of what one eats (a sa of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins — half a sa sufficing only for wheat, the sa being four mudds), handing it to the Imam or his appointee, bringing it out before the breaking of the fast, making it up if delayed, and giving its value in silver or gold if one lacks the food; a woman with no husband present pays for herself and her dependants.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The Inner Nursing cites the Prophet's saying that the fitra is lawful neither for him nor for the people of his house.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad in the Concealed Epistle holds that the Prophet obliged every Muslim head — male, female, small, great, even an infant born that day, and the child in the womb — to pay a sa, and explains that zakat al-Fitr is therefore named 'the charity of the head'.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan's Mafatih al-Nima distinguishes fitra from ordinary charity by timing — before sunrise it is fitra, after sunrise mere sadaqa — and defines fitra as bringing out what is owed to God and to His appointed guardian, as ransom and offering.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Two residual riddle-rulings hold that zakat is lawful to a man who owns a thousand dinars but owes a thousand (so no zakat is due from him), and to a well-off polytheist who has found no Muslim to receive his zakat, who then has more right to it than anyone.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited as stating that fasting is a shield from the Fire covering the tongue, hearing, eyes and all limbs, so that it is not about food and drink alone: every limb has its portion, and whoever abandons part of it diminishes the merit of his fast proportionally.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Per the same source, fasting Ramadan is obligatory on every Muslim, male and female, who is of age, sound of mind, healthy and resident, and there is no fasting for a hypocrite disobedient to God.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: The book al-Idah qualifies the rulings on fasting by sighting the crescent: they apply only to one absent from the presence of the Imam who does not know the measures of the crescents.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, in his epistle The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations addressed to the people of Yemen, rebukes them for failing to honor the month as God and His Messenger prescribed.
entities: The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: His specific charge is that the month must be named with the word 'month' placed before it, as in the Quranic 'shahr Ramadan', whereas the people say 'Ramadan' alone, which neither intellect nor guidance approves, since one does not address a beloved person without a title before his name.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: He supports this by al-Qadi al-Numan's Mukhtasar al-Athar al-Sharif, reporting Imam al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali as saying: do not say 'Ramadan', but say as God said, 'the month of Ramadan'.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: He argues that one who has heard this saying and still turns from it makes light of God, of His month, and of al-Baqir's word, and that one who transmits the book without acting on it falls under the Quranic censure 'why do you say what you do not do?'

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah is cited as holding that fasting becomes obligatory upon a boy once he can distinguish his right hand from his left.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: The fourteenth Mustansiriyya majlis divides fasting into seven obligatory kinds: Ramadan yearly; two consecutive months for deliberately breaking a fast-day when no slave can be freed; two consecutive months for killing a believer by mistake plus blood money; two months for zihar expiation lacking a slave; three days for breaking an oath lacking feeding, clothing or freeing; ten days for tamattu pilgrimage lacking an offering; and the fast of a vow.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: The same majlis lists twelve fasts of practice and commendation: itikaf, Shaban, the first Thursday, middle Wednesday and last Thursday of each month, the three white days, the fast of Dawud (alternate days, the most rigorous), Friday joined to Thursday or Saturday but never alone, Arafah for the non-pilgrim, the boy's fast at seven, recompense for game taken in the sacred state as ruled by the one entrusted, and the fast for shaving the head due to harm.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Zaid ibn Muhammad's Concealed Epistle states that God imposed the fast of the month of Ramadan after prayer and zakat, commanding one month of twelve be fasted, and that this obligatory fast is thirty days.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib in his Four Hundred Manners is quoted: fasting three days of every month and fasting Shaban drive away the whisperings of the breast and the disquiet of the heart.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The author reports from the Book of Clarification that the transmitted rulings tying fasting to the sighting of the crescent are addressed only to those absent from the Imam's presence and ignorant of the crescents' measures.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Sulayman ibn Hasan, in his epistle the Ijadiyya, explains that after the moon parts from the sun and travels twenty-eight stations it must cross two more to overtake the sun, since the sun has itself advanced two stations and a degree, so the meeting occurs at thirty stations, which reckoners count as one month.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Al-Muayyad fil-Din, in the forty-second of his Wisdom Sessions, refutes those who make fasting depend on sighting the crescent and argues that Ramadan is always complete and never deficient.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The opponents' proof is the Prophet's saying 'Fast when it is seen and break your fast when it is seen; if it is hidden, complete thirty,' which they take to make Ramadan sometimes twenty-nine days.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The reply is that the hadith was spoken in answer to companions asking how to act in the Prophet's absence, so sighting is only an emergency rule when neither the Messenger nor the Imam standing in his place is present; when either is present one fasts by his fasting.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Al-Muayyad argues on two legal grounds that the Prophet never fasted by sighting: Gabriel came to him morning and evening with certain news, making search unnecessary, and he declared he knew the roads and stations of the sky better than others know those of the earth.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The rational ground is that the Prophet knew crescent risings differ by place and elevation, so he could not have imposed a single sighting-standard on all people, nor can one and the same day be Shaban in one place and Ramadan in another.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Quranic proof is drawn from 'fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you' — taken to mean the Christians, who fast by calculation not sighting — and from 'a counted number of days,' which implies a fixed, unvarying number.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
