points.text: Further arguments for Ramadan's completeness: the year alternates six complete and six deficient months so that Ramadan falls complete; the Prophet said 'Shaban is never complete and Ramadan never deficient'; Shaban alone has a true middle night (the fifteenth) while Ramadan has none; and the expiation for breaking the fast is sixty days or sixty poor persons, matching two complete thirty-day months.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: In an anecdote from his autobiography, al-Muayyad debates a Zaydi sharif before King Abu Kalijar al-Daylami of Shiraz, who cited the hadith 'We are unlettered, we do not reckon' with the gathered fingers; al-Muayyad answered that the Prophet, honored with the ascension, could not have been unable to say 'thirty' or 'twenty-nine' and gestured like a herdsman, and the Alid withdrew in shame amid laughter.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Some summoners frame the case as a formal question to all Muslim scholars, asking who 'those before you' are, how many the counted days are, what 'witnessing the month' means, and whether the completed count is thirty, twenty-nine or twenty-eight, invoking the Prophet's rule that reports contradicting the Book are not his.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Grammatically, the lam in 'fast for its sighting' is read as the lam of anticipation or outcome (as in 'mothers nourish their children for death' and 'for the Day of Reckoning'), so the hadith means: let the crescent rise while you are already fasting, and while you are already breaking the fast.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the epistle al-Maknuna on the eclipse prayer, teaches that God made the first creation a proof for the last age, setting the moon's eclipse at fourteen nights (sometimes thirteen) and its concealment at twenty-eight nights, absent forty-eight hours before rising again.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The section closes by introducing the next text: the epistle al-Lazima on the fast of Ramadan and its proper time, by Ahmad Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, proof of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author writes in response to a brother's request to justify the Shia practice — and specifically the command issued from the Pure Presence in the year 400 requiring the fast to begin two days before the crescent was visible to the eye — against opponents who reproach them for fasting before the general public.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author frames the opponents' disagreement not as honest error but as arrogance, envy, and refusal to obey those charged with the Command to whom Quran 4:59 and 4:83 direct disputed matters to be referred.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The disputed proof-text, accepted by nearly all Muslim sects and relied on by the people of the outward, is the Prophet's saying 'Fast at its sighting and break the fast at its sighting.'

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Because Allah created all things in pairs — and the Prophet made pairing the governing principle of the law (prayer/alms, adhan/iqama, Hajj/Umrah, Safa/Marwa) — sight too must be of two kinds: natural vision and vision of the soul.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Natural vision occurs by the eye and apprehends only colors and shapes; vision of the soul occurs by way of knowledge through heart and soul and apprehends causes hidden from the eye, as in the Quranic 'Have you not seen what your Lord did with the companions of the elephant?' addressed to a Prophet who did not witness that event.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author concludes that vision of the soul is prior, more exalted and subtler, and that in discharging Allah's obligations one is bound to take the more excellent instrument, since settling for the lesser when the greater is present is a judgment of ignorance.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: By analogy with the man who knows the prayer time without hearing the adhan, and the man eating before dawn who knows dawn has broken though a barrier blocks his eye, the fast becomes binding once knowledge is obtained that its cause — the moon's separation from the sun after conjunction — has occurred, whatever bars sight: light, cloud, dust, or mountain.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author argues that the sun's light is itself merely a barrier like cloud or a wall — proven by stars becoming visible during a solar eclipse — so the crescent genuinely exists after separation even when unseen, and the soul is not barred from seeing it as it truly is.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Against the opponents' principle that a man knows nothing until his sight falls upon it, the author raises three refutations: they affirm Allah whom they have not seen; they judge the world originated in time by proof not sight; and they permit breaking the fast after thirty days without sighting the crescent — each forcing them back to the vision of knowledge.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Since the soul receives and retains the image of a sensed thing at first apprehension and thereafter needs no second sensing, and since the crescent's shape, color, thinness and thickness are no condition of the fast, what is sought in 'seeking the crescent' is knowledge that it now lies west before the sun — a fact grasped by the soul, not by sight, which apprehends only shapes and colors.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author argues from the Arabic letter lam in 'li-ru'yatihi' — parallel to 'set this in order for so-and-so's arrival' and 'work for the Hereafter' — that the act must precede that for which it is done, so the hadith means the community should already be fasting when the crescent is sighted.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: To the objection that the lam in 'Establish the prayer at the declining of the sun' does not require the prayer to precede the declining, the author replies with a geometric figure distinguishing point ب, the true declining seen by the soul, from point ج, the later sensible declining — so that here too the worshipper is already praying when sense perceives the shadow turn.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author notes that eyesight errs about things as they truly are — seeing large as small, thin as thick — whereas the seeing of knowledge scarcely errs, so the people of the true call have taken hold of the non-erring instrument.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: To the final objection that the Prophet's 'If it is obscured from you, then count thirty days' requires eye-sighting, the author begins by reasserting that the vision of the soul has been established as the nobler of the two.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author holds that both sightings — the hidden vision of the soul (knowledge) and the sighting of the eye — are valid foundations for discharging obligatory duties, but the vision of the soul is the more excellent and belongs to the possessors of knowledge, while the eye's sighting belongs to the generality, who must follow the learned, the relation between them being like the first and second times of a prayer.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author generalizes that every matter is either hidden (known only to the select) or apparent (known to select and common alike), and each group is bound to act on what it knows — as with the one at the pre-dawn meal who knows dawn has broken while the ignorant must follow the learned.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: Against reading 'if it is obscured from you, count thirty days' as referring to eye-sighting, the author argues that eye-sighting yields months of twenty-nine days, so that reading would have the Prophet binding his community to a doubtful rule that adds or subtracts an obligation, contradicting the Quranic demand for sincerity in worship ('they were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion').
entities: فإن غم عليكم فعدوا ثلاثين يوماً

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author concludes that the Prophet's fixing the month at the full count without deficiency points instead to the vision of the soul, whose numbers neither increase nor decrease, in line with 'and that you may complete the count.'

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author objects that eye-sighting makes the fast differ between regions — cloud in Kirman versus clear sky in Shiraz — whereas, just as a prayer's time binds the whole community once it arrives regardless of individuals, so the fast's time binds the community as one.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: A second argument: counting thirty requires knowing a month's first day, yet crescents are often unseen in turbid regions like Tabaristan, the mountains, coasts and islands, so the eye-reading would make the Prophet burden his community beyond capacity, contrary to 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity' — hence either the report is unsound or must be read as the vision of the soul.
entities: لا يكلف الله نفسا إلا وسعها

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author argues from the other pillars — prayer, zakat, Hajj, jihad, all entrusted to the Imam standing in the place of the Messenger, with the community bound to follow and not to advance or delay — that it is inadmissible for the fast alone to be left to the community's own ijtihad, which he calls presumption against Allah.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: To the objection that on the conjunction-and-separation principle a single day would be part Shaban and part Ramadan, the author answers with a doctrine of two causes for every obligation — a preceding general cause and a second specific cause that fixes its time (day/declining sun; wealth/passing year; ability/the greatest day at Mecca; opposition/the commanding head) — so that fasting's general cause is the moon's separation from the sun and its specific cause is the dawn that follows.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author presents an interpretive correspondence in which the sun — noblest and most luminous body, source of light, cause of growth and of all causes — indicates the rank of the Prophet/Speaker, and the moon — below the sun, receiving most of its light, giving light in darkness, intermediary in generation — indicates the rank of the Foundation (الأساس), who receives from the Speaker and expounds his sealed symbols and parables to the community.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The moon's successive states are read as stages of the Foundation's affair: illumination at conjunction as the Prophet's instruction of the Foundation ('I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate'), hiddenness beneath the sun's light as his rank known only to the elect, the crescent's appearance as the explicit designation near the Prophet's death, absence of moonlight by day as his having no affair during the Speaker's life, initial faintness and dispute over sighting as the disagreement over his Imamate, and fullness at fourteen days as his Imamate's universal recognition at the passing of the seven repetitions at the cycle's end.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: Ramadan, noblest of months, is taken to stand for the Foundation, and the author reads 'the month of Ramadan in which the Quran was sent down' interpretively — since the Quran descended over twenty-three years, not all in Ramadan — while 'whoever witnesses the month, let him fast it' is read as the command to attend the Foundation's assembly in silence, with the sick-or-traveling exception covering the doubter or learner who speaks to gain benefit.
entities: شهر رمضان الذي أنزل فيه القرآن
لا ترفعوا أصواتكم فوق صوت النبي

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: As a worked case the author defends the people of truth's entering the Ramadan fast of the year 400 two days before the eye-sighting: conjunction fell on Monday night, the moon stood only about six degrees from the sun at sunset (beneath the ray, invisible), the Shawwal conjunction fell Wednesday night making Wednesday the festival, so breaking earlier would have left only twenty-nine days — whereas 'Shaban is never complete and Ramadan never deficient' and 'the day of your fasting is the day of your sacrifice,' the sacrifice at Mecca having fallen on Monday.
entities: ما تم شعبان ولا نقص رمضان

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: Answering the charge that this reasoning is the forbidden science of the stars, the author replies that it would be an unjust division (قسمة ضيزى) to permit astronomical determination of the qibla and prayer times but forbid it for the fast, and that the prohibition applies only to one who takes up astronomy before the divine and revealed sciences and so falls into the position of Ptolemy's followers and those who deify the heavenly bodies — whereas after the religious sciences it increases certainty in Allah's oneness, as the Quran's oaths by the stars attest.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The treatise closes by concluding that the Prophet's ل in 'لرؤيته' means the sighting of knowledge — requiring that the people already be fasting when the crescent is seen by eye — and seals with praise, prayer upon Muhammad, Ali, the pure Imams as 'moons amid the darkness,' and upon the Imam of the age al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, affirming that knowledge descends and obedience ascends, meeting in the one whom Allah appoints.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: Quoting some noble books, the author reports the teaching that faith has eight levels, the first of which is charity toward parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is a relative, the neighbor nearby, the companion at one's side, the traveler, and those whom one's faith obligates one to care for — a list established in the Book of God.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The same source asserts that whoever undertakes the worship of God and the call of the People of the House without knowledge and without action cannot bear the name of faith, and has no bond with God nor covenant or honor with His guardian, because he has departed from it.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The author announces that he will next distinguish faith (iman) from Islam, setting out what each encompasses and what lies beyond them.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: Reporting from the fourth of the Mustansiriyya Councils (the Councils of Exposition and of Wisdom), the author states that the Imams of religion are seven, recurring in the world as the days of the week recur until the rising of the Qa'im, while the twelve proofs (hujjas) are spread throughout the world — and that this constitutes knowledge of the sum of the limits of the testimony.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The author interprets that saying to mean the limits of testimony only, and holds that fulfilling the rights owed to those limits consists of seven obligations of religion — guardianship, purity, prayer, almsgiving, fasting, pilgrimage and struggle — corresponding to the seven Imams.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: Corresponding to the twelve proofs are twelve incumbent practices: honoring parents, maintaining kinship ties, protecting the neighbor, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, truthfulness in one's home, good conduct with one's spouse, kindness to dependents, spreading the greeting of peace, feeding others, keeping the bond among the brethren, and visiting the sick.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: The Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, in a Friday sermon, likened himself in the physical world to the Pen in the spiritual world, setting four ranks beneath it, each preceded by a spiritual rank guiding it upward, so that the foundation faces the tablet and engraves upon it what it derives from the spiritual world.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: 'Ali answers that what is not God's is a partner, what is not with God is injustice, and what God does not know is that the Messiah is God's son — citing 'Do you inform God of what He does not know?' — since the nonexistent has no object of divine knowledge; the questioner then professes Islam and 'Ali's walaya, and 'Ali has al-Hasan and al-Husayn distribute the money to the Muslims.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: The Syrian testifies that al-Hasan is the son of the Messenger of God and that 'Ali is Muhammad's guardian with more right to the affair than Mu'awiya; and Ibn al-Asfar, on receiving the answers, tells Mu'awiya they come only from the mine of prophecy and the seat of the message, not from him, and refuses him even a dirham.

retained.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
retained.text: The author, citing the twenty-third of the Mustansiriya councils, states that the revelation of peace divides into seven sections from above (from God and His angels) and twelve sections from below (those coming from human beings).

retained.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
retained.text: The author interprets 'Ya Sin' as our Prophet Muhammad and 'the family of Ya Sin' as the family of Muhammad, the family of Ali, so that the seventh Qur'anic peace is addressed to the Imams of the Prophet's house.

retained.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
retained.text: Citing the twenty-fourth assembly, the author holds that the offering of peace is an obligatory Sunnah of Islam expressing affection and submission, and that al-Salam is one of the names of God, possessed of majesty and honor.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: Al-Muizz li Din Allah, in his Sunday supplication, sets out a descending order of ranks: beneath the Foundation (al-Asas) the Terminus (al-Mutimm) facing Israfil, beneath the Terminus the After (al-Lahiq) facing Michael, and beneath the After the Wing (al-Janah) facing Gabriel.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: Al-Muizz holds that these three (the Grandfather/al-Jadd, the Opener/al-Fath, and the Imagination/al-Khayal — i.e. Israfil, Michael, Gabriel) transmit to the respondents from the Speaker and the Foundation in the bodily world, just as three transmit from the two roots, the Pen and the Tablet, in the spiritual world.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: In his Friday supplication al-Muizz enumerates seven hudud — the Speaker, the Foundation, the Terminus, the After, the Wing, the Authorized (al-Madhun) and the Respondent (al-Mustajib) — together with twelve proofs ranked across twelve regions, which the author correlates with the Quranic 'over it are nineteen'.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: Ali prohibits both exaggeration and falling short concerning the Imams: believers must say the Imams are servants under a Lord, though they may say whatever they wish of their excellence — and he adds that the exaggerator will return to them and they themselves will raise up the one who falls short.

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: The Mustansiriya councils (seventeenth) place righteousness toward parents as the first of the twelve practices corresponding to the letters of the testimony, after the seven obligatory rights corresponding to its seven clauses.

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: Righteousness toward parents (eighteenth council) has seven obligatory parts and twelve manners, and extends to four levels: the bodily parents who caused his physical form, the two parents in religion who cause his form in knowledge (the Imam of the age and his proof), the two fathers of the community (the Prophet and the legatee, per the report 'I and you, O Ali, are the two fathers of this community,' and the Imams from their progeny), and finally righteousness toward one's own soul.

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: The twenty-fourth council names three obligatory rights God will not accept unless discharged in full: the right of God (to leave what He forbade and enter what He commanded), the right of parents (thankfulness for what has passed and obedience in what remains), and the right of the child (to be raised with tenderness, nourished, and taught the Book and wisdom); Ali adds that whoever goes against his parents has been undutiful to them.

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: The nineteenth council divides a person's relatives into twelve categories (children; full brothers al-ashqa'; half-brothers by another mother banu al-'allat; half-brothers by the mother al-akhyaf; paternal grandfathers and grandmothers; maternal grandfathers and grandmothers; paternal uncles and aunts; maternal uncles and aunts), with anyone related through one of these taking that one's ruling, and requires keeping the tie, giving, drawing near, and loving even when the relatives cut off, withhold, push away, and abandon — and Ali adds that no oath binds in the severing of kinship.

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: The twentieth council divides safeguarding the neighbor (per the verse on the neighbor who is kin, the neighbor who is a stranger, and the companion at your side) into seven ranks — the believing kin-neighbor with three rights (neighborliness, kinship, faith); the kin-neighbor without faith with two; the believing stranger-neighbor with neighborliness and faith; the companion at your side who differs in religion with the right of neighborliness; the companion aboard the ship with the right of nearness; the sharer of one's litter; and the one who sits with you to receive wisdom, whose sanctity is the most binding and whose claim is most obligatory.

retained.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
retained.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred maxims are cited for rules on study: no daylong silence except in remembrance of God, no reverting to desert life after the migration, and no recitation of the Quran while ritually impure until one purifies oneself.

retained.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
retained.text: The obligatory knowledge no believer may lack is enumerated as: knowledge of God's oneness and His transcendence above likeness (tashbih), above the stripping of attributes (tatil), and above nonexistence; acknowledgment of all messengers and their delivery of the message; acknowledgment of Muhammad as Seal of the Prophets and all he brought; acknowledgment of the Imams of his progeny whom God commanded be taken as guardians and to whom questions must be referred; and recognition of the Imam of the age, belief in his Imamate and walaya, submission to his command, and taking knowledge from him.

retained.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
retained.text: This obligation rests on the doctrine that God has never left the earth without a proof (hujja) against His servants and an Imam calling them to obedience, supported by 'Obey God, obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you,' 'On the day We shall call every people by their Imam,' 'You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide,' and 'Ask the people of remembrance if you do not know'; and a believer's degree is raised in proportion to what he knows after acknowledgment.

retained.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
retained.text: The Trusted of the Imam, the Banner of Islam, in the fifth council of Majalis al-Bayan and Majalis al-Hikma (the Councils of al-Mustansiriyya), teaches that each of the seven obligations of Islam itself contains seven obligations and twelve practices, mirroring the honored number nineteen formed from the testimony's seven and twelve letters.

retained.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
retained.text: Walaya is the first and most excellent of the obligations, and in every allusion made by these numbers the ranking of the friends of God is the utmost aim and intention.

retained.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
retained.text: Purity follows walaya in rank, and its lesser purity (ablution) has seven obligations: pure water, intention, washing the face, washing the hands, wiping the head, wiping the feet, and order — beginning with what God began by mentioning.

retained.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
retained.text: The greater purity — washing of the whole body — likewise has seven obligations: washing from janabah, from menstruation, of the unbeliever entering Islam, of one recovering from unconsciousness, from the blood of nifas, after immersion in impurity, and of the dead, which is an obligation upon the living until one of them performs it.

retained.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
retained.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl in al-Risalah al-Maknunah divides purity and filth into two kinds: outward purity is achieved by outward water, cleansing the outward filth of urine and excrement, while inward purity is achieved by inward water — which is knowledge — cleansing the inward filth of doubt and ignorance.

retained.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
retained.text: The same author reads the seven acts of wudhu as seven bounds — three Sunnah (rinsing the mouth, drawing in water, istinja), two washings and two wipings, one of each bounded and one unbounded — and interprets the mouth as the sole conveyor of nourishment to the senses, the nostrils as the breath by which the body lives, and the face, with its seven openings, as bearing the meaning of the Speaker, since as a person is known by his face so no one is known except through his prophet and there is no deliverance except by turning toward him.

retained.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
retained.text: The author of al-Risala al-Maknuna grounds the ghusl in Quran 'and if you are junub, purify yourselves' and the Prophetic saying 'beneath every hair there is janabah,' and defines junub etymologically as 'the one far from a thing,' concluding that the obedience of one in janabah is void and false.

retained.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
retained.text: The section closes by interpreting Ali's saying 'whomever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him' esoterically: water purifies and is not itself purified, and so likewise is the knowledge of the Imam — whomever it does not purify, God does not purify.

retained.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
retained.text: The reported norms are that the least of menstruation is three days, the least of purity is ten days, and the most of menstruation is ten days; if bleeding exceeds ten days the woman is a mustahadah, distinguished by the fact that menstrual blood is thick and turbid while istihadah blood is thin.

retained.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
retained.text: The author himself concludes decisively that the postpartum woman is pure once clean of blood after twenty days, thereafter relying on her custom, and that if blood exceeds her custom she judges by whether it has changed — changed blood being istihadah, unchanged blood keeping the original ruling.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: The author holds that one who abandons the prescribed prayers for a long period without excuse is not counted a Muslim during that period and has no deed accepted — citing the Prophet's 'There is nothing between the servant and disbelief except the abandonment of prayer' and Ali's 'Prayer is the pillar of religion' and 'There is no share in Islam for one who abandons prayer.'

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: Upon sincere repentance (tawbah naṣūḥ, Q 66:8, whose 'you who believe' the author glosses as those affirming the two testimonies) God accepts him, he becomes truly a Muslim with all lawful deeds accepted, and he is not required to make up the prayers missed before repentance — though doing so is rewarded — whereas deliberately broken Ramadan fasts from that period must be made up with expiation.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man ibn Muhammad, in the book of the interpretation of the Sharia, defines the five prayer times as hidden and known only by indications (Dhuhr when a thing's shadow equals its length, 'Asr when double, Maghrib at the setting of the disc, Isha' al-Akhirah at the vanishing of the white twilight, Fajr from daybreak to near sunrise), so that ten things are present each day and night — five outward prayers and five inward times.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: Al-Nu'man further sets prayer's four boundaries, like a house's — the time, the qibla, the wudu, the intention — and its seven obligatory elements: takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, glorification, tashahhud, and the sealing.

retained.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
retained.text: The objection of many common people — that Muhammad may be granted best of humankind but not Ali, since prophets are among humankind — is answered by the author as obstinate and self-refuting, since all Muslims accept that Muhammad's community is 'the best community brought forth for the people' though earlier communities contained prophets.

retained.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
retained.text: Al-Hakim's argument runs: al-Hasan and al-Husayn are masters of the youth of the people of the Garden, the people of the Garden are youths who never age and include Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and the Prophet said their father is better than the two of them — therefore Ali is the best of humankind alongside the Prophet; the preacher then professes belief and al-Hakim tells the dai to give the call as he wishes, since none will oppose him.

retained.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
retained.text: The author answers that even conceding error in both, adder and subtractor are not of equal degree, for four reasons: the subtractor misled vastly more people; he preceded the alleged addition by over four hundred years; he not only subtracted but also added the feeble sentence 'prayer is better than sleep'; and he dropped the Prophet's phrase from all five prayers while attaching his own only to the dawn prayer.

retained.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
retained.text: A hadith of the Prophet cited in the questions states that the earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification except for the bathhouse, the cemetery, and the latrine, and the answer given is that one prays in none of those places at all and builds no mosque beside graves.

retained.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
retained.text: Al-Majalis al-Mustansiriyya grades prayer in seven ranks by place — house (one), market mosque (twelve), tribal mosque (twenty-five), congregational mosque (one hundred), the Farthest Mosque (one thousand), the Mosque of the Messenger (ten thousand), and the Sacred House of God (one hundred thousand).

retained.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
retained.text: A list of twelve disqualifications from leading prayer is given: the sick may not lead the healthy, nor the leper, nor one with white leprosy, nor the madman, nor one on whom a prescribed penalty (hadd) has been carried out, nor the child of adultery, nor a bedouin leading emigrants, nor one in fetters leading the unfettered, nor one who performed dry ablution leading those who used water, nor the mute leading those who speak, nor a traveler leading residents, nor one hostile to the Prophet's household leading those who follow it.

retained.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
retained.text: Precedence in leading prayer is ranked among seven, per Jafar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq: earliest in emigration, then best reciter, then most learned in jurisprudence, then eldest; the owner of a mosque has the better right to his own mosque; and the Imam and whomever the Imam appoints outrank all of them.

retained.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
retained.text: Rank among licensed men governs multiplicity and substitution: two imams are not gathered in one unpartitioned place unless the later is the more excellent; only one granted unrestricted leave may appoint a substitute if his prayer is interrupted; a broken ablution requires appointing a replacement before the imam leaves the mosque or the congregation's prayer is spoiled; and only one whom the summoner designates may step forward to the niche.

retained.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
retained.text: Al-Ikhtisar sets the minimum by which prayer is completed at five limits — opening takbir, standing for whoever is able, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the tashahhud — valid for one who forgets or does not know more, whereas one who knows the limits and deliberately omits an obligation or sunnah has no prayer and must repeat it, and the ignorant person is obliged to learn.

retained.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
retained.text: The Dai Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives a different seven obligations — intention, first takbir, standing, recitation, bowing, prostration, taslim — plus four limits of prayer (place, time, purity, intention), and interprets 'the one who abandons my sunnah is cursed' esoterically as abandoning the Prophet's legatee, adding that the outward prayer itself neither forbids nor commands.

retained.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
retained.text: The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya enumerates seven obligatory prayers (residence, travel, Friday, fear, tawaf of Hajj, tawaf of Umrah, the bier) and twelve sunnah prayers, and in each of the five daily prayers seven obligations and twelve sunnahs, the twelfth being that a prayer lacking a first sitting has a qunut counted in its place while one with two tashahhud sittings has no qunut.

retained.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
retained.text: The seven supplications are distinguished by bodily posture: asking (palms facing the face), seeking refuge (backs of palms facing the face), humble submission (grasping the shoulders, done only in solitude), devotion (pointing with the index finger), entreaty (moving the finger), fervent appeal (both palms spread and raised to the sky), and abasement in the dust (cheeks turned upon the ground).

retained.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
retained.text: The twelve foundations of answered supplication are: sending ahead repentance, charity, a fast, or a prayer (per the verse that to God ascends the good word and the righteous deed raises it); purifying intention; beginning with God's praise; blessing the Prophet at start, middle and end; drawing near through the imams of religion named one by one up to the imam of one's own age; seeking access through him and them; asking the good of this world and the hereafter; seeking refuge from their evil; and finally asking whatever one loves.

retained.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
retained.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in his book on the inward nursing, enumerates fourteen "doors" that are the supporting pillars of prayer and without which it is not complete: ablution, opening, call to prayer, standing call, turning toward God, recitation, bowing, praise, glorification, prostration, testimony, salutation, the supplication of the standing invocation, and the supplication of the odd-numbered prayer.

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: Tawil al-Shariah states that the sermon precedes the two-cycle Friday prayer, is divided in two by a sitting, is distinguished from ordinary noon prayer by the raised voice, and that the call to stand comes after the sermon; it also makes the summoner's assembly parallel to the Friday congregation, so that silence and attentive listening become obligatory once the preacher faces the people.

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl's Hidden Epistle reads Friday esoterically: it points to Muhammad, gate of the Garden, who has an outward summons to the zahir of his law and an inward summons to its interpretation; the two cycles replace four because the sermon substitutes for two, and the sitting within the sermon is the separation between the upper and lower lights with which the Qaim rises.

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: The section reports that tashriq, said to be incumbent only in a congregational city, means the prayer of the two festivals — so named because it is prayed at sunrise and its performer is called al-mushriq — and that the twenty-three magnifications from Arafah to the last day of tashriq are a likeness of the summons of the five speakers of firm resolve corresponding to the five prayers, the ten spiritual and ten bodily ranks, and the speaker of the cycle, his executor, and the Imam of the age.

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: The Hidden Epistle derives fitr from the sense of splitting open, appearing and beginning — as earth, tree and camel's tooth 'break forth' — so that, fasting being silence and concealment as in Maryam's vow of a fast of silence, the breaking of the fast is the day the veiled command and hidden secrets are manifested; and the festival-of-sacrifice sermon uniquely begins with four magnifications rather than praise, signalling that the command appears otherwise than in past cycles.

retained.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
retained.text: The Mustansiriyya councils (ninth council) enumerate seven places of omission in prayer, in six of which the two prostrations of omission are proper — including forgetting a prostration, forgetting the first or second tashahhud, saluting after two rakahs in a four-rakah prayer, and rising to a fifth rakah — while the seventh, inattention behind the Imam, requires none because the Imam bears it for the worshipper.

retained.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
retained.text: The same source divides doubt into twelve cases: in five (doubt about bowing while still praying, or over one/two, two/three, three/four, two/four rakahs) the worshipper builds on what is certain — the lesser — and prostrates for omission; in the remainder, where the doubt arises only after the relevant act has been passed (e.g. doubting the takbir after bowing, or anything after the salaam), nothing at all is due.

retained.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
retained.text: Against the maxim that deeds are accepted only with intentions, the answer given is that the intention resides in the heart and the tongue's utterance is merely verbal expression, as stated in the Pillars, so that an act intended in the heart is complete even if never voiced.
entities: Book of the Pillars of Islam

retained.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
retained.text: The governing rule for the traveler is that he shortens the prayer and breaks the fast from leaving his dwelling until he returns to it, but he prays and fasts in full if he stops for five prayer times with his wife or with a resident blood relative (kin of lineage), while relatives by marriage and by nursing do not produce this effect.

retained.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
retained.text: In the absence of the imam of the age, the right to lead the funeral prayer belongs first to his appointed judge or officeholder, then to the highest in station among those the imam has advanced, then to the appointed prayer leader, and only if none is present to the most entitled guardian.

retained.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
retained.text: In the questions-and-answers collection attributed to our master Idris, the obligations owed from a dead man's estate are ranked in a fixed order of priority: zakat first (because it is a debt and not part of his wealth), then the Hajj, then the khums, then expiation, then al-Shurwa.

retained.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
retained.text: Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inner Nursing, enumerates five zakats paralleling the five prayers: the khums of earnings (which belongs to the Imam), the zakat of already-purified wealth at one dinar in forty (due to the Hujja), the tenth of crops, one head in forty of livestock, and the zakat of the soul — the shurwa redeeming the believer's neck and the fitra of his fast.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: Against the objection that obligatory duties may not be performed outside their appointed times, the answer given is that delivering the fitra to a rightful recipient suffices whenever done, since no fixed time was set for advancing or delaying it — the sole prohibition being that one must not break the fast before delivering it.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: The thirteenth Mustansiriyya session, following on the prior session about zakat owed by the wealthy, presents zakat al-Fitr as the zakat obligatory in every condition and even upon those of small means, comprising seven obligations and twelve Sunnah practices.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: The seven obligations are that a man pay it for himself, for the elder and the younger of his household, the free and the enslaved among them, and the males and the females among them.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: The Sunnah practices include bringing it from the middle sort of what one eats (a sa of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins — half a sa sufficing only for wheat, the sa being four mudds), handing it to the Imam or his appointee, bringing it out before the breaking of the fast, making it up if delayed, and giving its value in silver or gold if one lacks the food; a woman with no husband present pays for herself and her dependants.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad in the Concealed Epistle holds that the Prophet obliged every Muslim head — male, female, small, great, even an infant born that day, and the child in the womb — to pay a sa, and explains that zakat al-Fitr is therefore named 'the charity of the head'.

retained.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
retained.text: The fourteenth Mustansiriyya majlis divides fasting into seven obligatory kinds: Ramadan yearly; two consecutive months for deliberately breaking a fast-day when no slave can be freed; two consecutive months for killing a believer by mistake plus blood money; two months for zihar expiation lacking a slave; three days for breaking an oath lacking feeding, clothing or freeing; ten days for tamattu pilgrimage lacking an offering; and the fast of a vow.

retained.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
retained.text: The same majlis lists twelve fasts of practice and commendation: itikaf, Shaban, the first Thursday, middle Wednesday and last Thursday of each month, the three white days, the fast of Dawud (alternate days, the most rigorous), Friday joined to Thursday or Saturday but never alone, Arafah for the non-pilgrim, the boy's fast at seven, recompense for game taken in the sacred state as ruled by the one entrusted, and the fast for shaving the head due to harm.

retained.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
retained.text: Al-Muayyad fil-Din, in the forty-second of his Wisdom Sessions, refutes those who make fasting depend on sighting the crescent and argues that Ramadan is always complete and never deficient.

retained.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
retained.text: The reply is that the hadith was spoken in answer to companions asking how to act in the Prophet's absence, so sighting is only an emergency rule when neither the Messenger nor the Imam standing in his place is present; when either is present one fasts by his fasting.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: The author writes in response to a brother's request to justify the Shia practice — and specifically the command issued from the Pure Presence in the year 400 requiring the fast to begin two days before the crescent was visible to the eye — against opponents who reproach them for fasting before the general public.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: The author frames the opponents' disagreement not as honest error but as arrogance, envy, and refusal to obey those charged with the Command to whom Quran 4:59 and 4:83 direct disputed matters to be referred.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Because Allah created all things in pairs — and the Prophet made pairing the governing principle of the law (prayer/alms, adhan/iqama, Hajj/Umrah, Safa/Marwa) — sight too must be of two kinds: natural vision and vision of the soul.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Natural vision occurs by the eye and apprehends only colors and shapes; vision of the soul occurs by way of knowledge through heart and soul and apprehends causes hidden from the eye, as in the Quranic 'Have you not seen what your Lord did with the companions of the elephant?' addressed to a Prophet who did not witness that event.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: The author concludes that vision of the soul is prior, more exalted and subtler, and that in discharging Allah's obligations one is bound to take the more excellent instrument, since settling for the lesser when the greater is present is a judgment of ignorance.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: By analogy with the man who knows the prayer time without hearing the adhan, and the man eating before dawn who knows dawn has broken though a barrier blocks his eye, the fast becomes binding once knowledge is obtained that its cause — the moon's separation from the sun after conjunction — has occurred, whatever bars sight: light, cloud, dust, or mountain.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Against the opponents' principle that a man knows nothing until his sight falls upon it, the author raises three refutations: they affirm Allah whom they have not seen; they judge the world originated in time by proof not sight; and they permit breaking the fast after thirty days without sighting the crescent — each forcing them back to the vision of knowledge.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Since the soul receives and retains the image of a sensed thing at first apprehension and thereafter needs no second sensing, and since the crescent's shape, color, thinness and thickness are no condition of the fast, what is sought in 'seeking the crescent' is knowledge that it now lies west before the sun — a fact grasped by the soul, not by sight, which apprehends only shapes and colors.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: The author argues from the Arabic letter lam in 'li-ru'yatihi' — parallel to 'set this in order for so-and-so's arrival' and 'work for the Hereafter' — that the act must precede that for which it is done, so the hadith means the community should already be fasting when the crescent is sighted.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: To the objection that the lam in 'Establish the prayer at the declining of the sun' does not require the prayer to precede the declining, the author replies with a geometric figure distinguishing point ب, the true declining seen by the soul, from point ج, the later sensible declining — so that here too the worshipper is already praying when sense perceives the shadow turn.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author holds that both sightings — the hidden vision of the soul (knowledge) and the sighting of the eye — are valid foundations for discharging obligatory duties, but the vision of the soul is the more excellent and belongs to the possessors of knowledge, while the eye's sighting belongs to the generality, who must follow the learned, the relation between them being like the first and second times of a prayer.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author generalizes that every matter is either hidden (known only to the select) or apparent (known to select and common alike), and each group is bound to act on what it knows — as with the one at the pre-dawn meal who knows dawn has broken while the ignorant must follow the learned.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: Against reading 'if it is obscured from you, count thirty days' as referring to eye-sighting, the author argues that eye-sighting yields months of twenty-nine days, so that reading would have the Prophet binding his community to a doubtful rule that adds or subtracts an obligation, contradicting the Quranic demand for sincerity in worship ('they were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion').
entities: فإن غم عليكم فعدوا ثلاثين يوماً

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author concludes that the Prophet's fixing the month at the full count without deficiency points instead to the vision of the soul, whose numbers neither increase nor decrease, in line with 'and that you may complete the count.'

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: A second argument: counting thirty requires knowing a month's first day, yet crescents are often unseen in turbid regions like Tabaristan, the mountains, coasts and islands, so the eye-reading would make the Prophet burden his community beyond capacity, contrary to 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity' — hence either the report is unsound or must be read as the vision of the soul.
entities: لا يكلف الله نفسا إلا وسعها

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author argues from the other pillars — prayer, zakat, Hajj, jihad, all entrusted to the Imam standing in the place of the Messenger, with the community bound to follow and not to advance or delay — that it is inadmissible for the fast alone to be left to the community's own ijtihad, which he calls presumption against Allah.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: To the objection that on the conjunction-and-separation principle a single day would be part Shaban and part Ramadan, the author answers with a doctrine of two causes for every obligation — a preceding general cause and a second specific cause that fixes its time (day/declining sun; wealth/passing year; ability/the greatest day at Mecca; opposition/the commanding head) — so that fasting's general cause is the moon's separation from the sun and its specific cause is the dawn that follows.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author presents an interpretive correspondence in which the sun — noblest and most luminous body, source of light, cause of growth and of all causes — indicates the rank of the Prophet/Speaker, and the moon — below the sun, receiving most of its light, giving light in darkness, intermediary in generation — indicates the rank of the Foundation (الأساس), who receives from the Speaker and expounds his sealed symbols and parables to the community.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The moon's successive states are read as stages of the Foundation's affair: illumination at conjunction as the Prophet's instruction of the Foundation ('I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate'), hiddenness beneath the sun's light as his rank known only to the elect, the crescent's appearance as the explicit designation near the Prophet's death, absence of moonlight by day as his having no affair during the Speaker's life, initial faintness and dispute over sighting as the disagreement over his Imamate, and fullness at fourteen days as his Imamate's universal recognition at the passing of the seven repetitions at the cycle's end.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: Ramadan, noblest of months, is taken to stand for the Foundation, and the author reads 'the month of Ramadan in which the Quran was sent down' interpretively — since the Quran descended over twenty-three years, not all in Ramadan — while 'whoever witnesses the month, let him fast it' is read as the command to attend the Foundation's assembly in silence, with the sick-or-traveling exception covering the doubter or learner who speaks to gain benefit.
entities: شهر رمضان الذي أنزل فيه القرآن
لا ترفعوا أصواتكم فوق صوت النبي

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: Answering the charge that this reasoning is the forbidden science of the stars, the author replies that it would be an unjust division (قسمة ضيزى) to permit astronomical determination of the qibla and prayer times but forbid it for the fast, and that the prohibition applies only to one who takes up astronomy before the divine and revealed sciences and so falls into the position of Ptolemy's followers and those who deify the heavenly bodies — whereas after the religious sciences it increases certainty in Allah's oneness, as the Quran's oaths by the stars attest.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The treatise closes by concluding that the Prophet's ل in 'لرؤيته' means the sighting of knowledge — requiring that the people already be fasting when the crescent is seen by eye — and seals with praise, prayer upon Muhammad, Ali, the pure Imams as 'moons amid the darkness,' and upon the Imam of the age al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, affirming that knowledge descends and obedience ascends, meeting in the one whom Allah appoints.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The book is titled Isʿaf al-Talib fi Jamiʿ al-Matalib (The Student's Aid in All Demands), begun on 7 Rajab in the year 1051 of the Prophetic migration.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author wrote at the repeated request of a patron, to gather into one place what is scattered across the books of the saints and their callers — the paired and authoritative books, the brief abridgements on Sharia matters, and expansive treatments of juristic paths and legal opinions — so that these paths become easier to travel.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The work is situated in the Tayyibi Ismaili dawa, dedicated to the caller Jafar ibn Sulayman ibn al-Hasan ibn Yusuf ibn Sulayman and his successor the caller Muhammad ibn al-Fahd, in service to the Imam al-Tayyib.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author disclaims originality: whatever is correct in the book derives from the guardian of his favor and his successor, while every slip or error is his own shortcoming.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author states as a qualification that these twelve practices are not obligatory upon women.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author cites 'Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts to the effect that the Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects and this community will divide into seventy-three, of which one is in the Garden and the rest in the Fire.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: The author cites Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman's Book of the Foster-Suckling, which reads 'the righteous of the believers' in Q 66:4 as designating 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Imam of every believing man and woman.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: On the same authority, Qur'anic uses of 'righteous' — 'their father was righteous' and 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' — are interpreted as referring to an Imam and to the Imams among God's servants.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: In an account from Uns al-Afidah al-Muniba, a messenger of the king of Rum brings money to Medina to test the Prophet's successor with three questions: what is not God's, what is not with God, and what God does not know.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: Abu Bakr and 'Umar each fail to answer and instead accuse the questioner of disbelief, which 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas criticises for not even admitting ignorance, before directing the group to 'Ali.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: In a report from Abu al-Jarud via al-Harith al-Awar, a Syrian sent secretly by Mu'awiya brings eleven questions originally posed by Ibn al-Asfar (the Byzantine ruler), who promised to follow and pay tribute to whoever could answer them.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: 'Ali first detects the stranger's foreignness, grants him safety on the principle that 'when war lays down its burdens there is no harm,' and denounces Mu'awiya and the community that severed his kinship, denied his right and diminished his station.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: 'Ali defers the questioning to his sons, presenting al-Hasan and al-Husayn as the sons of the Messenger of God and Muhammad (ibn al-Hanafiyya) as his own son, and the Syrian chooses al-Hasan.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: Al-Hasan answers all eleven questions — truth and falsehood are four fingers apart (the eye sees truth, the ear hears much falsehood); heaven and earth are separated by the oppressed one's prayer and the reach of sight; east and west by the sun's day-course; the galaxy is the lamps of heaven from which rain descends; the rainbow is God's bow and safeguard from drowning; the moon's darkening is God's erasure of the night's sign per Q 17:12; the first thing to appear on earth was the valley of Dab and the first to stir the palm tree; the polytheists' souls flee to a spring called Salma; the hermaphrodite is identified by emission, menstruation or breasts, else by how the urine strikes a wall; and the ten ascending strengths run stone, iron, fire, water, cloud, wind, angel, Angel of Death, death, and the command of God.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: In a further report, 'Ali resolves four of 'Umar's unanswered puzzles: dreams seen while the soul is loosened from the body (per Q 39:42) are true visions of the kingdom while those seen as it returns are Satan's delusion; instinctive love or hatred stems from souls meeting and scenting one another in the air two thousand years before the bodies; and forgetting and recalling are caused by a film over the heart like the film of the moon — after which 'Umar affirms his truthfulness and prays not to outlive him.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The seven higher instances are enumerated in descending order of exaltedness: God's 'Peace be upon you'; 'O Noah, descend in peace from Us'; 'Their greeting on the day they meet Him is peace'; 'they will be met therein with greeting and peace'; the angels' entry saying 'peace be upon you'; the command that believers pray for the Prophet and submit; and 'Peace be upon the family of Ya Sin'.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: Of the twelve human greetings, the first four are named as: the greeting of the people of the right hand to the Prophet and his noble family ('Peace be upon you for your patience'); the greeting on entering houses/the mosque; the peace concluding the ritual prayer; and the believer's 'peace' answer when the ignorant address him.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The fifth through ninth divisions set an order of precedence in initiating the greeting: the camel rider greets the horse rider, the horse rider the donkey rider, the donkey rider the walker, the walker the one standing, and the one standing initiates and then returns it.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The author distinguishes three kinds of reply to a greeting: the virtuous reply (better than what was offered), the complete reply (in kind), grounded in 'return it with something better, or return it as it is', and the just reply.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The just reply is reserved for dhimmis, who do not initiate the greeting; if one does, the answer is 'And upon you', because some were reported to say 'al-sam alaykum' ('death be upon you') instead of 'al-salam alaykum', so that whoever said good receives its like and whoever said evil receives its like.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The author cites al-Muizz li-Din Allah's Sunday prayer naming the five lower borders — the spokesman, the foundation, the culmination, the successor, and the wing — and his Saturday prayer over the seven days and twelve months.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: Prayers of the saints of the religion are reported invoking blessings on the seven proclaimers, seven culminations, seven caliphs and twelve successors, together with their gates, proofs, and preachers, and on the Imams of Muhammad's station and the proofs of their ages.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: From the Four Hundred Counsels of Amir al-Muminin the author reports the command to return a greeting better or in kind, to shake hands with an enemy even if he dislikes it on the authority of 'Repel with that which is better', and to answer 'May God greet you with peace' with 'You are the peace of God, and the finest of abodes and stations'.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: Citing the questions of Shaykh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi answered by Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris, the author records the ruling that peace to sheikhs and teachers should be proclaimed aloud rather than by the Indian custom of bowing, that is better.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The same source rules that audibility in returning a greeting and in blessing a sneezer is a courtesy and not an obligation, with no fault in omitting it — except that returning a greeting in general remains required, whether aloud or silently.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Jafar bin Mansour al-Yemen, in the book of the Esoteric Nursing, interprets the Quranic verse 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' as referring to the Imams among God's servants.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: On the same authority, 'those who were made weak in the land' whom God will make Imams and heirs means the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib, weakened in the person of Ali himself, who is the proof of Muhammad and whose likeness is the earth.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's supplication of victory and awe invokes numbered ranks — the six transmitted, the seven beheld, the nine signs, the ten words, the twenty-one, the eight who encircle the Throne, the eleven who prostrate and the twelve counted ones who bow.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: In his Four Hundred Manners Ali names seven Imams, seven successors, seven witnesses and seven substitutes, and declares that whoever holds fast to them joins the truth while whoever holds to another way is undone.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Muhammad bin Tahir, in a supplication, seeks nearness to God through the Imams' gates, proofs, preachers, authorized ones, the respondents of their cycles, and all who incline toward, shelter in, follow or are guided by them.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Ali's commandment to those who love the Imams requires doing their work with God-fearing restraint, not sitting with those who revile them, and not praising them openly before the enemy — so that love of them be plain and hatred of them concealed — together with truthfulness, patience, and not burdening the Imams with intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Further maxims from the Four Hundred Manners: beware disputation, for it bequeaths doubt; reckon speech as part of deeds; hasten to good works and let most speech be remembrance of God; sins withhold provision; the best deed of the believer is awaiting the relief; and blessed is he admonished by another's case.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: The nineteenth of the Mustansiriya councils teaches that the kinship God commands to be joined contains a seven and a twelve, the seven being the Imams of the religion indicated by 'I ask you no reward except affection toward my kin', recurring like the days of Friday.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred manners, forbids despising weak believers (saying God belittles and detests whoever despises a believer, and will not bring the two together on the Day of Resurrection unless he repents), forbids making a brother ask when his need is already known, and commands mutual visiting, tenderness, and giving, warning against being like the hypocrite who describes what he does not do.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Ali teaches that the Muslim is the mirror of his Muslim brother: on seeing a brother's slip one must not band together against him but guide, counsel, and treat him gently, and must avoid discord, which leads a person away from the path.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Ali forbids backbiting, citing the Qur'anic rebuke about eating the flesh of one's dead brother, and commands that believers meeting one another shake hands and show a bright face, so that by parting their burdens have lifted.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: In a reported question-and-answer, Shaykh Shimon bin Muhammad al-Ghuri al-Hindi asked whether the Indian custom of asking neighbors for water, salt, or food (when one could afford to buy but lacks them at the moment) is permitted, and Sayyidina Hassan bin Idris (Badr al-Din) answered that there is no harm in it, since it belongs to the purity of affection and the excellence of brotherhood.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: The author notes that in both Qur'anic verses enjoining goodness toward parents, God commands goodness to both yet credits the child's account with the mother's deed alone (carrying him in hardship, in weakness upon weakness), so the one God distinguishes by mention must be distinguished with honor and righteousness.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Righteousness toward one's own soul, the seal of this righteousness, consists in making the truth plain to the soul and establishing it there, magnifying it so as to awaken longing, placing fear in it, dealing gently with it, delivering it from what would destroy it, and rescuing it from what has bound it.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: The twelve manners toward parents include honoring their dwelling, rising for them, answering their call, lowering the voice, not rebuking them, lowering the wing of humility, not walking ahead of them in light or darkness, never opposing their command or saying a word of complaint, desiring life for them in old age as they desired it for him in childhood, and providing for their needs as they provided for his.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Twelve manners of neighborliness are enumerated — not peering into the neighbor's house, not listening in on his speech, not disclosing what one learns of him, not letting him hear or see what he would hate, not withholding a household implement when asked, not acting haughtily when of higher station, not envying him when he is above, helping when he seeks help, covering his 'awrah if exposed, causing him no injury, and bearing his injury with patience — these being the deeds of a people whose hearts God has tested for piety.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Ali is cited warning believers not to let the Murjiah prevail over them with their opinion, marking certain schools as sources whose word must be refused.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: In a question from Shaykh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi answered by Sayyidina Hasan ibn Idris ibn al-Hasan ibn Abdullah al-Anf, it is asked — citing Hamid al-Din's al-Hadi wal-Mustahdi, al-Numan's al-Daaim, and Idris ibn al-Hasan's Zahr al-Maani — whether al-Sadiq's concealed license to al-Shafii later lapsed as with al-Mughirah and Abu al-Khattab, or whether the ignorant merely invented his school as factions falsely claimed the Imamate for Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and Abdullah ibn Muawiyah.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: The answer given is that al-Sadiq had granted al-Shafii license solely because of his acknowledgment of the excellence of the Ahl al-Bayt, and for no other reason.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Asked how the Prophet's saying that whoever looks into his brother's book without permission is as one looking into the Fire squares with members of a school freely consulting each other's books, the answer distinguishes the book of inner truth (haqiqa), which may be opened only by permission of the one who granted access, from all other books, where the rule is mere good manners and not binding.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: A borrower who finds a Quran or other book damaged and disordered may correct and set it right without the owner's permission — there is no harm in doing so, but it is not obligatory upon him.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Books of the dawah belonging to a deceased man may not be used to settle his debts, because they belong to the dawah and are not inherited.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Those granted license (al-mafsuhin) may read the benefits of religion to women in a mixed gathering only if a screen stands between them so she hears without being seen, and no man may be alone with a woman unless another woman is with her or another man is with him.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Analogy in religion is prohibited outright: Ali is cited that the religion cannot be measured by analogy, that a people will come who do so and they are its enemies, and that the first to reason by analogy was Iblis.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan in Mafatih al-Nimah cites al-Sadiq distinguishing referring an obscure teaching back TO the Imams — so they may establish its proof and disclose its interpretation (tawil) — from throwing it back AT them by calling it false and turning away, the latter being forbidden.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: The duty of concealment and precaution is affirmed by Ali's maxim that whoever divulges the secret of the Imams, God will give him the cold of iron to taste.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: A Question-and-Answer book arranged on the order of the doors of Daaim al-Islam, containing questions from teachers of the Indian lands and answers from the summoners (duat) of the Yemeni lands, is cited as an authority on purity.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Asked whether the prohibition on urinating beneath fruit-bearing trees means trees actually bearing fruit or trees whose property it is to bear fruit, the Yemeni respondents answer that it covers both.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Though the dawah books forbid greeting or speaking to one in a state of hadath, the answer given is that once he has risen from that place (having cleansed himself with a stone or otherwise) he may be greeted, must return the greeting, and may speak.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Reusing a stone or clod of earth used for cleansing after urination is permitted once it has dried, provided no impurity and no moisture are evident upon it.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf lists the nullifiers of ablution as sleep, whatever issues from the front or rear passage (including a stone or wind), an enema, fainting, insanity, and the disappearance of the glans into the front passage of a living or dead person.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Tawil al-Daaim reports that one who interrupts his ablution may build upon what he has already done, so long as the water has not dried upon the limbs already washed; and Mukhtasar al-Musannaf holds that one whose hands are amputated above the elbows is relieved of the obligation to wash them.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: The twelve practices (sunan) of ablution are istinja, washing the hands before entering the vessel, pronouncing God's name on sitting down, rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose, moving the ring, combing water through the beard, wetting the eyes, giving the right precedence over the left, wiping the inner and outer ears, the second and third washings of the face (the first being the obligation), and the siwak.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: The twelve practices of the greater purity are the washings of Friday, of Eid al-Fitr, of Eid al-Adha, for ihram, for entering the Haram, the Kabah, and Madinah, on the day of Arafah, on the nights of the nineteenth, twenty-first and twenty-third of Ramadan, and after washing the dead.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred maxims of conduct, commands cleansing with water from foul odor, prescribes invocations on entering the privy and on looking at what has passed, and states that when sleep mingles with the heart ablution becomes obligatory.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The book of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of Daaim al-Islam rules that one who prayed while a known impurity was upon him — having forgotten the istinja — must repeat the prayer, since prayer is not permitted while a man carries an impurity of which he knows until he washes it away.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The same source distinguishes obligation from excellence: the Imams' concealment of themselves in water was mentioned for the excellence of good manners, so a man who uncovers himself where no one sees him commits no harm and prays validly with that purity, though concealment is better.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah lists twelve manners of the wudhu governing the privy — entering with sandals, advancing the left foot, covering the head, not facing or turning the back to the qiblah, concealing oneself, leaning on the left leg, not sitting long, not cleansing with human excrement or worn bone or animal droppings but with three fresh stones, cleansing with the left hand, not pouring water on excrement, not speaking, and advancing the right foot on leaving.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The section holds, on the authority of the Prophet, that prayer is not valid or accepted without ablution and purification, and reports his forbidding urination in burrows because they are the lairs of serpents and snakes.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Manners is cited for rinsing the mouth and drawing water into the nose as Sunnah purification, istinja with cold water cutting off piles, ablution after purification earning ten good deeds, the formula 'In the name of God — make me among those who repent and purify themselves' said before touching water, concealing oneself because Satan covets the uncovered man, not baring the thigh before a company, and washing children's hands of food-grease lest Satan smell it and harm the two recording angels.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
