dropped.text: A key distinction is drawn between acts that are Sunnah and acts that are obligatory for another reason: rinsing the mouth, drawing in water and istinja are Sunnah practices not to be deliberately abandoned, and omitting them does not spoil the prayer — yet the istinja remains obligatory insofar as the removal of impurity is itself obligatory.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Rulings of accommodation are given for the injured and incapacitated: one with a wound or boil that water cannot touch wipes over the bandages, and performs tayammum if removal would harm him through cold or severe injury or if he is sick; in the greater purification he pours water in a stream, and performs tayammum if he fears for himself, whether traveling or at home; and a man whose hands are cut off has the wudhu performed for him by his bondmaid or wife, failing which he performs tayammum and prays.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: On water, the answers hold that water above the Shariah-stated measure which overpowers impurity remains valid for purification, whereas water in a vessel in which an impurity has become apparent becomes impure and is not made valid by pouring more water in a stream unless it rises above the measure after the vessel is purified; a pool eight cubits in length and breadth, even a span deep, is valid; rainwater running with filth into a great pool is valid so long as color, taste and smell are unchanged; and used water and used dust may be used for purification once and many times.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The saying 'Whoever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him' is interpreted esoterically: water purifies and is not itself purified, and likewise the knowledge of the Imam — whomever it does not purify, nothing else will purify him.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Majalis al-Bayan enumerates the seven obligations of wudhu (pure water, intention, washing face, washing hands, wiping head, wiping feet, and the order in which God mentioned them), its twelve Sunnah acts, the seven obligatory forms of ghusl (including washing the dead as a collective obligation on the living), the twelve Sunnah forms of ghusl, and the twelve places where prayer is disliked.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The section closes with Ali's ruling that there is no dissimulation (taqiyyah) permitted in the drinking of intoxicants or in wiping over the socks, consistent with Tawil al-Shariah's report that the Prophet forbade wiping over the socks and forbade abandoning the audible saying of the basmalah.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: The answers given hold that one who fears harm from water — whether resident or traveler, weak or sick — performs tayammum and prays, and is NOT required to repeat the prayer later, contrary to the ruling in certain Shariah books that he must wash and repeat it.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: The esoteric interpretation given is that the washing from janabah is a likeness of the removal of doubt, since marital relations are a likeness of imparting and receiving, and doubt arises precisely at the moment of imparting and receiving.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Doubt itself triggers obligation: one who revives from unconsciousness not knowing his condition, and one who wakes finding traces of semen without recalling an emission, must perform the ghusl.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: The one in janabah, the menstruating woman and the woman in post-natal bleeding are ruled alike: it is better that they leave off removing hair or nail until purified, and neither may deliberately recite the Quran, nor Quranic matter within supplications or books, nor the basmalah with the intention of Quranic recitation.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Procedural rulings from Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: one who forgets the ablution until after the ghusl simply performs it with no penalty; and if minor impurity occurs mid-ghusl, he completes the ghusl and performs the ablution afterward for prayer.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Yemeni summoners answering Indian dignitaries ruled that when water suffices for only one of a living junub and a corpse, the living one in janabah performs the ghusl and tayammum is performed for the deceased.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his Four Hundred Manners, forbids the Muslim to sleep while junub or without purity, prescribing tayammum with earth if no water is found, because the believer's spirit ascends to God who receives and blesses it — keeping it in the finest form if its term has come, or returning it by trusted angels if not.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: On material purity the answers hold: vomit does not render impure what it falls upon (though washing is better); ground is pure once the impurity's substance and smell are gone, since sun and light purify it, unless it is ground set aside as a privy; and a small amount of impurity — wet hair, the produce of filth-eating animals — is excused.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Ali's ruling that touching a corpse after it has grown cold necessitates ghusl is interpreted to mean 'after it has become impure' — the corpse's moisture transmits impurity to the living — while the corpse-washer's own washing is Sunnah.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Garments made by polytheists are pure until the polytheist has worn them or visible impurity appears, per al-Daaim's dispensation; but the answer of the master insists that what polytheists have bleached and washed with soap is not pure except by washing, while cloth merely sprinkled with impure water during weaving and then dried may be prayed in.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Against the common people's claim that a garment large enough that moving one end does not move the other may be prayed upon at its pure portion, the answer rules that prayer upon such a mixed garment is not permitted at all; likewise prayer is not complete without a pure garment, tayammum being prescribed for ritual impurity and never for the impurity of garments.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The section's rulings are taken chiefly from a book of questions and answers that one of its compilers arranged according to the chapter order of Daʿāʾim al-Islām, supplemented by Sharḥ al-Akhbār, Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim, Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf, al-Muntakhaba, and question-sets addressed to Yemeni masters.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: On the siwāk, the answer given is that the tooth-stick is the mainstay and there is no objection to the Indian custom of scraping the tongue afterward with split bamboo, though one should not pick the teeth with a knotted stalk of dried grass, and using the siwāk while in janāba (major ritual impurity) is disliked.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Two definitions of al-rayḥān are reported: Sharḥ al-Akhbār says it is every fragrant plant, with the myrtle (al-ās) singled out by that name; Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim says it means linguistically the tips of any sweet-scented plant when its blossom appears, and is a comprehensive name for fragrant plants, the myrtle being singled out as the most lasting and strongest.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is quoted from his four hundred points of etiquette as saying the siwāk pleases the Lord, sweetens the mouth, and belongs to the sunna.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Tayammum is not permitted to a settled (non-traveling) person except for cause; it is licit for the traveler who is far from water, or who cannot perform ablution before the prayer time lapses, or for whom reaching the water would endanger his person or property.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Tayammum requires dust: on a smooth rock fixed in the ground one may perform it only if dust lies on it, and al-Muntakhaba directs one who finds no earth to beat out felts and garments and use that dust even if nothing is seen to fly up.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: A series of traveler's cases is resolved: tayammum suffices for both prayer and fast for one who forgot the ghusl; one who fears illness from ablution performs tayammum; the dead on a journey are given tayammum; prayer with tayammum is valid both in its time and as a make-up; a junub imam who performs tayammum leads only those who have likewise performed it; scarce water goes first to washing an impure garment; and a new convert who finds no water performs tayammum and prays.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Where a deceased person and a person in janāba compete for water enough for one washing, the junub washes himself and the deceased is given tayammum — a ruling repeated in both the question-collection and Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Finding water breaks a tayammum performed for janāba and returns the man to that state, so he must repeat tayammum until enough water for the full washing is available; once he is pure from janāba, remaining water is used for ordinary ablution rather than tayammum.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Al-Nuʿmān's book of purity is cited for the case of a traveler with only a little water: he cleanses himself after relieving himself with stones or the like and then performs the ablution, since the absence of water is itself the cause, and no tayammum is called for.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Tayammum is made valid by intention for oneself: of two men who prayed together, the prayer of the one taught the tayammum was valid while the teacher's prayer, who struck the earth only to instruct, was invalid because he formed no intention for himself.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: A woman who becomes pure from menstruation in Ramadan before sunset and fears harm from the full washing, and a man who has a nocturnal emission and fears illness from washing at night, may each perform tayammum and fast, and neither must make up that day; a traveler's wife who becomes pure and finds no water likewise performs tayammum, after which intercourse is lawful — and a Christian or Zoroastrian wife is to be taught the tayammum by her husband.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: On food, the governing principle is that any liquid in which an animal with flowing blood has died may not be eaten and may not be fed to animals lawful to eat, though soap may be made from it provided the buyer is told of its corruption and the washed garment is afterward rinsed with pure water; and the dung of any animal unlawful to eat is impure, so neem oil pressed from stones passed by crows may not be eaten, sold, or bought.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Small admixtures are tolerated — a little lime chewed with betel, or a little earth in drinking water — unless gross enough to harm the one who takes it.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The food of unbelievers is treated by distinction: their slaughtered animals were forbidden only because they neither pronounce God's name nor turn the animal to the qibla, while their other foodstuffs are lawful in themselves and defiled only by their wet touch — so one must avoid their handiwork where an alternative exists, but in need nothing is forbidden except their slaughtered animals and their moisture.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Corroborating positions are cited: Ḥusayn ibn Idrīs answering Shaykh Ḥasan ibn Nūḥ holds that slaughtered animals of the People of the Book may be eaten if a Muslim witnessed the qibla and God's name, and their other food is lawful by the text of the Qurʾān but impure if touched with their moisture; and the Yemeni masters answering Shaykh Ḥasan al-Hindī permit eating the cooking of a serving girl who is not careful about ritual purity.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: A collection of questions and answers, arranged by the chapter order of the book Daaim al-Islam, supplies rulings on cleanliness and the purifications of the natural disposition (fitra).

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: The responding authority rules that no uncircumcised male is left so in Islam even to eighty years, and that a woman who has grown old without the circumcision of girls (khafd) still undergoes it rather than being left without it.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: On hair, the answers require that the head be parted in two halves from front to back (against the Indian custom of parting toward the middle), permit trimming only from the two sides of the beard (al-aridayn) and nothing else from the beard, and allow shaving, shortening or plucking of other body hair.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Several Indian customs are dismissed as having no basis — the dislike of a husband and wife sharing one comb, and the belief that leaving the hair uncombed on Friday night is binding — with the reply 'no reliance is to be placed upon that.'

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: The answers distinguish forbidden from permitted adornment: the engraving of dye (tattooing with henna patterns) is forbidden, while dyeing the teeth, filing uneven teeth for women, and piercing the ears of women and infant girls carry no harm.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Henna for men is ruled discouraged but not sinful in the question-and-answer collection ('no sin upon one who does it'), whereas Jafar ibn Sulayman's epistle condemns men's henna as imitation of women and an act of disobedience to God.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Ali is reported as instructing women not to take the circumcision of daughters to the utmost but to leave something of it, as better for the face and more favored by the husband, and the respondent confirms one acts accordingly.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: The Prophet's prohibition of a menstruating (adult) woman taking a qassa or jumma is glossed: the jumma is plaiting hair from the side locks to the nape, the qassa is cutting the head hair leaving about a quarter at the front, and the qunzua — gathering the hair with portions left standing — is likewise forbidden.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Qadi al-Numan, answering his district governor al-Khattab ibn Wasim, ruled that an uncircumcised married father must still be circumcised, with the exceptions that one born circumcised (as some prophets were) is excluded and that a man whose glans or most of it is exposed is not compelled.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: In his epistle al-Sayf al-Aqta fi Ibtal al-Bida, addressed to his people in the Island of Yemen, Jafar ibn Sulayman argues that women shaving their heads or their crown-edges and temples inverts the God-given order — men's adornment being the beard, women's the length of their head hair — citing the Prophet that hair is 'one of the two beauties.'

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Jafar's decisive proof against women shaving is Qadi al-Numan's ihram ruling in Daaim al-Islam: the bald and scalp-diseased man passes the razor over his head, while the woman released from ihram only cuts from the ends of her plaits and shaves neither it nor anything of it — so if shaving is barred even there, it can never be a standing custom.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Jafar condemns a double inversion of timing: girls are circumcised too early (within ten to forty days) when Ali forbade it before seven years, while boys are circumcised too late though Ali commanded haste — even the People of the Book circumcise on the seventh day.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Jafar further rules that the circumcision of girls must be done in concealment — known only to the girl, the woman performing it, and a few household women — without gathering, hospitality or call to prayer, since such public ceremony belongs only to the purification of male children and the matter falls under modesty, which the Prophet called part of faith.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: On a girl who dies before seven, Jafar ibn Sulayman (answering the author's questions from Yemen to India) holds the stated age-limit may not be transgressed, and Muhammad ibn Fahd al-Mukarrami rules explicitly that she is not circumcised — whereas a male child who dies uncircumcised is, by preferred sunna, circumcised after death.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Ali's four hundred counsels close the section with the command to circumcise children on the seventh day regardless of heat or cold, since it purifies the body and the earth cries out to God from the urine of the uncircumcised upon it.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: The author draws this section's rulings chiefly from a previously mentioned book of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of Daʿāʾim al-Islām, supplemented by Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim, Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf, Mukhtaṣar al-Āthār, Kitāb al-Akhbār, al-Iqtiṣār and Kitāb al-Zīna.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: The answer given is that impure garments, the skins of carrion, the skins of beasts of prey, or garments washed by polytheists' hands transmit impurity to the body when contact occurs while either is wet, so the body must then be washed.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: Taʾwīl al-Daʿāʾim rules that the goat, unlike the sheep, is not shorn while alive — hair shorn from a living goat counts as carrion — but its hair, skin, flesh and bones become lawful and pure if taken after proper slaughter, so prayer upon them is permitted.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: Regarding wool, fleece or hair shorn from a lawful animal while it is alive, the text is reported as holding that prayer in it is not permitted until it is washed, yet the material is not itself impure — a qualified position, not a declaration of impurity.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On vessels made of carrion skins in Waghar used to carry ghee or oil to Ahmedabad, the answer is that the contents become impure and a garment they touch cannot be prayed in, but the ghee and the soap made from it may be sold and bought provided the buyer is told they are impure, whereas the carrion skins themselves may never be sold or bought.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf rules that a broken human bone may be patched only with the bone of a properly slaughtered edible animal; one who used carrion bone, inedible-animal bone or human bone must remove it and repeat every prayer prayed, and the ruling authority compels him if the case becomes known — but it is not removed after death if it was unknown and he himself did not know.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On menstruation, the answer permits the husband to touch his menstruating wife's whole body short of intercourse, but holds it better that he avoid what is beneath the wrapper worn from navel to knees, lest fluid reach her womb.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: The mustahadah does not pray, does not enter the mosque and is not approached by her husband while the menstrual blood is present; when it departs and the flow thins she purifies herself, prays, fasts, enters the mosque and her husband may come to her, performing ablution whenever blood appears, since it is an ailment.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On the term of nifas the authorities differ: Hasan ibn Nuh and Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf make it depend on the woman's customary duration; the Sharia texts give forty or sixty days; Hasan ibn Idris answers that it may be less than forty days though forty must be reckoned; and a book of the people of the House sets the least at twenty days, the middle at forty and the most at sixty.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: Citing al-Nuʿman's al-Muntakhaba, the author rules that when postpartum blood turbid, thick and foul exceeds her custom she abstains from prayer, fasting and her husband until two months pass; if it continues beyond two months she is unquestionably a mustahadah, washes, and makes up the abandoned prayers and fasts from her customary term to the two months by way of precaution, since menstruation may have followed the nifas.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: Hasan ibn Idris answers that neither the menstruating woman nor the one in janaba may recite any portion of the Quran, whether in supplications or books, nor recite the basmala with the intention of Quranic recitation, and the menstruating woman does not touch the mushaf.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On istibra, the clearing of the womb: a marriage contract with a woman one has fornicated with is invalid until her womb is cleared; Mukhtaṣar al-Muṣannaf sets the withdrawal at two months; Kitāb al-Akhbār transmits forty-five nights for a mature woman who has not menstruated and nine months for such a virgin deflowered by the seller; and by the maxim al-walad lil-firāsh wa-lil-ʿāhir al-ḥajar the fornicator has no claim on the child's lineage.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The author reports Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts as teaching that night prayer benefits the body, earns God's pleasure, opens one to mercy and conforms one to prophetic character, and that one must not pray in laziness or drowsiness, must limit wandering thought (receiving only as much of the prayer as one attended to), and must not look aside, since God says 'I am better for you than that toward which you have turned.'

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Also from Ali: prayer is the offering (qurbān) of every godfearing person, no deed is more beloved to God than prayer, and worldly affairs must not distract from its appointed times — God having reproached those 'neglectful of their prayer' (Q 107), meaning heedless of it.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The author cites riddle-questions from a book of legal questions: the man for whom prayer is impermissible yet inexcusable is the one drunk to unconsciousness ('Do not approach prayer while intoxicated'); prayer in a state of purity may still be invalid if performed behind a bedouin (a'rābī), since bedouins are harder in disbelief and hypocrisy and it is impermissible to pray behind them; and an obligatory prayer without bowing or prostration is that of a swimmer unable to reach dry land.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The governing distinction throughout the question-and-answer material is between adā' (prayer performed within its appointed time) and qaḍā' (making up after the time has passed), applied separately to the obligatory prayer, its sunnah, and its optional (nāfilah) prayer.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Responsa rule that missed prayers (fawā'it) take precedence over the current prayer if time remains — one sins by neglecting them — that the sunnah's time is before the obligatory prayer except in Maghrib, whose sunnah is prayed as adā' after the obligatory prayer provided nothing separates them, and that one arriving while the imam prays 'Asr during the Dhuhr time intends Dhuhr with him if Dhuhr's time still holds.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Making up missed prayers or praying voluntarily at sunrise, at the sun's meridian standing, and at sunset is disliked (makrūh), on Friday and other days alike; and the reports record agreement that there is no prayer after Fajr until the sun declines except for making up or obligatory prayers (the consecration prayer, the two rakahs of circumambulation, the two festival prayers and the like), with Friday excepted on the ground that 'the fires are not stoked on it.'

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The author expressly qualifies this 'disbelief': it means only that nothing is accepted from him since he stands in a disbeliever's position — he is not subject to the poll tax, killing, enslavement of offspring, ritual impurity, or prohibition of his slaughtered meat, because the two testimonies place him within the rulings of Islam.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The author reports, from questions of Sulayman ibn Hasan answered by Dawud ibn Ajab, the same ruling: one who cut himself off from prayer and cannot reckon what he missed bears no guilt for the past if he repents sincerely and enters the noble covenant and does not lapse again — and from Muhammad ibn al-Fahd ibn Salah's epistle, that a bequest paid for making up a dead person's prayers is applied in order (obligatory portions, then shaf' and witr, then sunan), prayer taking precedence over the obligatory fast.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: In the same epistle the case of the boy who killed his mother before puberty is answered: he should undertake her release and discharge as known in the books of the friends of God, and convey good deeds to her — above all Hajj, since Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq told a wealthy questioner that charity equal to the weight of Mount Abu Qubays would not attain the reward of Hajj — but if she was not a believer or did not pray, he must make up her prayer as far as he is able, since prayer is the first deed God examines.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Al-Nu'man reports Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah's answer that the Fajr prayer belongs neither to night nor day — for if to night the faster could eat at its time, and if to day its recitation would not be aloud — since two prayers belong to the day's portion, two to the night's, and one stands midway, this being 'the far-reaching wisdom.'

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inward Nursing, prescribes the witr as three units reciting al-A'la, al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas respectively with the standing qunut after bowing, followed after a separation by two seated units reciting al-Falaq and al-Nas, and identifies the dawn prayer — four units, two voluntary and two obligatory, containing the qunut — as the 'middle prayer' of Q 2:238.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The author closes with Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim's answer (sent from Yemen to Hind in 1145 AH to Muhammad 'Ali ibn Salih al-Badri) that making up prayer follows the rule of fasting — only men make it up on behalf of men — while an aged man too weak to make up prayer prays what he can, another makes up on his behalf, and expiation is made.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: A question-and-answer book arranged by the chapter order of Daa'im al-Islam records that a man of the call appointed by a tyrannical sultan as imam, muezzin or teacher and paid from the port levy or jizya may lawfully consume such pay only if the public treasury (bayt al-mal) is administered by the judgment of one appointed by the friends of God, and not otherwise.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Idah reports from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ali that giving the call while walking or mounted is permissible provided one faces the qibla at the moment of the testimony, while the author states that the books attributed to the Ahl al-Bayt agree that the iqama is invalid unless the person is standing upon the ground.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf holds that the muezzin should say inwardly 'I bear witness that Ali is the friend of God' after each testimony to Muhammad's messengership, and 'the family of Muhammad are the best of humankind' after each 'Come to the best of deeds'.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf further rules that no one in the mosque should leave after the call before praying, except for a necessity or to perform ablution with the intention and expectation of returning, and that one who misses the congregation prays alone or with another congregation without fault.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shari'a rules that the adhan may be given without ritual purity but the iqama only by one who is pure, that the muezzin faces the qibla and forms intention first, and that the obligatory prayer is prayed at the iqama while the supererogatory is joined to the adhan and comes first.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Idris ibn Sayyidina Hasan records in the sixth part of Uyun al-Akhbar that under the caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah the muezzins publicly proclaimed 'I bear witness that our mawla Ali is the friend of God' and 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of humankind and their kindred the best of kindred', in confirmation of the Prophet's Ghadir declaration.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The author argues from Ibn Abbas's answer that the 'near kindred' are Ali, Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and rejects the report from Abu Bakr that 'we are the kindred of the Messenger of God' on the ground that Abu Bakr's only tie was remote Qurashi lineage.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The author supports Ali's pre-eminence with the Prophet's hadith of the two weighty things and the ark of Noah, and the saying 'Ali is the best of humankind, and whoever refuses this has disbelieved'.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The narrated anecdote of al-Hakim at al-Gharafa has him settle a dispute at Atfih between a preacher who rejected the new call and the dai who gave it, by a chain of reports the preacher himself concedes sound.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The author announces that he will next reproduce in full the epistle al-Muriba 'amma jarat bihi al-mubahatha by his sayyid and father Muhammad ibn Fahd, which debates whether the formula 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of humankind' is an illicit innovation or a thing commanded by the Noble Book and upheld by obedience to those whose command must be obeyed.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The section is framed as a recorded debate in which one jurist challenges another over the call-to-prayer formula 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of human beings, and their kindred are the best of kindred,' noting no other Islamic group says it.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The respondent's first reply is that, per Q 41:46 and Q 6:164, a righteous act benefits only its doer and a wrong burdens only its doer, so the formula harms no one else; the questioner accepts this but demands a plain proof that Ali equals the Prophet in excellence, conceding the Prophet's primacy as master of the messengers is already established.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proof one: the purification verse (Q 33:33) establishes the people of the household as equal to the Prophet in purity, and since Ali is the most excellent of them and the Prophet's guardian and successor, likeness to the Prophet is established for him.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proof two: 'Peace be upon the family of Yasin' (Q 37:130) refers to the Messenger's household, and only the best of human beings could be the most excellent of that family, which is Ali, whom the Prophet chose as guardian over his community.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proof three: 'You are the best community brought forth for humankind' (Q 3:110) is read as addressed specifically to the Prophet's household, and since Ali is first and most excellent among them, he is the best of human beings after and alongside the Prophet.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proof four: because Moses' request for Aaron as minister, back-strengthener and partner in his task was granted (Q 20:29-36, 28:34-35), and because God's way admits no change or alteration and Muhammad is told to follow earlier prophets' guidance, the Prophet was obliged to appoint Ali as his minister, brother and partner — confirmed by the hadith 'Ali stands to me in the station of Aaron to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me.'

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proof five: the guardianship verse (Q 5:55) — 'Your guardian is only God, His Messenger, and those who believe who give alms while bowing' — designates Ali as the Messenger's partner in guardianship over the believers, reinforced by the Ghadir Khumm declaration 'whoever's master I am, this Ali is his master.'

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proofs six, seven and eight argue respectively that Q 98:7 makes the household 'the best of creation,' that Q 3:33-34's election of Abraham's and Imran's families implies the Prophet's family surpasses them since he surpasses Adam and Noah, and that Q 44:30-32's choosing of the Children of Israel over the worlds shows the Prophet's kindred are best not only in their era but over all prior eras.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: An objection is reported: that Umar's removal of 'hayya ala khayr al-amal' from the adhan is unproven from the opponents' books, was in any case a legitimate exercise of judgment, and that if it were an error then the added testimony 'I bear witness that our master Ali is the guardian of God' would equally be an error, since adding to the adhan is like subtracting from it.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The author rejects as void slander the ascription of the wilaya testimony to al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah — noting the Twelver Shia use it despite differing from him in school — and instead traces the phrase to Ali himself testifying to his own guardianship after the Prophet, as the Prophet testified to his own prophethood and God testifies to His own oneness (Q 3:18).

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The author dismisses the appeal to the opponents' books (Sahih al-Bukhari, the five, al-Mishkat) on the ground that their own scholars dispute those books' soundness and they contain fabrications, and holds that al-Qadi al-Numan's narration from Jafar al-Sadiq predates their compilation and was likely suppressed by them to avoid censure.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The compilation distinguishes a mosque given over to public use, which its owner may not pull down (though he owes nothing if it collapses on its own), from one belonging to him alone and not so dedicated, which he may pull down.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: A man who builds the congregational mosque or another on his own property does as he wishes and need not seek the governor's permission.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The 'neighbor of the mosque' is defined as the one who hears the call to prayer; the prayer of a man without congregation counts as a single prayer, and for the neighbor of the mosque it is disliked to pray alone at home without an excuse.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Answering a question about the Prophet refusing to plaster his leaking mosque and saying 'No; a shelter like the shelter of Moses,' the reply explains it to mean that this is not like the plastered shelter of Moses.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The rulings distinguish a mosque opened to the people, in which the greeting prayer is prayed and which may not be relocated, from a prayer-place confined within a house and never made open, in which no greeting prayer is prayed and which the owner may absorb into his house.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Two imams do not lead prayer at one time in one assembly, and a congregational prayer is not held twice in one mosque — a later imam and his people pray individually — except that an imam overtaken by something breaking his state may appoint a substitute; yet a separate congregation on the mosque roof is allowed.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: A worshipper is permitted to pass the nearer mosque for a farther one because its licensed man is of greater rank, and no blame attaches to him.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The greeting prayer is not prayed while an obligatory prayer is owed (except the Sunnah of dawn, which is joined to the obligatory prayers) and only at times when supererogatory prayer is permitted.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: On the qibla: one ignorant of it exerts his judgment and prays; learning of error mid-prayer with little time left, he turns toward the House and completes it if he was between east and west, but if his back was to the Kaaba only repetition suffices; and if two (or four) directions are confused with none prevailing, he prays toward them all — a ruling repeated from Mukhtasar al-Musannaf.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Muhammad ibn al-Fahd rules in his epistle that prayer is permitted in a dome or mosque built for prayer into which a grave was later introduced, but that a structure built on account of a pre-existing grave has the ruling of a cemetery and prayer in it is never permitted — matching the rule given earlier in the answers.
entities: The Clear Highway of the Path of Guidance

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Muhammad ibn al-Fahd further rules that the greeting prayer is obligatory only within the mosque proper and not its courtyard or forecourt, though performing it there is good since they fall within the mosque's bounds, so that one who steps out to the courtyard and returns need not repeat it.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Majalis al-Bayan lists twelve places where prayer is disliked, including the cemetery, slaughterhouse, bathhouse, latrine, camel resting places, facing a sleeper, without a screen, on impure ground, on food, in places of worship, churches, and Magian houses unless sprinkled with water.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib in his four hundred rules of conduct teaches that sitting in the mosque from dawn to sunrise is swifter for seeking provision than travel, forbids spitting toward the qibla (with forgiveness sought if done forgetfully), blowing on the place of prostration, food or incense, praying with a sword before one, and approaching the mosque after eating offensive foods.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: The section is compiled from a question-and-answer book arranged according to the chapter order of Daʿaʾim al-Islam, supplemented by Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, Mukhtasar al-Athar, al-Ikhtisar, al-Muntakhaba, al-Idah, al-Majalis al-Hatimiyya, al-Majalis al-Mustansiriyya, and epistles of al-Qadi al-Numan and later summoners of Yemen answering Indian questioners.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: The disqualification is relative, not absolute: each of these persons may validly lead others who share his own condition.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: A woman may lead women in prayer but does not stand ahead of them — they stand to her right and left — and a woman may never stand ahead of a man while he prays behind her.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: Recitation that alters the meaning of the Quran voids the leadership: one who substitutes or distorts vowels (e.g. a kasra on the lam in "Allah is free of the polytheists and His Messenger," or a fatha on the ha in "and among them are those whom God guided") may not be taken as imam, must correct his recitation lest he exchange a verse of mercy for one of punishment, and one who does recite well is obliged to lead when the people call him and he is acceptable to them.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: Taqiyya licenses modification but not omission of prayer elements: the licensed imam may lower the recitation of the basmala so only he hears it, and may omit "rabbana laka al-hamd" when common people are present — but he must not omit it for any cause other than taqiyya.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: A man of the summons who repeats a prayer outside its time purely for taqiyya before those not of the People of the House commits no sin, even if others of the summons follow him with him as their intended imam.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: The blind man's imamate is conditionally allowed: al-Ikhtisar permits it when there is need, al-Muntakhaba requires that he be set straight on a given day and sets aside the nasib if he led from the side, and al-Qadi al-Numan wrote that there is no harm if he is set straight — but in every case he is not to be taken as a standing (permanent) imam.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: The follower must never precede the imam: he begins each act after him, returns to his prior position if he forgets and precedes, may not stand in front of him (that follower's prayer is void though the imam's is valid), and the Prophet warned that one raising his head before the imam risks having his head turned into a donkey's.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: The Prophet, injured by a fall from a horse, led his companions seated and signalled them to sit, then declared that the imam exists to be followed — when he magnifies, magnify; when he recites, be silent; when he says "God hears him who praises Him," say "our Lord, to You be praise"; when he gives the greeting, greet; and when he prays seated, all of you pray seated.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: Rows must be complete and continuous with the space of a prostrating body between them, none in Mecca closer to the Kaaba than the imam, and a latecomer finding no room prays alone alongside the imam without joining his row — save the imam's hujja, who alone may step level with the imam, by explicit text.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: On women praying behind a screen, Sayyidna Jafar ibn Sulayman answers Sayyidna Ali ibn Sulayman that if the place is connected by an opening or lattice the prayer is complete and looking at the men is forbidden before or after entering the sanctified state, cutting off the prayer if directed at non-kin; if the place is not connected, the woman nearest the men takes a single glance at their garments before the sanctified state, and that suffices for all of them — this against the Daudi position that she must keep her gaze on the men during bowing and prostration or none of them has a prayer.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: A question-and-answer compilation arranged by the chapter order of Daaim al-Islam divides al-mufassal into long (al-Hujurat to al-Mujadila), middle (al-Mujadila to 'Amma yatasa'alun') and short (from 'Amma yatasa'alun' to al-Nas) portions, and explains that Ali's recitation of 'So be patient' against Ibn al-Kawwa was a rebuke to silence him, not the opening of a surah in prayer.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: The same source lists acts that break the covenant: abandoning prayer or any prescribed work without excuse, disbelieving a believer who has sworn by God after being accused, fornication, killing a believer, reviling the summoner or his appointee, and refusing without excuse the summoner's command to strive with person and wealth.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that if the intention for prayer slips away before one enters it — through preoccupation, forgetfulness or anything else — the prayer subsequently performed does not suffice, and that one may not recite inwardly what the tongue has not uttered.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: On the tashahhud, performing the first does not excuse one from the second, though the second does suffice in place of the first.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Particular bodily rulings are given: a woman places her hands above her knees on her thighs so as not to raise her hindquarters, the seated worshipper folds the left leg beneath him and keeps the right upright, and tawajjuh comes after the takbirat al-ihram with recitation beginning after it.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Those behind the imam answer 'God has heard the one who praised Him' quietly with 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise,' the sole exception being the appointed relayer who raises his voice with that and with the takbir but not with the tasbih.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman's epistle al-Sayf al-Aqta fi Ibtal al-Bida rebukes Yemeni adherents who profess walaya yet never prostrate, arguing from 'between the servant and unbelief is abandoning the prayer' and Ali's 'there is no portion in Islam for one who abandons the prayer' that no one may claim walaya to the friends of God except by holding fast to the hem of the prayer.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: That epistle classifies neglecters of prayer into two kinds — those of tribal temper wholly absorbed in animal nature, and those of arrogance and coarse insolence, especially women — and notes that even unbelievers, including those of India, retain an inherited worship, so that such arrogance falls under the threat that those too proud to worship God enter Hell abased, worship benefiting only the worshipper since God has no need of it.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah numbers the obligations of prayer as seven — first takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, tasbih, greeting, taslim — and forbids moving the foot, speaking, or shifting place from the opening takbir to the taslim, along with prophetic prohibitions on reciting while bowing, disturbing pebbles, turning like a fox, squatting like a monkey, pecking like a crow, and drooping the head below the level of the back.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Ali's Four Hundred Etiquettes forbid clasping the hands while standing in imitation of the People of the Book, treat gross turning about as cutting off the prayer so that it must be begun again with adhan, iqama and takbir, and direct the solitary worshipper to make himself hear his recitation and to turn to his right when finishing.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Answering Muhammad Ali ibn Salih al-Badri, head of the island of India, the master Hibat Allah rules that since no text of the friends of God forbids it, reciting al-Falaq and al-Nas in an obligatory prayer leaves the prayer complete — one who recited al-Nas first repeats it in the last rakah, one who recited al-Ikhlas first recites al-Falaq in the second — but one should not deliberately recite so, putting it in the position of the sunnah.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: In the question-and-answer book arranged by the chapters of the Pillars of Islam, it is answered that the guiding call's teaching that supplication is not recited after the afternoon prayer applies both to the supplication of drawing near and to all other supplications, yet no sin falls on one who does supplicate.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The same source answers that wiping the face at the place of prostration is permitted only after the afternoon and dawn prayers, this being commanded by the masters as received from the pure Imams, and that prolonging supplication after the afternoon prayer, though discouraged, incurs nothing.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The book on the interpretation of the Sharia holds that daytime prayers are recited low, night prayers aloud, and the dawn prayer, offered in the last darkness, is announced aloud.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: In the Eleventh Mustansiriyya Council, the author states that having completed the jurisprudence of prayer — outward given exposition, inward given sign and intimation — he now treats the supplication closing the prayer and its seven and twelve.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The author states that each of the seven supplications has a mention in the Quran to be brought forward later, since all set down so far are roots awaiting the branching of boughs and bearing of fruit.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib is quoted in his Four Hundred Etiquettes teaching that God accepts supplication when His right is remembered and guarded, that the gates of heaven open at six times (rainfall, the advance of battle ranks, the call to prayer, Quran recitation, the sun's decline, and dawn), that supplication turns back even a firmly settled decree, that it should be used to repel affliction before it descends since affliction reaches the believer faster than a mountain torrent or galloping horses, and that one who supplicates without deeds is like an archer with no bowstring.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: Ali is further quoted that whoever recites Surat al-Ikhlas ten times and Surat al-Qadr until sunrise will not be touched by sin however hard Iblis strives.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The question-and-answer book rules that deliberate throat-clearing without excuse cuts off the prayer — the imam being alerted instead by words of glorification or a gesture — and that habitual deliberate throat-clearing requires repeating the prayer.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The same source rules that a woman may not occupy herself in prayer by carrying her child even to quiet his weeping, that food placed in the mouth out of necessity for pain incurs nothing, that a braid wound inside the turban around to the forehead is permitted since the forbidden binding is turning hair back on its root and gathering it to the middle of the head, and that holding a gemstone, dirham or object in mouth or hand does not void the prayer if it does not prevent proper formation of letters or fulfilling the prayer's limits — though being free of all such things is more fitting.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The abridgment of the compiled book rules that eating or drinking in prayer cuts it off whether done forgetfully or deliberately, and the interpretation of the Sharia adds that recitation precedes bowing, that one must not raise his voice above the imam's, that noon and afternoon recitation is kept low while night recitation is aloud, and that the Prophet forbade wiping over leather socks and forbade omitting the audible basmala; once the opening magnification is pronounced the worshipper does not speak until the salutation.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: The answer in the question-and-answer collection arranged by the chapters of Daaim al-Islam holds that prayer on a mat or cloth bearing depictions is permitted only if the depiction does not occupy the worshipper's attention, with the standing exception that one does not pray toward images.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: A later answer in the same collection states more strictly that prayer in or upon a rug or garment bearing figures is not permitted when the figures are seen, and permitted when they are not seen.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Questions of dye and fabric are assigned to the domain of etiquette rather than validity: wearing safflower-dyed or deeply red cloth does not invalidate the prayer of man or woman, and only pure silk is singled out as disliked for men.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Because the whole of a woman is 'awra, the answer given is that prayer is not permitted to her if any part of it is exposed, and this holds whether she knew the ruling or was ignorant of it — a ruling applied directly to the women of the people of the dawa in India who do not wear the long shift and head-veil.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: The abridgment of the Musannaf draws an asymmetry: a man who prays with his 'awra uncovered unknowingly repeats the prayer once he learns of it, whereas a free or slave woman's prayer with uncovered 'awra is spoiled whether she knew or not.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Prayer is valid only in pure garments — the worshipper strips off whatever is impure — yet carrying wrought or unwrought gold and silver in the waistband does not affect the prayer's validity.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: On impure clothing the rule is that one who has only an impure garment and no water prays in it and repeats when a clean garment or water is found, and one who has two garments of which one is impure but unidentified must pray the prayer in each, intending the fulfilment of the obligation.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Obligatory prayer is not permitted upon stone, unbaked brick, or the like — only supererogatory and sunna prayer — and Idris ibn al-Hasan grounds the general principle in the Prophet's saying that the earth was made a place of prostration and a means of purification, concluding that whatever of the earth is unfit for dry ablution is unfit to pray upon.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman holds in the book of the obligations and limits of religion that a man may lawfully uncover his head and pray bareheaded, and that holding an object in mouth or hand does not void the prayer so long as it does not impair the letters or the required postures, though being free of it is better.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Another transmitted position holds that a man is not to pray bareheaded without turban and mantle unless he finds neither, and that praying with only a small handcloth on the shoulders is impermissible when another garment is available.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: The interpretation of the Daaim explains the technical garment terms — belting a single thick shirt so the private part does not show when bowing, the 'two wings of the swallow' wrap used when nothing else is found, and the forbidden ishtimal al-samma, which is invalid because it pins both hands and prevents bowing, prostration, and the raising of the hands.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred counsels of etiquette require a clean garment before God, forbid praying in a loosely draped shirt as the practice of the people of Lot, and forbid prostrating upon an image, a rug containing one, a heap of wheat or barley, anything edible, or bread — while allowing coins to be carried in a clean money belt or cloth.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Ancillary rulings permit prostration on plaster over which carrion was burned because fire purified it, deny validity to prayer in the resting places of camels while allowing it in sheep folds once swept and sprinkled, and tolerate a small amount of milk or butter from animals that feed on filth.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: A cited question-and-answer collection, arranged by the chapters of Daaim al-Islam, rules that Friday prayer may be established in two congregational mosques only if three miles or more separate them — and the answer extends this: if the distance is less than three miles, Friday is established in only one of them, whether the mosques belong to one city or two.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Against al-Muayyad's sermon wording that condemns abandoning Friday prayer 'under a just imam or an unjust one', the answer distinguishes two senses: praying behind the people of injustice is impermissible except under taqiyya (dissimulation), whereas 'the unjust' in the sermon means an appointed summoner in whom transgression has appeared, behind whom prayer remains obligatory while the people refer the matter to the holder of authority.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali is reported as instructing that prayer behind a nasib or a haruri not be counted, the leader being treated as a mere pillar of the mosque while one recites for oneself as if praying alone.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Al-Husayn ibn Ali is reported to have let Muawiya's governor lead the prayer over al-Hasan, saying 'were it not for the practice I would not have put you forward', which the text glosses as the People of the House's practice of dissimulation, summed up in an Imam's saying that 'dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my fathers'.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf supplies the practical rules of Friday: prayer behind the Imam of the Muslims surpasses prayer behind his deputies; the binding call is the one given before the seated preacher; a broken purity lets the Imam withdraw, wash, and either repeat the sermon or simply pray; a seated sermon suffices for illness; and omitting the sitting between the two sermons is disliked but not grounds for repetition.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: The number of cycles depends on when the congregation disperses: if all but one man leave after the sermon the Imam prays four, if they leave after one completed cycle he prays Friday as two, and if they leave before he bows he restarts as the four-cycle noon prayer.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah forbids the respondent to 'give suck' unless appointed to it by his summoner, and forbids him to press proposals or demand branches of knowledge from the summoner, who 'knows better how to raise his children'.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: The festival prayer has neither call to prayer nor call to stand, requires a congregation of five including the Imam like Friday, is obligatory where someone establishes it, and is not prayed in congregation at Mina — where, per al-Numan's Tawil al-Daaim and Idris ibn Hasan, each prays it alone.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The author distinguishes omission (sahw, inattention) from doubt: the one who commits an omission is certain of what he omitted, whereas the doubter is not certain of what he doubts — a distinction many jurists confuse by treating doubt as if it were omission.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The two prostrations of omission are called al-murghimatan, 'the two that rub down the nose', because they rub down the nose of the devil when the corruption of forgetfulness is repaired by them.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع) is quoted in his four hundred manners: whoever is certain of something and is then struck by doubt should act on his certainty, for doubt neither dispels nor diminishes certainty.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: If a doubter is certain of nothing at all — not knowing whether he added to or fell short of his prayer — he begins the prayer again from the beginning, and so likewise does the Imam.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The prostration of omission is not multiplied: repeated omissions in a single prayer, or three separate omitted obligations, still require only the two prostrations.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: Where no explicit text (nass) exists — as with neglecting the first tashahhud and remembering before the salaam, or repeating a single surah after the Opening — it has not been stipulated that the worshipper must prostrate, though the answerers add that such things should not be done deliberately.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The Imam bears responsibility for a follower's omission, except in the bowing and the opening takbir, which the follower must not neglect; conversely a latecomer prostrates for his Imam's omission even if he caught only the opening takbir with him, and prostrates on his own account for errors made while praying alone.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: On interruption, the author cites the report that three things interrupt the prayer — a woman, a donkey, and a black dog — alongside the Prophet's own statement that nothing interrupts a believer's prayer but one should ward off what one is able, and Ali's dictum that smiling does not interrupt the prayer while loud laughter does.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: Broken purity or bodily impurity during prayer is governed by position and orientation: one who breaks purity before the tashahhud repeats the prayer but one who breaks it after the peace upon the Prophet and the righteous need not, and one who cleans blood or vomit without turning his face from the qibla builds upon his prayer, whereas turning from the qibla obliges repetition from the beginning.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd, in his epistle The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided, answers that a latecomer who reaches the Imam before the Imam raises his head from the bowing and enters with a single takbir has attained that rakah, provided the intention is contracted in his heart.
entities: The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib is reported as instructing that boys be taught the prayer and held to it when they reach eight years, and more generally taught what God will benefit the parents by.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Ibrahim ibn Husayn al-Hamidi reports in Ibarat al-Bishara a saying of Amir al-Muminin that the boy sheds milk teeth at seven, reaches maturity at fourteen, completes his stature at twenty-one, and completes his intellect at twenty-eight.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Athar directs that children be separated in their sleeping places at that stage, as a precaution since they have drawn near to maturity and the stirring of desire.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: A distinction is drawn between the two grounds for praying in full: stopping five prayer times with blood kin or a resident wife, and forming the intention to reside ten days, the latter being the stipulated limit of residence.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Idris ibn Hasan answers that residence-intention governs: one prays in full while the intention of residence remains and shortens from the moment he resolves on travel; an intention to return to the first lodging carries over to a nearby lodging, otherwise a fresh ten-day intention is required.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Distances are defined: the barid is four farsakhs, the farsakh three miles, and the mile three thousand cubits, being a thousand even paces of a single leg.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Whoever enters Mecca prays in full without shortening, on the basis of the Quranic words that the resident and the visitor stand equal, though Ismail ibn Sayyidina Hiba held that the full prayer applies only within the sanctuary of the House of God and that in Mecca itself the prayer is shortened.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Six categories are reported from Amir al-Muminin as not shortening prayer or fast despite travel: collectors on circuit, merchants moving market to market, princes circuiting their emirate, hunters, shepherds seeking rain-fed pasture, and warriors who cut the road — and Idris extends this to shaykhs touring villages to visit believers, likening them to the prince.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: A traveler may lead residents when he is the more excellent, saluting after two rakahs while they rise to complete, and a traveler following a resident imam may either withdraw after two rakahs or wait for the imam's salutation — though Muhammad ibn Fahd restricts the traveler-as-imam dispensation to the people of the high ranks.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd reports that one who has performed tayammum may lead those who performed ablution only among the people of the high ranks, citing the Dai Jafar ibn Sulayman, who at Haraz performed tayammum unseen and led the congregation, then explained the dispensation as granted for weighty matters serving the guiding dawa.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sayyidina Sulayman answers in Ghurufat al-Jinan that an imam with only a shortening follower behind him need not raise the takbir aloud once that follower has withdrawn, since raising the voice exists for the follower.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states in Kitab al-Rida al-Batin that shortening applies to three four-rakah prayers — the first, afternoon, and late evening — reducing twelve rakahs by six.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: The sick man prays seated or cross-legged with bowing and prostration; if unable to gesture with his head he gestures with his eyes, and failing that with his heart, and he need only make up the obligatory prayer, the sunnah and supererogatory being meritorious but not obligatory to make up.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that one who loses his reason through a medicine or any act of his own must repeat the prayers missed in that state, regardless of whether the act was obedience or disobedience.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: The answer to the eclipse question, attributed to the pure Imams and the ranks below them, is that a lunar eclipse falls at the dawn of the fifteenth or sixteenth while a solar eclipse may fall at either the beginning or the end of the month, contrary to the Brethren of Purity's treatise on astronomy which said a solar eclipse occurs only at the month's end.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: The eclipse prayer may not be prayed until the eclipse is actually seen with the eye: it is not prayed on the word of an astrologer or anyone else, and if cloud intervenes it is postponed until visible (book of purity).

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: A latecomer to the eclipse prayer counts his joining as the beginning of his own prayer, follows the imam in bowing and prostration, sits poised while the imam testifies, and after the imam's salutation completes the remaining bowings himself, not counting the first two prostrations done with the imam.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: In extreme combat — crossing of swords and thrusting of spears — prayers are converted into takbir, one takbir in place of each bowing, and the takbir is shortened just as shortening is obligatory in the prayer of fear.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Per مُخْتَصَرُ الْمُصَنَّفِ, the prayer of fear requires at least three men praying with three standing guard, since the term 'party' does not apply to fewer than three; and if eclipse, funeral, and fear coincide the imam prays the funeral, the eclipse prayer, and the prayer of fear.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: The rain prayer includes a hundred takbirs facing the people, a hundred glorifications to the right, a hundred declarations of oneness to the left, and a hundred praises, with two sermons as at the two feasts, delivered leaning on an Arabian bow as the Messenger of God did; and whoever delivers the sermon before the prayer must pray and then deliver it again.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: On the qunut the answers distinguish: deliberate abandonment in the witr requires repetition, forgetting it requires no repetition since there are no prostrations of forgetfulness in sunnah prayers, its least measure is three glorifications or three takbirs, and it is recited after 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise'.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Judge al-Numan in المنتخبة holds the witr may be divided by the salutation without intervening actions or speech, though if one is compelled to speak there is no harm provided the talk is not prolonged.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd, in لاحبة سبيل الهدى للمهتدين, answers that one who prayed dawn before the true dawn keeps his shaf and witr but must repeat both the sunnah and obligation of dawn — unless dawn was close upon him, in which case the sunnah prayer stands, on account of a noble inner meaning permitting it.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Praying tarawih behind an imam who recites the whole Quran is permitted only for the sake of protective concealment (taqiyya) and with the intention of a voluntary prayer, and the believers do not take him as a leader; likewise the reliance for numbers of sunnah bowings is upon الدعائم, and sunnah omitted for concealment must be made up.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman rules that the prayer of Umm Daud has a text from Mawlana al-Sadiq only for the month of Rajab and for the day of 'Arafah, so Qasim ibn Fir of the Daudi faction, who commanded it in Rabi al-Awwal and Ramadan of 1042, acted without a text — for no practice is valid without a supporting text, and 'little action in a sunnah is better than much action in an innovation.'

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim answers (year 1135) that the prayer of the prophets and Imams at times of calamity was praise and thanksgiving for what God disclosed to them, and that followers may pray it at all times when sunnah and voluntary prayers are permitted, prohibition applying only to the forbidden times.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: For the Quranic prostration a distinction holds: the binding prostration verses oblige all present to prostrate (though not a second time in the same sitting), while the remaining ones are optional, prostrating being better; and 'Ali's four hundred points urge prolonging prostration since Iblis was commanded to prostrate and disobeyed while the son of Adam obeyed and was saved.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The 'dying state' (siyaq) is defined as the moment when death draws near and the passage from this world to the hereafter is imminent, per the book interpreting the pillars.
entities: book of the interpretation of the pillars

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Asked whether people may relocate to flee epidemic and plague believing they will escape it, Idris ibn Hasan answered that they may go wherever they wish, since the matter is in Allah's hand.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman's epistle 'The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations' — written to admonish his heedless followers among the people of the island of Yemen where he had settled — rebukes them for being slow to visit the sick, citing the pillars' report from the Commander of the Faithful that seventy thousand angels pray for a Muslim who visits a sick person from the hour of his visit until sunset (or sunrise, if by night).
entities: The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The Prophet forbade the visitor from eating in the sick person's presence, and Allah nullifies (in another wording, casts behind him) the reward of such a visit, the stated reason being that eating in a poor sick man's house burdens him and inwardly galls his household.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Whoever knows such rulings is obliged to pass them on, since the learned are few, and the one who gives the warning has thereby discharged his duty.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: From 'Ali's four hundred points of conduct: one must not sleep in the prohibited posture nor on one's face (and the sleeper on his face is to be woken), a woman is not to sleep stretched on her back, and refuge is sought from severe affliction because the gravest affliction is loss of one's religion.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: On lifespans: they are fixed terms that neither increase nor decrease, yet the reported 'increase and decrease' is sound in the sense that what is diminished in the past cycle is added in the future one.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The saying that 'the wretched is he whom the Hour overtakes while alive and not yet dead' is interpreted to mean that the Hour comes upon him while he is still in the animal (bahimi) condition, not having passed to the angelic life.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Husayn ibn Idris ruled, answering Hasan ibn Nuh's tenth question, that a living formed child in a dead mother's womb must be extracted if a skilled woman is present and it is possible, or if the fetus is six months or more with hope of life; otherwise the mother is not buried until the child's death is confirmed.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: 'Ali taught frequent remembrance of death, the rising from graves and the standing before Allah so that calamities sit lightly, described fever as death's forerunner and Allah's prison on earth which strips away sins as hair is stripped from a camel's pores, and said that a Shi'a who departs from a prohibition is afflicted in property, child or self so that his sins are purged before meeting Allah — the dead of their Shi'a being a truthful witness (siddiq shahid).

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
