dropped.text: Innovations of mourning are condemned: no shaving hair, lighting lamps or cutting nails for the dead; placing weapons beside the corpse or holding a vigil beside it obligatory has 'no reliance to be placed upon it'; and the gathering of women to lament for nights and days with singing and play, as if it were a prescription at fixed times, disgraces the believers before Allah and His friends.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Wailing is forbidden by narration: Jafar ibn Muhammad bequeathed that no cheek be struck and no collar torn for him (the woman who tears her collar has a rent in Hell that grows as she adds to it), 'Ali wrote to Rifaah ibn Shaddad his judge over al-Ahwaz to forbid wailing where he held authority, and the Prophet named two accursed voices — howling at calamity and a voice raised at a blessing — i.e. wailing and singing.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The account of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah shows the dead/dying are punished by the living's words: he saw an angel with a fiery iron mace who struck at his skull each time a woman shrieked 'O my mountain!' or 'O my might!', desisting only when he answered 'No, rather Allah', and the Prophet confirmed it saying, 'What is the matter with your dead, that they suffer by the words of your living?'

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The decisive distinction: the Prophet wept at the death of his child and declared he had not forbidden weeping but only wailing and lamentation, weeping being a tenderness and mercy Allah places in whom He wills; he licensed tears at calamity ('the soul is stricken, the eye sheds tears') while commanding only speech pleasing to Allah and forbidding foul speech (hujr).

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Correspondingly, the singing forbidden at calamity is permitted at weddings and banquets solely to distinguish lawful marriage from fornication — the Prophet, hearing music among the Banu Zurayq, approved it, saying there is no secret marriage until smoke is seen or a tambourine heard, and that the beating of the tambourine is what separates nikah from sifah.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: 'Ali commanded households to speak well over their dead, citing Fatimah — when the daughters of Hashim mourned with her at her father's death she said 'Grieve with restraint, and hold fast to supplication' — and he ruled that whoever strikes his thigh at a calamity forfeits his reward.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The washing of the dead requires the ablution performed three times together with three washings, though performing the ablution at the last washing suffices, as stated in the Book of Reports.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Where water is scarce, the answer given is that a living man in janabah uses the water and the dead is given tayammum with earth; another report permits a washer in janabah to wash the dead, performing tayammum first if washing would harm him, when no one else can be found.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: A martyr is normally not washed, but the Mukhtasar of al-Musannif rules that a martyr who was in janabah is washed on account of that janabah, and one found dead with no mark upon him is washed, given hanut, and shrouded.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The Mukhtasar al-Athar rules that the drowned and the burned are washed, as is any severed limb whose separation would preclude life, each detached limb being washed and set in its own place before shrouding; no hair is shaved and no nail trimmed from the dead.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Answering the author's question from Hind, Jafar ibn Sulayman rejects the wrapper arrangement used by the Daudi group and by unbelievers, ruling that the Pillars prescribes only an izar from navel to knee with water passed beneath it and the washer's cloth-wrapped hand reaching under it, while conceding that a screen is the better course, especially for a woman.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The best shroud, per Jafar ibn Muhammad in The Pillars of Islam, is three garments: a shirt neither buttoned nor hemmed, a wrapping sheet, and a waist wrapper.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan's term 'tajir' for a woman's shrouding is defined as gathering the shirt at the navel down over the clothing and tucking it into the izar's fastening — a mark distinguishing women from men, like the head covering.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Ali's counsel that whoever touches the body of the dead after it has grown cold must perform the washing is glossed as meaning after his end has come and he has been washed according to the sunnah, since the dead body has become impure and its moisture renders a living man impure.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: For conjoined twins, the summoners of Yemen rule that separation is done only if slight and safe; if dangerous they are left, their life and death counting as one, and if one dies the adhering part is cut from the dead one only where the living feels no pain.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The shroud and outfitting are taken from the estate first — before debt and bequest — according to the deceased's station even if costly and even if the debt exceeds the estate.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Hanut is any perfume placed on the places of prostration and named parts of the body, but wars and saffron are excluded for men and included for women; the dead himself is not incensed — only his shroud and the place of washing — and Ali forbids any fragrance but camphor since the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: One who dies in a state of pilgrim consecration has his head and face left uncovered and no perfume brought near him, because he remains consecrated during days that are numbered.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Walking before the bier is disliked only for an enemy of the family because angels of wrath attend it; for believers, encompassed by angels of mercy, position does not matter though walking behind is more excellent, and the call to prayer at the bier is disliked while announcing the death without a public call is permitted.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The Prophet turned back women following a bier, telling them they neither pray over it, carry it, lower it, nor cover it, and so should return excused but unrewarded.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The funeral prayer is a communal obligation on every Muslim who knows of it until one performs it, may be offered anywhere and even in disliked hours or at an eclipse, and the supplication between takbirs may be recited or left to the imam.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The funeral prayer is offered over martyrs, grave sinners, those executed under prescribed punishment or retaliation, and even one who has taken his own life; the supplication is quiet by day and aloud by night.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The dead is buried in the burial ground of the town where he died and not carried to another, unless he dies in open wilderness, in which case he may be carried to the nearest burial ground.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Burial in another's land requires his leave, but once done without consent the owner may claim only the value of the grave sites and may not have the bodies removed.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Baked brick, stone, and whatever else is available may be placed over the dead, contrary to the dislike of it held by the people of the outward sense, and the questioner is told to rely on this except where prudent concealment requires otherwise.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Ali counsels visiting the graves of those who have a claim upon one and seeking provision there, since the dead rejoice at such visits, and a man should ask his need at his parents' graves after praying for them.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Prophet is cited as saying that charity (sadaqa) is not lawful for him nor for the people of his house, and a later answer specifies that 'people of the House' here refers to the Imams.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman teaches that whoever pays the khums is thereby excused from the tithe except voluntarily, but paying the tithe alone does not excuse the khums, because the tithe does not encompass the khums as the khums encompasses the tithe.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman also holds that one whose standing in the call, after his obligations are discharged, is shown by outward abundance of wealth pays from it what he wills, apart from the fitra, of obligatory rights and voluntary giving.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Prophet is quoted as saying there is no prayer for one who does not pay zakat, and that the withholder of zakat is in the Fire.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the Hidden Epistle, lists ten things upon which God imposed zakat: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, dates, raisins, wheat, barley, and grains.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in the Four Hundred Counsels, says: treat your sick with charity and fortify your wealth with zakat.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils place zakat after the jurisprudence of guardianship, purity and prayer, as one of the rights of the testimony, and assign it seven obligations and twelve sunnahs, matching the number of the clauses and letters of the testimony.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: According to the Mustansiriyya Councils, zakat must be received by the Imam and is taken from seven things: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, crops, and minerals.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Councils name eight recipients falling into seven divisions — the poor and needy, the collectors (as wage), those whose hearts are reconciled (as bond of protection), the freeing of necks, the debt-burdened among the people of allegiance, the way of God as a struggle of sufficiency, and the wayfarer understood as those cut off from the road of guidance.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The twelve sunnahs of zakat include waiting for the year to run its course, nisabs of twenty dinars for gold, two hundred dirhams for silver, five grazing camels, thirty grazing cows and forty sheep, taking the middling livestock rather than the best or poorest, not joining what is separate nor dividing what is joined, exempting the stud animal, giving from crops below the nisab of five awsaq by bundle and handful on the harvest day per Qur'an 6:141, and no zakat on dwellings, ornaments, or things for use.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: In the question-and-answer book arranged after Daaim al-Islam, the prohibition on concealing zakat from one's imam is explained as applying to one who brings out only part of the zakat, whereas one who withholds it entirely has abandoned the obligation altogether.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The same source explains that the 'hamala' which makes charity lawful for a recipient means either a penalty imposed by a tyrannical ruler or the bearing of blood money on behalf of the 'aqila.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Ali's covenant to Muhnaf ibn Sulaym forbids a resident of his domain to pay charity to the enemy, and the answer interprets the exemption for territory not encompassed by his horsemen as meaning zakat is not demanded from one seized by the enemy who is not of the Shia holding the allegiance.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: It is transmitted from the people of the House that zakat handed to other than the one God commanded does not suffice, even if it is afterwards plundered or stolen, until it is handed to the guardian of the affair or one who receives it by his command.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils hold that one who keeps the outward prayer and believes its inner reality but does not spend the zakat of his wealth, the khums of his earnings, the purchase of his own self and the redemption of his pledge falls short of the one God praises as spending from what He provided.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: The same responsa hold that these debts take precedence over inheritance, that khums is taken from the entire estate including houses and servants, and that a guardian or kinsman who discharges them secretly, without the other guardian's knowledge, commits no wrong.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Where heirs refuse to purify the deceased's wealth by paying the khums, the answer invokes the Quranic verse 'There is no compulsion in religion' rather than coercion.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: The nisab that defines 'means' (yasar) is ownership, after a full hawl, of either two hundred dirhams of silver or twenty gold dinars — specified in Arab ounces and in Gujarati kadiyana and wal weights — and since gold and silver prices vary by age, the pious believer should reckon by whichever of the two coinages is the cheaper.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Once khums has been paid on capital, khums on subsequent profit is due only on what remains in hand after household expenses; paying khums on the whole profit is a merit (fadl), not a binding obligation.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf sets the general condition of zakat — that the property reach its nisab unencumbered and that a hawl pass over it — and applies it to altered deposits, to undivided estates (assessed per heir's share, not on the whole), to debtors (zakat only on the surplus over the debt), and to trade goods exchanged for trade goods.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Al-Akhbar reports that an apostate begins his zakat afresh and owes nothing for the period of his apostasy, and that there is no zakat on the wealth of an orphan or of one who has lost his reason — to which Ta'wil al-Da'aim adds the qualification that this exemption covers only wealth held for the owner's own use, while any part held for trade is valued and does bear zakat.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, cited in Ta'wil al-Shari'a, taught that zakat is five dirhams for five classes of poor and that its meaning is mutual consolation, since all creation is a single soul whose limbs all turn to treat the one limb that suffers pain, and he added that if anyone were untouched by defect death would never reach him.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad's al-Risala al-Maknuna gives the graduated livestock scales — a sheep for every five camels up to twenty, then bint makhad at twenty-five, bint labun at thirty-five, hiqqa at forty-five, jadha above sixty and two hiqqas at one hundred and twenty; tabi' at thirty cattle and musinna at forty; one sheep at forty sheep rising to two sheep at two hundred — with defective animals and the flock's ram excluded, and he explains the hiqqa at sixty as resembling the stallion in what she can bear.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: On produce, the responsa note a tension: the Pillars make zakat due on everything the earth brings forth and the masters' practice was to take the tenth from little and much alike, whereas the Shari'a sets a nisab of five awsaq (the wasq being sixty sa') — and the tenth is due on what sky and rivers water, half the tenth on what wheels and beasts water.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Al-Akhbar distinguishes land of the tenth (Arab land and mountain land cultivated by its own people, unconquered by horse or mount) from kharaj land (Sudan and lands taken by force), and holds that the ruling attaches to the land's produce and not to its owner, so that sale between Muslim and protected non-Muslim does not change it.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: The Book of the Inner Nursing reads the tenth as an outward ruling by which the Messenger judged: whoever pays it in truth and keeps back only nine tenths has discharged his outward obligation even unasked, while whoever retains more than nine tenths has not truly obeyed the ruler over his outward affairs.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: The khums is grounded in the Quranic spoils verse naming five recipients — God, the Messenger, the near of kin, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer — is extended by Da'ud ibn 'Ajab to the seed of lands already purified (seeds falling under the word 'thing'), and is taken from mines, treasures and spoils, as Ja'far al-Sadiq's report of the Prophet's distribution confirms.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Answering a question about the Indian custom of mixing four grains (rice, maize, wheat, salt) and taking their monetary value, the reply is that reliance is on the Book of the Pillars: a sa of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins.
entities: Book of the Pillars of Islam

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: A reported saying holds that the fitra should be from the best of what one eats and the purest of what one stores, yet mixing it from everything eaten during Ramadan suffices, and one who ate nothing but barley may give barley.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that a dhimmi who accepts Islam before dawn on the day of Fitr owes zakat al-Fitr, while one who converts after dawn owes nothing.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Reports state the fitra is paid on behalf of the mukatab; the Landmarks of Religion that it is due for a child born before dawn on the day of Fitr; and the Book of the Pillars that it has also been said to be paid for the child still in the womb.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: The Landmarks of Religion gives the sa as four and a half Meccan ratls, five ratls less a third by the ratl of Medina, and nine and a tenth Baghdadi ratls, while the Selected Book allows a sa of dried curd or half a sa of wheat.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: The Inner Nursing cites the Prophet's saying that the fitra is lawful neither for him nor for the people of his house.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan's Mafatih al-Nima distinguishes fitra from ordinary charity by timing — before sunrise it is fitra, after sunrise mere sadaqa — and defines fitra as bringing out what is owed to God and to His appointed guardian, as ransom and offering.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Two residual riddle-rulings hold that zakat is lawful to a man who owns a thousand dinars but owes a thousand (so no zakat is due from him), and to a well-off polytheist who has found no Muslim to receive his zakat, who then has more right to it than anyone.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited as stating that fasting is a shield from the Fire covering the tongue, hearing, eyes and all limbs, so that it is not about food and drink alone: every limb has its portion, and whoever abandons part of it diminishes the merit of his fast proportionally.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Per the same source, fasting Ramadan is obligatory on every Muslim, male and female, who is of age, sound of mind, healthy and resident, and there is no fasting for a hypocrite disobedient to God.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: The book al-Idah qualifies the rulings on fasting by sighting the crescent: they apply only to one absent from the presence of the Imam who does not know the measures of the crescents.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, in his epistle The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations addressed to the people of Yemen, rebukes them for failing to honor the month as God and His Messenger prescribed.
entities: The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: His specific charge is that the month must be named with the word 'month' placed before it, as in the Quranic 'shahr Ramadan', whereas the people say 'Ramadan' alone, which neither intellect nor guidance approves, since one does not address a beloved person without a title before his name.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: He supports this by al-Qadi al-Numan's Mukhtasar al-Athar al-Sharif, reporting Imam al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali as saying: do not say 'Ramadan', but say as God said, 'the month of Ramadan'.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: He argues that one who has heard this saying and still turns from it makes light of God, of His month, and of al-Baqir's word, and that one who transmits the book without acting on it falls under the Quranic censure 'why do you say what you do not do?'

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah is cited as holding that fasting becomes obligatory upon a boy once he can distinguish his right hand from his left.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Zaid ibn Muhammad's Concealed Epistle states that God imposed the fast of the month of Ramadan after prayer and zakat, commanding one month of twelve be fasted, and that this obligatory fast is thirty days.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib in his Four Hundred Manners is quoted: fasting three days of every month and fasting Shaban drive away the whisperings of the breast and the disquiet of the heart.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The author reports from the Book of Clarification that the transmitted rulings tying fasting to the sighting of the crescent are addressed only to those absent from the Imam's presence and ignorant of the crescents' measures.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Sulayman ibn Hasan, in his epistle the Ijadiyya, explains that after the moon parts from the sun and travels twenty-eight stations it must cross two more to overtake the sun, since the sun has itself advanced two stations and a degree, so the meeting occurs at thirty stations, which reckoners count as one month.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The opponents' proof is the Prophet's saying 'Fast when it is seen and break your fast when it is seen; if it is hidden, complete thirty,' which they take to make Ramadan sometimes twenty-nine days.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Al-Muayyad argues on two legal grounds that the Prophet never fasted by sighting: Gabriel came to him morning and evening with certain news, making search unnecessary, and he declared he knew the roads and stations of the sky better than others know those of the earth.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The rational ground is that the Prophet knew crescent risings differ by place and elevation, so he could not have imposed a single sighting-standard on all people, nor can one and the same day be Shaban in one place and Ramadan in another.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Quranic proof is drawn from 'fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you' — taken to mean the Christians, who fast by calculation not sighting — and from 'a counted number of days,' which implies a fixed, unvarying number.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Further arguments for Ramadan's completeness: the year alternates six complete and six deficient months so that Ramadan falls complete; the Prophet said 'Shaban is never complete and Ramadan never deficient'; Shaban alone has a true middle night (the fifteenth) while Ramadan has none; and the expiation for breaking the fast is sixty days or sixty poor persons, matching two complete thirty-day months.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: In an anecdote from his autobiography, al-Muayyad debates a Zaydi sharif before King Abu Kalijar al-Daylami of Shiraz, who cited the hadith 'We are unlettered, we do not reckon' with the gathered fingers; al-Muayyad answered that the Prophet, honored with the ascension, could not have been unable to say 'thirty' or 'twenty-nine' and gestured like a herdsman, and the Alid withdrew in shame amid laughter.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Some summoners frame the case as a formal question to all Muslim scholars, asking who 'those before you' are, how many the counted days are, what 'witnessing the month' means, and whether the completed count is thirty, twenty-nine or twenty-eight, invoking the Prophet's rule that reports contradicting the Book are not his.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Grammatically, the lam in 'fast for its sighting' is read as the lam of anticipation or outcome (as in 'mothers nourish their children for death' and 'for the Day of Reckoning'), so the hadith means: let the crescent rise while you are already fasting, and while you are already breaking the fast.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the epistle al-Maknuna on the eclipse prayer, teaches that God made the first creation a proof for the last age, setting the moon's eclipse at fourteen nights (sometimes thirteen) and its concealment at twenty-eight nights, absent forty-eight hours before rising again.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The section closes by introducing the next text: the epistle al-Lazima on the fast of Ramadan and its proper time, by Ahmad Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, proof of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: The disputed proof-text, accepted by nearly all Muslim sects and relied on by the people of the outward, is the Prophet's saying 'Fast at its sighting and break the fast at its sighting.'

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: The author argues that the sun's light is itself merely a barrier like cloud or a wall — proven by stars becoming visible during a solar eclipse — so the crescent genuinely exists after separation even when unseen, and the soul is not barred from seeing it as it truly is.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: The author notes that eyesight errs about things as they truly are — seeing large as small, thin as thick — whereas the seeing of knowledge scarcely errs, so the people of the true call have taken hold of the non-erring instrument.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: To the final objection that the Prophet's 'If it is obscured from you, then count thirty days' requires eye-sighting, the author begins by reasserting that the vision of the soul has been established as the nobler of the two.

dropped.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
dropped.text: The author objects that eye-sighting makes the fast differ between regions — cloud in Kirman versus clear sky in Shiraz — whereas, just as a prayer's time binds the whole community once it arrives regardless of individuals, so the fast's time binds the community as one.

dropped.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
dropped.text: As a worked case the author defends the people of truth's entering the Ramadan fast of the year 400 two days before the eye-sighting: conjunction fell on Monday night, the moon stood only about six degrees from the sun at sunset (beneath the ray, invisible), the Shawwal conjunction fell Wednesday night making Wednesday the festival, so breaking earlier would have left only twenty-nine days — whereas 'Shaban is never complete and Ramadan never deficient' and 'the day of your fasting is the day of your sacrifice,' the sacrifice at Mecca having fallen on Monday.
entities: ما تم شعبان ولا نقص رمضان
